docs.title: js-contrib
docs.text:
GPU-accelerated X-SCAPE heavy-ion simulations, driven from Python, with the data out in the open.

js-contrib is the contrib package of the JETSCAPE / X-SCAPE event generator, much like fastjet-contrib is for FastJet. It takes the full multistage simulation (3+1D viscous hydrodynamics, MATTER + LBT jets with the medium response, Cooper–Frye particlization and hadronization) and makes it fast enough, scriptable enough and portable enough to produce large event samples. Those samples are used for physics analyses and as training data for machine-learned surrogates.

  • GPU acceleration

    MUSIC hydro runs on the GPU: CUDA on NVIDIA cards, Metal on Apple Silicon. Several jobs share one GPU, so a single workstation produces thousands of Au+Au events with jets per hour.

    GPU acceleration

  • Python and PyTorch

    The whole framework is available in Python. You can run events, read results as numpy or awkward arrays, write your own modules in Python, and put a live PyTorch FNO in place of the hydro.

    Python and ML

  • Runs anywhere

    Choose a production container (Docker or Apptainer, NVIDIA GPUs), a native Mac wheel (Metal), a lightweight analysis environment, or a full source build in conda.

    Choose your setup

  • Open data on the OSDF

    Productions are shared on the Open Science Data Federation and can be read without an account, either by downloading them or by opening them in place over osdf://.

    Data on the OSDF

docs.title: From zero to an analysed event
docs.text:
Linux + NVIDIA GPU (container)Mac, Apple Silicon (wheel)Any computer (analysis only) 
docker pull jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126
mkdir -p work
docker run --rm --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/work:/work" -w /work \
  jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 bash -c \
  'xscape-examples /work/examples && cd /work/examples/pythonic &&
   python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir /work/out_oo'

One O+O event goes through the whole chain, and its hadron files are written to ./work/out_oo/. Other CUDA versions, Apptainer and Jupyter are covered in Production container.

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh        # once; then open a new Terminal
VER=0.1.0                                              # latest: github.com/jhputschke/xscape-macos/releases
mkdir -p ~/xscape && cd ~/xscape
curl -LO https://github.com/jhputschke/xscape-macos/releases/download/v$VER/xscape-$VER-cp313.lock.txt
uv venv --managed-python ~/.venvs/xscape-$VER --python 3.13
source ~/.venvs/xscape-$VER/bin/activate
uv pip sync xscape-$VER-cp313.lock.txt
xscape-fetch-data lbt                                  # the LBT tables (240 MB download)
xscape-examples ~/xscape/examples
cd ~/xscape/examples/pythonic && python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir ~/xscape/out_oo

The same event runs on the Mac's GPU in under a minute. See Mac (xscape wheel).

git clone https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib.git && cd js-contrib
./utils/analysis_env/setup_analysis_env.sh             # venv in ~/.venvs/js_analysis
source ~/.venvs/js_analysis/bin/activate
python utils/analysis_env/check_env.py /path/to/out    # opens every file of a production

This gives you no GPU and no X-SCAPE build, only what you need to read and analyse the files, including files on the OSDF. See Analysis environment.

From there, the site follows the order you work in:

  1. Install: choose one of the four setups.
  2. Run: start with your first event, then run the productions: Au+Au with jets, O+O with initial-state radiation, Z+jet in Pb+Pb, and at scale on clusters.
  3. Analyse: hadrons, jets with FastJet, hydro and hadrons together (the jet wake), O+O, and ROOT.
  4. Extend in Python: the Pythonic interface, your own modules, and the live PyTorch FNO hydro.

Status

js-contrib follows the X-SCAPE contrib branch and MUSIC4GPU XSCAPE. The Mac wheel's first regular release is v0.1.0. The production container images are tagged by CUDA version (cu126, cu130, cu124). See Contribs and repositories for the full list of components.

docs.title: About js-contrib
docs.text:
js-contrib is the contrib package of the JETSCAPE / X-SCAPE heavy-ion event generator (and of C-SCAPE, which is in development). It plays the same role for X-SCAPE as fastjet-contrib does for FastJet. The framework and its physics modules stay in X-SCAPE. js-contrib adds what is needed to run them at scale and to use the results: GPU hydrodynamics, Python bindings and a Python layer, machine-learning hydro modules, HDF5 writers, the production scripts, containers and a Mac wheel, an analysis environment, and data sharing on the Open Science Data Federation (OSDF).

The physics is the standard X-SCAPE multistage chain: a 3D Monte Carlo Glauber initial state with dynamical strings, PYTHIA 8 hard scatterings, MATTER + LBT jet energy loss with recoils, energy–momentum deposition of the jet into the fluid, 3+1D viscous MUSIC hydrodynamics, Cooper–Frye particlization with iSS and string hadronization of the jets. js-contrib's productions run this chain on the GPU for large event samples: Au+Au with a jet and its medium response, O+O with initial-state radiation, and Pb+Pb Z+jet.

This section explains why the package exists, what physics the productions contain, how the GPU and Python parts fit in, and what to cite. To get going right away, see Install and Run.

  • Why js-contrib

    What it adds on top of X-SCAPE: large GPU productions with jets and their wake, ML training data, Python access to the framework, portable setups and open data.

    Why js-contrib

  • The physics

    The event chain as the productions configure it, stage by stage, from the initial state to the hadrons, with the parameters and the publications behind each module.

    The physics

  • GPU acceleration

    MUSIC on CUDA and Metal: what runs on the GPU, how close it is to CPU MUSIC, and the throughput per machine.

    GPU acceleration

  • Python and machine learning

    The framework in Python, modules written in Python, and Fourier neural operator (FNO) hydro with PyTorch.

    Python and machine learning

  • Publications and citing

    The papers behind the framework and every module, and how to cite js-contrib.

docs.title: GPU acceleration
docs.text: The viscous hydrodynamics is the most expensive part of an X-SCAPE heavy-ion event, and js-contrib runs it on the GPU with MUSIC4GPU, a port of MUSIC to CUDA (NVIDIA) and Metal (Apple Silicon). This page explains what runs on the GPU and what does not, how closely the GPU results agree with CPU MUSIC, what throughput to expect on the machines it was measured on, and the launch settings that give that throughput. Read it before you plan a campaign or pick hardware. To launch jobs, see Clusters, GPUs and monitoring.

docs.title: What runs on the GPU
docs.text:
MUSIC4GPU is a direct port of MUSIC 3.1: the same equations and the same numerical scheme (KT flux, Newton reconstruction, second-order Israel–Stewart viscous evolution). It adds no new physics. Two back ends share the same compute kernels and host code, and are chosen when MUSIC is built:

back end hardware used by CUDA NVIDIA GPUs, discrete (V100 … H100, RTX) and Grace-Blackwell (GB10) the production container, source builds on Linux Metal Apple Silicon (M1 or later) the Mac wheel, source builds on macOS

When a configuration is supported, the whole per-cell hydro time step runs on the GPU: ideal evolution and reconstruction, shear stress and bulk pressure, velocity gradients, temperature-dependent η/s and ζ/s, the regulator, and the integration of the hydro source terms. The X-SCAPE productions (zero net baryon density, 3+1D grid) fall entirely inside it. Configurations outside it fall back to the CPU path, correct but slower: baryon diffusion, vorticity terms, a finite-μB EOS or μB-dependent shear.

Everything else in the event runs on the CPU:

flowchart LR
  IC["3D MC-Glauber strings<br/>CPU"] --> M1["MUSIC_1: background<br/><b>GPU</b>"]
  H["Pythia hard process<br/>CPU"] --> E["Matter + LBT<br/>CPU"]
  M1 --> E
  E --> L["CausalLiquefier droplets<br/>CPU"]
  L --> M2["MUSIC_2: jet leg<br/><b>GPU</b>"]
  M1 --> S["freeze-out surfaces<br/>CPU, OpenMP"]
  M2 --> S
  S --> W["HDF5 writers<br/>CPU"]
  W --> P["iSS particlization,<br/>hadronization<br/>CPU (stage 2)"]
  • On the CPU: the initial state, Pythia, the jet energy loss (Matter, LBT), the liquefier's droplets (the source is evaluated on the CPU and integrated on the GPU), the freeze-out surface search (Cornelius), the HDF5 output, and the whole second stage: iSS particlization and hadronization. Stage 2 needs no GPU at all, so it runs on CPU nodes.
  • One GPU per MUSIC. MUSIC uses the first GPU it sees, so a machine with several GPUs runs one campaign per GPU (each with its own CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES).
  • The CPU path is still there. MUSIC_FORCE_CPU=1 runs the double-precision CPU path of the same binary, for validation.

The GPU is no longer the bottleneck

After the speed-ups, an Au+Au jet event on an RTX 3090 needs about 2 GPU-seconds but about 35 host core-seconds (24 core-seconds for a job alone); the GPU computes for about 2 s of a 15 s event (where the time goes). On a discrete GPU the host cores, not the GPU, set the rate. That is why the launch settings below are mostly about cores and threads, and why several jobs share one GPU.

docs.title: Precision choices
docs.text:
• Single precision on the GPU. The kernels compute in FP32 (CUDA builds with --use_fast_math); the CPU path computes in double precision. Apple GPUs have no FP64, so Metal stays FP32. An FP64 build option has been assessed but not built.
  • Vacuum cells at rest. In FP32, dilute vacuum cells could reach large u⁰ and stall an evolution. MUSIC4GPU puts vacuum cells (e < 10⁻⁵ fm⁻⁴, u⁰ > 10) at rest and zeroes non-finite viscous fields with a warning; MUSIC_ABORT_ON_NONFINITE=1 stops the run instead.
  • The reconstruction solvers stop at float resolution. No switch; the change is at the level of float rounding.
  • A larger time step late in the evolution (on by default in the production XMLs): Δτ = 0.02 → 0.05 fm/c from τ = 3 fm/c, with the stored frames and freeze-out checks kept every 0.1 fm/c, so the output format does not change. It roughly halves the MUSIC steps and changes the medium at the 10⁻³ level, below the GPU-vs-CPU difference. The wake field differs cell by cell by ~5 %, almost all at scales below ~1 fm; at hadron level no change is seen within ±2 %. Keep one setting per campaign; --late-dtau 0 gives a constant step.

docs.title: How close is the GPU to CPU MUSIC?
docs.text:
Method. The same Au+Au 0–10 % jet job (6 jet events on 3 backgrounds, PythiaGun p̂T 50–70 GeV, Matter + LBT + liquefier) was run twice with identical options, once on the GPU and once with MUSIC_FORCE_CPU=1. Only MUSIC's arithmetic differs. The comparison goes cell by cell through the hydro fields, then the freeze-out surfaces, then hadrons: iSS was run on both paths' surfaces with the same seeds and correlated sampling, so the hadrons are identical wherever the surfaces agree and the difference is measured with little noise. It was done with CUDA on a GB10 and repeated with Metal on an M3 Max.

Result. The two paths agree to about 0.2–0.3 %, with identical freeze-out times. The small remaining difference is systematic, and the same with CUDA and Metal:

quantity GPU vs CPU freeze-out times (all 9 MUSIC runs) identical energy density above freeze-out, energy-weighted |Δe|/e 2×10⁻³ temperature |ΔT|/T, velocity |Δv| above freeze-out 3×10⁻⁴, 1.6×10⁻⁴ energy above freeze-out / in the dilute fluid below it −0.3 % / +0.4 % freeze-out volume −0.19 % charged hadrons −0.20 ± 0.02 % ⟨pT⟩, v₂, v₃, momentum anisotropy equal within errors jet wake (events with the same showers) fields 0.1–1 %, integrals ~1 %

What it means.

  • Within one campaign the difference is negligible: far below model and tuning uncertainties.
  • Between paths it is a normalization offset that does not average out (it has the same sign in every event). Keep a campaign, and an FNO training set, on one path; don't mix in CPU-fallback jobs; and name the path when you compare with CPU or published MUSIC results.
  • Single events can differ in their jets. A 3×10⁻⁴ change in the temperature is enough to send Matter and LBT down another random sequence, so the same seed may give a different shower. Compare the two paths statistically.
  • Limits: 6 events, one centrality, one p̂T window. A large campaign compared with the CPU build has not been done.

Full details: MUSIC_CPU_vs_GPU.md. The physics of the productions themselves is on The physics.

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
Measured on specific machines

These numbers come from a handful of machines and code states, and they change as the code does. Each one is given with its hardware and settings. Re-measure on your own hardware before you size a campaign.

The productions:

  • Au+Au jets, campaign setting: prod_AuAu_0_10_jet (two stages: MUSIC_1 background, then MUSIC_2 with jet deposition) with --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 --jets-per-bin 5 --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both: one background per 15 jet events, pair file and particlize file written. An "event" is a jet event.
  • O+O, hadron files only: prod_OO_isr --bulk-hadrons 10 --no-particlize --no-hydro-file (bulk hadrons made in the job, nothing else kept).

The rates are events per hour for the whole machine, from the campaign's makespan.

docs.title: GPU vs CPU MUSIC
docs.text:
How much faster a production runs on the GPU than on MUSIC's CPU path (MUSIC_FORCE_CPU=1, same binary, same events) on the same machine. These are speed-ups over each machine's own CPU, not a comparison between GPUs. Two numbers answer different questions:

  • Single event: one job alone on the machine, GPU against CPU path. This is what a user running a few events sees.
  • Whole machine: each path with as many jobs at once as pays, best events/h against best events/h. This is what a campaign sees.
2 × RTX 3090, Threadripper 3960X (24 cores) GB10 (20 Arm cores, one integrated GPU) M3 Max (12 performance + 4 efficiency cores, Metal) code and setting current cu124 image, Au+Au campaign setting (2026-10-23) code of 2026-10-03 to 10-08 code of 2026-09 to 10-10 one job alone, CPU path 60.9 s/event (59 events/h) 230 s/event 302 s/event one job alone, GPU 11.3 s/event (319 events/h) 32 s/event 28 s/event single-event speed-up 5.4× 7.2× 10.8× (12.8× in a September test) CPU path, machine full 4 jobs × 12 threads: 62 events/h (1.05× one job) not measured; 1.0–1.1× assumed not measured; 1.05–1.25× assumed GPU, machine full 10 jobs per GPU, MPS: 2,846 events/h (8.9× one job) 6 jobs, MPS: 205 events/h (1.74× one job) 3 jobs: 284 events/h (1.69× one job) whole-machine speed-up ~46× (35× counting job startup and ramp-up) ~11–13× ~15–17×

The whole-machine speed-up is the single-event speed-up times what concurrent jobs add on the GPU, divided by what they add on the CPU path. The two differ this much because:

  • One GPU job leaves the machine mostly idle. On the 3090 box a job alone keeps the GPU 18 % busy and 4.4 of 48 threads. More jobs fill the spare GPU and cores: 20 jobs (10 per GPU) give 8.9× the rate of one.
  • One CPU-path job already fills the machine. MUSIC's OpenMP loops keep 42 of 48 threads busy, so 4 jobs × 12 threads gain only 5 %.
  • The 3090 box gains most because it has two GPUs and 24 fast cores, so 20 jobs fit. Its rate is now limited by the CPUs (22 of 24 cores busy, GPUs 62 % busy). The GB10 and the M3 Max each have one integrated GPU, which is ~85 % busy at 3–6 jobs; more jobs add nothing.

The GB10 and M3 Max numbers are older

Their CPU/GPU pairs come from the 2026-10-08 comparison (6 events, two per background, MUSIC's own grid); their concurrent-job gains from a setting with a new background every event and p̂T 50–70 GeV. Both predate the GPU-side speed-ups of 2026-10-11/12 (on the M3 Max a job alone got 43 % faster), while the CPU path gained only the late time step, so their speed-ups today are probably higher. One CPU-path and one GPU job with the current code (~15 minutes per machine) would settle them.

  • The CPU path is a fair reference. It takes the late time step, but MUSIC_2 starts from τ0 instead of restarting from MUSIC_1's state, which is how a CPU production would run. Both paths gave the same p̂T values and droplet counts.
  • MUSIC alone gains more than the whole event. Per time step: 9.1× on the 3090 (vs 48 threads), ~5.2–5.5× on the GB10 (vs 20 threads), 5.0× on the M3 Max (vs 12 threads). One O+O event (wall time, indicative): ~3.5×, ~5.5× and ~8×.

docs.title: Where an event's time goes
docs.text:
The stages of one Au+Au event at the campaign setting, for one job alone on the 3090 box, same image on both paths (measured 2026-10-23 and 10-25). Stage 1 is the GPU job; stage 2 is iSS on the saved freeze-out surfaces, run later on CPU cores. Times are per event in a 15-event job, so the background's hydro counts one fifteenth.

per event, one job alone GPU, 3 threads (campaign) GPU, 48 threads CPU path, 48 threads jet-leg hydro (MUSIC_2) 8.24 s 5.14 s 51.52 s  GPU kernels 2.07 s (GPU 25 % busy) 1.80 s (GPU 35 % busy) –  CPU work around them 6.17 s (1.8 cores) 3.34 s (7.6 threads) 51.52 s (45.5 threads) background hydro (MUSIC_1 + copy), ⅟₁₅ 1.00 s 0.36 s 3.78 s Pythia + Matter + LBT + liquefier 0.13 s 0.14 s 0.13 s pair file writer 4.34 s 4.36 s 4.18 s particlize file writer 1.32 s 1.27 s 1.27 s stage 1 15.0 s (hydro 61 %) 11.3 s (hydro 49 %) 60.9 s (hydro 91 %) stage 2, one core: iSS (400 oversamples) 6.45 s 6.45 s 6.45 s stage 2, one core: jet fragmentation + files 0.86 s 0.86 s 0.86 s both stages 22.3 s 18.6 s 68.2 s

Inside the jet leg's hydro (MUSIC_PROFILE=1, 3 threads): the RK steps, where the host waits for the kernels, take 1.96 s; putting the string and droplet source terms on the grid (CPU, OpenMP) 2.93 s; the freeze-out surface 2.64 s (Cornelius 1.93 s, on the CPU after a copy from the GPU); packing and copying the frames 0.35 s; init and other 0.36 s.

  • The GPU computes for about 2 s of a 15 s event. The rest of the hydro is CPU work around the kernels, which runs in parallel: 48 threads cut it from 6.2 to 3.3 s, while the GPU part stays at ~2 s.
  • Matter + LBT take 0.13 s per event, under 1 %, including Pythia and the liquefier, the same on both paths.
  • The writers take 5.6 s on one core, as long as the GPU-path hydro with 48 threads; the pair file alone 4.3 s (reading the frames, resampling, HDF5). --particlize-only skips it.
  • Counting stage 2 lowers the single-event speed-up from 5.4× to 3.7× (18.6 s against 68.2 s), since iSS costs the same on both paths. Stage 2 usually runs on a CPU cluster (slurm_hadronize.sh), where 4–5 cores keep up with 2,160 events/h; on the 3090 box itself it would cost ~17 % of stage 1's rate (~38× instead of 46× over the CPU path, an estimate).

iSS in stage 1?

Today the hydro (GPU and CPU parts) is about half of a stage-1 event. iSS at 400 oversamples adds ~7.3 s on one core, about as long as the hydro, so moving it into stage 1 drops the hydro to 30–40 % of the event if the job still writes its files (22.3 s and 18.6 s per event above). It stays near half only without the writers (--hadrons-only, ~16.6 s and ~13.0 s) or with few oversamples (1–10 oversamples cost mostly a fixed ~2.6 s per surface). But --hadrons-only writes no pair file, so there is no hydro history for FNO training and no surfaces to sample again. On a full 3090 box, already CPU-limited, iSS in stage 1 costs ~17 % of the rate either way. These rows add measured stage times; they were not run as jobs.

docs.title: Other speed-ups that matter
docs.text:
A pair event once took ~184 s on the GB10. Much of the way to today's rates came from the CPU side, with bit-identical output:

  • MUSIC's host work: the string source fill skips empty steps and bins strings by transverse reach (15.3 → 5.9 s per event); the jet source is prepared once per step and the liquefier evaluates only droplets that can deposit (pair event 184 → 60 s).
  • Parallel freeze-out surface: the surface search runs η-slices in parallel with OpenMP, deterministic across thread counts (9.6 → 1.2 s per event).
  • MUSIC_2 restarts from MUSIC_1's state at the step before the first droplet, instead of re-running the early evolution (two-stage job −19 % wall time, on by default).
  • iSS: the per-surface fixed cost fell from ~16.5 s to ~4 s, and the sampling loop was repacked; hadronize.py on both legs at 500 oversamples now takes ~10.6 s on one core (8.8 s with --correlated), against ~58 s before.
  • HDF5 writers and memory: Blosc-zstd compression and a background stored once for all its jet events take the pair file from 400 to 170 MB per event (15 jets per background); reading the legs one frame at a time and a slim copy of the hydro history for the jets took a job's memory from ~20 GB to ~6–7 GB.
  • Shared LBT tables (LBT_TABLE_CACHE): one read-only copy of LBT's 0.66 GB of tables for all jobs on a machine.

The complete list, with what is and is not bit-identical: OPTIMIZATION_CHANGES.md.

docs.title: Recommended launch settings
docs.text:
None of these settings changes the output; they only change how fast a campaign runs. They are not built into the scripts, because the best values depend on the machine's balance of cores, GPU and memory. These are the measured best values:

setting 2 × RTX 3090 (per GPU, Docker) GB10 M3 Max (Metal) SLURM cluster (slurm_prod_array.sh) jobs at once (run_jobs.sh -j) Au+Au 10, O+O 8 Au+Au 4, O+O 8 Au+Au 3 P=10 (default; see the per-GPU table) OMP_NUM_THREADS 3 Au+Au 5, O+O 2 5 cpus-per-task / P, at least 2 (set by the script) OMP_WAIT_POLICY passive passive (no measurable effect here) passive, with KMP_BLOCKTIME=0 passive (set by the script) MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC block block – (CUDA only) block (default) CUDA MPS (--mps) yes, one daemon per container yes, natively (not in a container) – (CUDA only) off (USE_MPS=0), never tried on a cluster LBT_TABLE_CACHE yes (Au+Au) optional (−0.6 GB per job) yes yes (Au+Au, default path) --stagger 12 s (Au+Au) – no gain 12 s (Au+Au, default)

What each setting does:

  • Jobs per GPU. One job alone leaves the GPU idle much of the time, so several jobs share it. Size the number by the cores (~2–3 per job) and host memory (plan ~7 GB per Au+Au job, 5 GB with --particlize-only; ~1.5–2 GB per O+O job). If a node gives fewer cores per GPU, lower -j, not the threads per job.
  • OMP_NUM_THREADS ≈ cores / jobs. By default every job starts one OpenMP thread per core, and several jobs then oversubscribe the cores. On the M3 Max, -j 3 with default threads gave only 1.1× one job; with the cores split, 1.6×. For one job alone, leave it unset: on the GB10, fewer threads made a single job 24 % slower.
  • OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive: idle OpenMP threads sleep instead of spinning and stealing cores from the other jobs.
  • MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block: the host thread sleeps while it waits for the GPU instead of spinning, ~30 % less CPU per event at the same throughput. The job log says [MUSIC-GPU] host sync: block.
  • CUDA MPS lets the kernels of several jobs run side by side instead of taking turns: +5–7 % on the 3090s, +12.5 % on the GB10 at 4 jobs. Try without it first; if the GPU is under ~60 % busy it won't help. The MPS daemon does not start inside a container on the GB10, and two daemons in one container hang the second GPU's jobs: use one container per GPU.
  • LBT_TABLE_CACHE=FILE: all jobs map one read-only copy of LBT's tables: −0.6 GB and 6–11 s of start-up per Au+Au job (on the M3 Max, start-up 14.5 → 3.0 s). Put the file on local disk, one file per LBT-tables version, not in the container's /dev/shm. O+O runs no LBT.
  • run_jobs.sh --stagger S: the first jobs start S seconds apart so that their memory peaks don't coincide (−11 GB at 20 jobs on the 3090 box).
  • OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 is set by the drivers; more threads don't help.
NVIDIA GPU, ~12 cores per GPUGB10Mac (Metal)

One RTX 3090-class GPU, Au+Au campaign setting (one run_jobs.sh per GPU):

mkdir -p /scratch/lbt_cache
OMP_NUM_THREADS=3 MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block LBT_TABLE_CACHE=/scratch/lbt_cache/lbt_tables_v1.bin \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 10 --mps --stagger 12 60 45 0 out_c --pthat-bins 10-20,20-30,30-40 \
  --jets-per-bin 5 --parton-ymax 0.6 --write-particlize both

With Docker on two GPUs, utils/launch_2gpu.sh (Au+Au) and utils/launch_2gpu_oo.sh (O+O) start one container and one MPS daemon per GPU, with the settings above as their defaults (Au+Au: 10 jobs and 3 threads per GPU, the LBT cache, --stagger 12).

OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC=block \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 4 --mps 20 25 0

For O+O: OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 and -j 8 --mps.

export LBT_TABLE_CACHE=/path/on/local/disk/lbt_tables_v1.bin
OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive KMP_BLOCKTIME=0 \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 3 --campaign test 20 25 0 ~/xscape/prod/out

-j 4 with 4 threads was not better than -j 3. --mps and MUSIC_CUDA_SYNC don't apply. Keep the Mac awake for long campaigns (caffeinate -i ./run_jobs.sh ...).

Let the wizard write the command

utils/prodwizard.py takes a production preset and a machine (2x3090, gb10, m3max, or a SLURM cluster with V100, A40, A100 or L40S) and writes the launch command with these settings, with estimates of events/h, duration, disk and memory. It never starts jobs.

Disk can become the limit

At 2,160 Au+Au events/h with the pair file, the 3090 box writes ~525 GB/h, more than the ~290 GB/h an upload to the OSDF takes. If you don't need the hydro history, use --particlize-only (0.097 instead of 0.243 GB per event) or a large local disk.

On another machine, measure: one job alone first (is the GPU mostly idle?), then a short sweep of -j with and without MPS, with OMP_NUM_THREADS ≈ cores / jobs. Use the same seeds in every run and compare events/h by makespan. If the GPU stays below ~75 % busy while the cores are full, the machine is host-limited: more cores per GPU pay, more jobs don't. How to launch and monitor: Clusters, GPUs and monitoring.

docs.title: Cost on HPC
docs.text:
None of the cluster GPUs has been run yet. Scaling the measured 3090 and GB10 numbers by GPU speed and cores per GPU gives these estimates for the Au+Au campaign setting, per GPU:

GPU jobs per GPU cores per GPU host memory per GPU expected Au+Au events/h limit V100 (16/32 GB) 8 12–16 64 GB 700–950 GPU A40 (48 GB) 10–12 16–24 90–100 GB 1,100–1,400 cores at 16, GPU at 24 A100 (40/80 GB) 10–12 16–24 90–100 GB 1,000–1,500 GPU or cores L40S (48 GB) 18–22 24–32 135–165 GB 2,000–2,900 cores

For NSF ACCESS resources, on well-sized nodes every option gives about 15–25 Au+Au events per ACCESS credit: faster GPUs cost proportionally more per hour. An H100 pays off only with at least ~24 cores per GPU; with 16 it runs at an A100's rate. About 50,000–55,000 credits of GPU time make a million Au+Au events. Storage (100–240 TB for those files) is the larger request. The first choice is NCSA DeltaAI (GH200, 72 Grace cores per H100, about 19–22 events per credit), the second NCSA Delta A40. Details, including Slurm settings per resource: REPORT_CLUSTER_ACCESS.md.

docs.title: Speed-up per GPU against the CPU path
docs.text:
A cluster hands out a GPU together with a share of a node's cores and memory, so the useful number is events/h per GPU against the CPU path on that same share. The 3090 column is measured; the NCSA Delta columns are estimates (nothing has run on Delta), and Delta's smaller memory share gives lower rates than the table above.

per GPU 2 × RTX 3090 box (measured) Delta A40 or A100 40 GB, 4-GPU node (estimate) share of the node 12 Zen 2 cores (24 threads), ~62 GB 16 Milan cores, 62.5 GB (one GPU's charge on a 64-core, 256 GB node) jobs per GPU 10, OMP_NUM_THREADS=3 8 with the pair file, 10 with --particlize-only; OMP 2; memory sets this GPU path, events/h 1,423 (1,080 by makespan), pair + particlize 800–1,100 with the pair file, 1,000–1,400 with --particlize-only; limited by memory, then cores, so the A100 adds nothing CPU path on the same cores, events/h 31 (half of the 62 measured on 24 cores) 47–62 (16 cores × 2.6 events/h per Zen 2 core × 1.15–1.5 for Milan) speed-up per GPU 46× (35× by makespan) 13–23× with the pair file, 16–30× with --particlize-only one GPU replaces ~550 Zen 2 cores (~420 by makespan) ~200–470 Milan cores events per ACCESS credit – 12–16 (pair), 15–21 (--particlize-only) at the A100 rate; about twice that on A40s if they cost half cost per event against Delta CPU nodes (3.0–3.9 events per credit) – 3–5× cheaper (pair, A100 rate); up to 8–14× (--particlize-only, A40 at half rate)
  • Delta's per-GPU speed-up is lower than the 3090 box's (13–30× against 35–46×): its 62.5 GB share holds only 8–10 jobs, too few to keep the GPU busy, and the CPU path does better on 16 newer cores than on 12.
  • The speed-up per credit is the per-GPU speed-up divided by ~4.2, because Delta charges a GPU-hour (66.7 credits, cores included) about 4.2× the 16 core-hours of the same cores. The A40 is charged below the A100 rate, but Delta does not publish the factor.
  • Stage 2 changes little: 7.3 core-s per event, about 0.002 credits on Delta CPU, against ~0.05–0.08 credits per event of GPU time.
  • Assumptions: ~5 GB per job with --particlize-only and ~7 GB with the pair file; 25–35 s per event in a loaded job; 45-event jobs; a Milan core 1.15–1.5× a Zen 2 core for both paths; the A40's GPU time per event 1.0–1.2× the 3090's, the A100's 0.9–1.4×. The CPU path's rate per Milan core is not measured; its hydro is bandwidth-heavy and could scale less well.
  • Delta's 8-GPU A100 nodes (more memory per GPU; check before planning) would lift the memory limit: ~1,100–1,700 events/h per GPU, about 18–36× the CPU path.
  • One short benchmark settles it: one A40 at -j 8 and -j 10, plus one CPU-path job on 16 cores (REPORT_CLUSTER_ACCESS.md §7).

docs.title: The physics
docs.text: This page describes what the js-contrib productions simulate, stage by stage, as their XML files and drivers configure it. It is meant for a reader who knows heavy-ion physics and wants to know which models, which parameters and which approximations are behind the files before analysing them. Every module is an X-SCAPE module or an X-SCAPE external package; js-contrib chooses the settings, chains the modules, runs them on the GPU and writes the results. The values below are taken from the production inputs in contribs/PyJetscape/example/config/. Every job also stores the XML it ran (prod_user_xml), so a file always records its own settings. Publications are linked where each model appears and collected in Publications and citing.

docs.title: The setups at a glance
docs.text:
setup system centrality hard process hydro hadrons Au+Au with a jet Au+Au, \(\sqrt{s_{NN}}\) = 200 GeV 0–10 % (\(b < 4.7\) fm) PYTHIA 8 dijet, \(\hat p_T\) 50–70 GeV by default background/jet pair of MUSIC runs iSS + Colorless, afterwards on CPUs (or in the job) Au+Au hydro only Au+Au, 200 GeV 0–10 % none one MUSIC run none (FNO training data) O+O with ISR O+O, 200 GeV \(b < 3\) fm (about 0–24 %) PYTHIA 8 + iMATTER initial-state radiation, \(\hat p_T\) 20–40 GeV by default one MUSIC run iColored in the job; iSS in the job or afterwards Pb+Pb with a jet Pb+Pb, 5.02 TeV 0–10 % (\(b < 4.95\) fm) PYTHIA 8 dijet background/jet pair iSS + Colorless Pb+Pb Z+jet Pb+Pb, 5.02 TeV 0–30 % (\(b < 8.57\) fm) PYTHIA 8 Z + parton, Z → ee, μμ background/jet pair iSS + Colorless

The Au+Au jet chain, which the other setups vary:

flowchart LR
  IS["3D MC-Glauber<br/>nucleons, strings"] --> HARD["PYTHIA 8<br/>hard scattering<br/>at a binary collision"]
  IS --> M1["MUSIC_1<br/>background leg<br/>strings only"]
  HARD --> EL["MATTER → LBT<br/>in MUSIC_1's medium<br/>recoils, holes"]
  M1 -. "T, s, u^μ" .-> EL
  EL --> LIQ["CausalLiquefier<br/>droplets"]
  IS --> M2["MUSIC_2<br/>jet leg<br/>strings + droplets"]

docs.title: 1. Initial state: 3D MC-Glauber with strings
docs.text:
The initial state is the dynamical 3D Monte Carlo Glauber model of Shen and Schenke (arXiv:1710.00881; its rapidity-loss and string deceleration model: arXiv:2203.04685):

  • Nucleons and quarks. Nucleon positions are sampled for Au and Pb (minimum distance 0.9 fm). For O+O they are read from O-16 configuration files with \(\alpha\) clustering (PGCM). The participants are valence quarks (useQuarks 1) whose momentum fractions come from parton distributions at \(Q^2 = 1\) GeV\(^2\).
  • Strings. Every binary collision can produce a QCD string (the number per NN collision fluctuates). The string ends decelerate with a parametrized rapidity loss (rapidity_loss_method 4; ylossParam4At2…At10 = 1.610, 1.685, 1.685, 2.95, variance 0.682) and the nucleon remnants lose a fraction 0.536 of the string's rapidity loss. The strings form at \(\tau_{\rm form}\) with mean 0.424 fm/c (Au+Au, Pb+Pb) or 0.5 fm/c (O+O). No baryon junctions; baryon number is not evolved in the hydro.
  • Centrality is selected on \(b\) only. Inside X-SCAPE the generator samples \(b\) with \(P(b) \propto b\) between b_min and b_max and requires two or more participants; the cenMin/cenMax tags act only in the standalone 3dMCGlauber program. The b_max values are geometric: \(\pi b_{\max}^2\) = 10 % of the Au+Au cross section (4.7 fm), and 10 % and 30 % of 7.7 b for Pb+Pb (4.95 fm, 8.57 fm). For O+O at 200 GeV this model's \(\sigma_{\rm inel}\) is 1.55 b, so \(b < 3\) fm is about 0–24 %.
  • Where the hard scattering happens. The hard process is placed at one of the event's binary-collision points, in \(x, y\), at \(z = t = 0\). Each event has exactly one hard scattering, while in nature the rate grows with \(N_{\rm coll}\): n_coll (or glauber_ncoll) is recorded per event so the analysis can weight with it.

The initial-state grid is \(|x|, |y| \le 15\) fm with 0.3 fm cells and \(|\eta_s| \le 6\) with 0.2 for Au+Au; \(\pm 20\) fm and \(\pm 8\) for Pb+Pb; \(\pm 10.5\) fm for O+O. MUSIC uses the same grid.

docs.title: 2. From strings to fluid: no separate pre-equilibrium stage
docs.text:
There is no pre-equilibrium model: the task list contains NullPreDynamics. Instead MUSIC starts on an empty grid just before the first string deposits anything, and the strings act as dynamical sources while they decelerate (MUSIC InitialProfile 131: all strings start at \(\tau = 0\), \(\eta_s = 0\)). The strings hand their energy and momentum to the fluid as they decelerate, each deposit smeared with a Gaussian of width \(\sigma_x\) = 0.207 fm and \(\sigma_{\eta}\) = 0.458, without an initial flow (stringPreEqFlowFactor 0). The hydro equations of the background are

\[ \partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = J^\nu_{\rm strings}. \]

The hydro start time therefore varies per event; it is recorded as tau0_music. Jet energy loss starts interacting with the medium at this time, at each point's own proper time; before it, partons propagate as in vacuum.

docs.title: 3. The hard process: PYTHIA 8
docs.text:
The hard scattering comes from PYTHIA 8 (arXiv:1410.3012, arXiv:2203.11601) through X-SCAPE's PythiaGun:

  • Processes: HardQCD:all = on (dijets) in a \(\hat p_T\) window, 50–70 GeV by default for Au+Au and 20–40 GeV for O+O. Pythia's initial-state radiation and multiparton interactions stay on; its final-state shower is off (FSR_on 0), because MATTER does the final-state shower; Pythia's hadronization is off.
  • Hand-over: the final partons above softMomentumCutoff = 2 GeV are handed to the energy-loss modules at the binary-collision vertex.
  • Several \(\hat p_T\) windows: a job can run several windows with one background each (--pthat-bins); each window's generated cross section and its error are stored, and the events carry weights.
  • Parton rapidity cut (optional): --parton-ymax keeps only events whose hardest partons pass \(|y| < Y\). Rejected events are regenerated before any shower or hydro, and the stored cross sections are corrected by the kept/tried fraction.
  • A pp reference: run_prod_vacuum.py runs the same PythiaGun and MATTER in vacuum, with no medium.

For O+O the hard process is PythiaIsrGun (section 12), for Z+jet a Z + parton process (section 13).

docs.title: 4. Jet energy loss: MATTER and LBT
docs.text:
The partons are showered in the medium by the JETSCAPE multistage approach (arXiv:1705.00050, arXiv:2204.01163): MATTER at high virtuality, LBT at low virtuality.

  • MATTER (arXiv:1301.5323, arXiv:1712.10055) is a virtuality-ordered shower with medium-modified splitting. It runs while a parton's virtuality is above \(Q_0\) = 2 GeV.
  • LBT (arXiv:1503.03313, arXiv:1803.06785) is a linear Boltzmann transport of on-shell partons with elastic scatterings and medium-induced radiation. It takes over below \(Q_0\). The switch between the two is arbitrated by <mutex>ON</mutex>; MATTER comes first in the XML because it sets the virtuality LBT takes over at.

  • Couplings and \(\hat q\). Both use \(\alpha_s\) = 0.25; LBT runs its coupling (run_alphas 1). MATTER's \(\hat q\) has the HTL form with one running and one fixed coupling and no virtuality dependence (QhatParametrizationType 1):

    \[ \hat q = C_A\,\frac{42\,\zeta(3)}{\pi}\;\alpha_s^{\rm run}(2ET)\,\alpha_s^{\rm fix}\,T^3 \ln\frac{2ET}{m_D^2},\qquad m_D^2 = \frac{4\pi\alpha_s^{\rm fix}\,T^2\,(6+N_f)}{6},\; N_f = 3. \]

  • Where the medium acts. Both modules interact only where \(T \ge\) 160 MeV (hydro_Tc), and only from the hydro start time on. The time step is 0.1 fm/c, up to 20 fm/c (Au+Au, Pb+Pb) or 50 fm/c (O+O).

  • Recoils and holes. MATTER runs with recoil_on 1 and LBT always produces them: a scattering kicks a medium parton out (the recoil) and leaves a hole, a negative-energy parton that carries the momentum missing from the medium. In the jet productions the soft part of this medium response goes into the fluid (next section); in O+O the holes close colour lines in the hadronization (section 10).
  • Which medium. In the two-leg productions, MATTER and LBT see the background leg's medium (temperature, entropy density and flow velocity per cell).

docs.title: 5. Energy–momentum deposition: the CausalLiquefier
docs.text:
The energy the jet loses to the medium is put back into the fluid by X-SCAPE's CausalLiquefier (Tachibana, Shen and Majumder, arXiv:2001.08321).

Droplets. After every energy-loss step the liquefier compares the four-momentum that came in with the four-momentum of the partons that are still tracked. A parton is no longer tracked when its energy in the local fluid rest frame is below e_threshold = 2 GeV, and holes are never tracked further. The difference \(\Delta p^\mu\) becomes a droplet at the step's space-time point: soft partons enter with a positive sign, holes with a negative one. Heavy quarks, photons and leptons are never liquefied. Each event's droplets are stored in the pair file (source/droplets: \( au, x, y, \eta_s, E, p_x, p_y, p_z\)).

Causal spreading. A droplet is not dropped into one cell. Its energy and momentum spread from its position by relativistic (causal) diffusion,

\[ \partial_t ho + abla\cdot\vec j = 0,\qquad au_{ m relax}\,\partial_t \vec j + \vec j = -D\, abla ho , \]

with \( au_{ m relax}\) = 0.1 fm/c and \(D\) = 0.08 fm, so the signal speed is \(\sqrt{D/ au_{ m relax}} \approx 0.89\,c\). The droplet is deposited in the hydro step that contains \( au_{ m drop} + au_{ m delay}\), with \( au_{ m delay}\) = 1 fm/c, using the diffusion kernel \(G\) at that time (smoothed with width_delta = 0.1 fm). The jet leg's hydro equations are then

\[ \partial_\mu T^{\mu u} = J^ u_{ m strings} + J^ u_{ m jet},\qquad J^ u_{ m jet}(x) = \sum_{i\,\in\, m droplets} \Delta p_i^ u\; G(x - x_i). \]

Each droplet is normalized on MUSIC's grid, so it deposits exactly its four-momentum. The liquefier's dtau must equal MUSIC's time step at the start (0.02 fm/c); when MUSIC lengthens its step later (section 7) it passes the new step to the liquefier.

docs.title: 6. The background/jet hydro pair
docs.text:
The jet productions run MUSIC twice per event, with X-SCAPE's two-stage hydro:

  1. MUSIC_1, the background leg: the strings only. It provides the medium that MATTER, LBT and the liquefier read.
  2. MUSIC_2, the jet leg: the same strings plus the droplets.

Both legs start from the identical initial condition and are bit-identical until the first droplet deposits (not before \(\tau_{\rm delay}\) = 1 fm/c). The difference of the two evolutions, jet leg minus background leg, is the jet's effect on the medium, without the event-by-event fluctuations of the fireball that would remain if one subtracted an average background. The same holds for the two freeze-out surfaces, and so for the hadrons: the background's bulk hadrons can be subtracted event by event.

Things to know about the pair:

  • The jet does not feel its own wake. Energy loss is computed in the background medium; the wake changes the fluid but not the jet.
  • Several jets per background. The background can be reused for several jets (--reuse, --pthat-bins); MUSIC_1 then runs once per background and MUSIC_2 once per jet. MUSIC_2 also starts from MUSIC_1's saved state just before the first droplet can deposit instead of recomputing the identical early steps; the output is the same.
  • Late droplets are lost. Droplets due after the jet leg has frozen out never reach the fluid; their energy is recorded (E_droplets_late).
  • A null test. With the deposition switched off (--no-deposit) the two legs must be identical, which the productions check.

In the O+O production there is only one MUSIC run per event, so there the medium response is part of the bulk and cannot be separated.

docs.title: 7. Hydrodynamics: MUSIC
docs.text:
The fluid is evolved by MUSIC, a 3+1D second-order viscous hydrodynamics code (arXiv:1004.1408, arXiv:1009.3244, arXiv:1509.06738), here through its GPU port MUSIC4GPU (the same equations and numerical scheme; see GPU acceleration). The settings are the tuned 3D-Glauber + MUSIC set of X-SCAPE, tuned at \(\sqrt{s_{NN}}\) = 200 GeV; the Pb+Pb inputs use it unchanged.

setting equation of state EOS 91: lattice QCD (HotQCD, arXiv:1407.6387) matched to a hadron resonance gas with the SMASH hadron list. EOS 9 (the same with the UrQMD list) is available for reruns of older campaigns. shear viscosity \(\eta/s(T)\), piecewise linear with a kink (below) bulk viscosity \(\zeta/s(T)\), a skewed Cauchy peak (below) second-order terms on (Include_second_order_terms 1) conserved charges none (Include_Rhob 0, Include_QS 0) numerics Kurganov–Tadmor scheme in single precision (beastMode 1); \(\Delta\tau\) = 0.02 fm/c, 0.05 fm/c from \(\tau\) = 3 fm/c on freeze-out \(T_{\rm fo}\) = 150 MeV (0.243 GeV/fm\(^3\) with EOS 91) stored evolution every 0.1 fm/c: \(e, v_x, v_y, v_z\), resampled onto the output grid

The transport coefficients use the functional forms of the JETSCAPE Bayesian analysis (arXiv:2011.01430) with these values:

\[ \frac{\eta}{s}(T) = \left(\frac{\eta}{s}\right)_{\rm kink} + a_{\rm low/high}\,(T - T_{\rm kink}), \qquad T_{\rm kink} = 206~{\rm MeV},\; \left(\frac{\eta}{s}\right)_{\rm kink} = 0.108,\; a_{\rm low} = -1.999,\; a_{\rm high} = 1.999~{\rm GeV}^{-1} \]

(with a floor of \(10^{-3}\)), and

\[ \frac{\zeta}{s}(T) = \frac{(\zeta/s)_{\max}}{1 + \left(\dfrac{T - T_{\rm peak}} {w\,[1 + \lambda\,{\rm sign}(T - T_{\rm peak})]}\right)^2}, \qquad (\zeta/s)_{\max} = 0.092,\; T_{\rm peak} = 180~{\rm MeV},\; w = 67~{\rm MeV},\; \lambda = -0.8 . \]

The larger time step after 3 fm/c keeps the freeze-out checks and the stored frames at 0.1 fm/c. It changes the medium at the \(10^{-3}\) level, so the files of one campaign are made with one setting, which every job XML records.

The output grid. The productions do not store MUSIC's native grid. They resample the evolution onto a grid set in a YAML file, the one the FNO models are trained on: for Au+Au 64 × 64 × 32 cells at 0.3875 fm × 0.3875 fm × 0.3125 in \(\eta_s\) (\(|x|, |y| \le\) 12.2 fm, \(|\eta_s| \le\) 4.84), \(\tau\) from 0.5 fm/c in steps of 0.1 fm/c; for O+O 0.3125 fm in \(x, y\). The freeze-out surface and the hadrons are made from MUSIC's own grid, not from this resampled copy.

docs.title: 8. Freeze-out surface: Cornelius
docs.text: MUSIC finds the \(T = T_{\rm fo}\) hypersurface with Cornelius (arXiv:1206.3371), checking every 0.1 fm/c. Each surface element carries its position \(x^\mu\), normal \(d\sigma_\mu\), flow \(u^\mu\), \(e\), \(T\), \(P\) and the viscous fields \(\pi^{\mu\nu}\) and \(\Pi\): exactly what iSS reads. The productions store these elements losslessly in the particlize file, one surface per jet leg and one per background, so hadronization can be repeated later with any settings.

docs.title: 9. Particlization: Cooper–Frye with iSS
docs.text:
The fluid is converted into hadrons with the Cooper–Frye formula (Cooper and Frye, Phys. Rev. D 10, 186 (1974)), sampled by iSS (arXiv:1409.8164):

\[ E\,\frac{dN_i}{d^3p} = \frac{g_i}{(2\pi)^3}\int_\Sigma p^\mu\, d\sigma_\mu \left[f_{\rm eq}\!\left(\frac{u\cdot p}{T}\right) + \delta f_{\rm shear} + \delta f_{\rm bulk}\right]. \]
  • Viscous corrections: shear and bulk \(\delta f\), Grad's 22-moment form (deltaf_type 20).
  • Hadron list: the SMASH list for EOS 91 (the UrQMD list for EOS 9), taken from the job's own MUSIC input so that EoS and hadron list always match.
  • Resonance decays: iSS decays the resonances itself. Channels that are closed at the pole masses (215 of them, such as \(\omega \to \pi\rho\), \(\eta' \to \eta\sigma\), \(f_2 \to \rho\rho\)) get Breit–Wigner masses for their unstable daughters. \(\eta\) and \(\Sigma^0\) stay stable, as in SMASH, so they are among the final hadrons.
  • Oversampling: one fluid is sampled many times (--oversample, 100 by default in the offline hadronization). The oversamples are independent Cooper–Frye samplings of one collision, not independent collisions, and the analysis tools treat their errors accordingly.
  • Correlated jet/background sampling (--correlated): iSS's random numbers are addressed by the surface cell, and the jet leg's samples use their background's seeds. Jet and background then give the same hadrons where their surfaces agree, and jet − background is about 8 times less noisy at \(|\eta| < 1\), with the same physics in each leg.

docs.title: 10. Jet hadronization
docs.text:
Au+Au, Pb+Pb and Z+jet: Colorless. The final partons are hadronized by Lund string fragmentation in PYTHIA 8, without their colour flow (the JETSCAPE choice for MATTER + LBT in A+A). LBT's recoils are included (take_recoil 1); partons the liquefier took into the fluid are not. A string that cannot be closed gets a beam remnant with 1/6 of eCMforHadronization, which is always set to the collision's \(\sqrt{s_{NN}}\). Hadron decays are done by Pythia. The productions store the final partons (in double precision), so the jets are hadronized afterwards on CPUs, as often as wanted (--n-frag fragmentations per event).

O+O: iColored. With initial-state radiation the jet hadrons are the whole hard nucleon pair: the dijet showered by MATTER and LBT, the ISR emissions, Pythia's MPI partons and the pair's beam remnants from 3dMCGlauber. iColoredHadronization fragments them along their colour flow. MATTER's recoils and LBT's partons carry colour tags, and the colour lines that end in the medium, at the holes, are closed by reconnection (<colour_closure>reconnect). Holes are not hadronized. Because it needs the beam remnants of the live event, this runs in the production job. The mechanism is described in X-SCAPE's README_ColourFlow.md.

docs.title: 11. Hadronic afterburner
docs.text: The productions do not run a hadronic afterburner: there is no hadronic rescattering after particlization. iSS decays the resonances of the SMASH list itself (section 9), so the stored hadrons are final-state hadrons as far as decays go. The outputs are prepared for SMASH (arXiv:1606.06642) to be added later: the hadron list is SMASH's, and the undecayed ("primary") bulk hadrons with their positions can be kept in their own files (--keep-primaries). Positions of the jet hadrons for a rescattering stage are not yet available.

docs.title: 12. O+O with initial-state radiation
docs.text:
The O+O production uses X-SCAPE's small-system chain (arXiv:2308.02650, arXiv:2407.17443), built from the <Hard><ISR> block of the XML:

IS: 3dMCGlauber (O-16, positions only)
 -> Hard: PythiaIsrGun at one binary collision      the hard scattering
          -> iMATTER                                 ISR, backward in time
          -> MCGlauberGenString                      strings from what the hard pair left
 -> MUSIC                                            one hydro per event
 -> Eloss: MATTER + LBT in MUSIC's medium            the final-state shower
 -> JetHadronization: iColored                       jet hadrons
 -> SoftParticlization: iSS                          bulk hadrons
  • Two-step initial state. 3dMCGlauber first makes only the nucleon positions and the collisions. PythiaIsrGun puts the hard scattering (\(\hat p_T\) 20–40 GeV by default) at a binary collision drawn uniformly; Pythia's own ISR is off, its MPI on.
  • ISR with iMATTER. The initial-state partons are showered backward in time, from \(t = 0\) to \(-t_{\max}\) = −50 fm/c, and the final-state shower starts there.
  • Strings from what is left. The strings are made after the ISR, and the hard partons' momentum is taken out of the colliding nucleons (Subtract_hard_momentum 1); the hard pair's remnants go to the jet hadronization instead of into strings. The energy bookkeeping closes exactly, per event: \(E_{\rm strings} + E_{\rm ISR,\,sub} + E_{\rm remnant,\,proj} + E_{\rm remnant,\,targ} = N_{\rm part}\sqrt{s_{NN}}/2\).
  • Tuned O+O set. 3dMCGlauber and MUSIC use X-SCAPE's tuned O+O settings at 200 GeV (\(\tau_{\rm form}\) = 0.5 fm/c, EOS 91, the viscosities and freeze-out above).
  • One MUSIC run per event, no background leg and no liquefier: the medium is made from what each event's hard scattering left, so a background cannot be reused.
  • Energy loss: MATTER (with recoils) + LBT with the Au+Au settings; there is no medium, and no \(\hat q\), before \(t = 0\).
  • Hard-triggered events. Every event has exactly one hard scattering; weight with \(N_{\rm coll}\) for the geometry of hard events. When the hard collision is the event's only one, no string forms and there is no medium (about 5 % of the events at \(b < 5.6\) fm).

What this means for an analysis is in O+O analysis.

docs.title: 13. Z+jet in Pb+Pb
docs.text:
The Z+jet input (PbPb_0_30_ZJet.xml) is the Pb+Pb jet setup at 5.02 TeV, 0–30 %, with a Z in place of the dijet. It is set up for comparisons with the CMS Z+jet (arXiv:1702.01060) and Z–hadron (arXiv:2103.04377, arXiv:2507.09307) and ATLAS Z-tagged hadron (arXiv:2008.09811) measurements.

  • Hard process: \(q\bar q \to Z g\) and \(qg \to Z q\), a pure Z (no \(\gamma^*\)), decaying to \(e^+e^-\) or \(\mu^+\mu^-\); Pythia's ISR and MPI on, FSR off. One parton is required next to the Z, and an event is kept only with the Z's lepton pair (<trigger>Z).
  • Acceptance in the generator: both leptons \(p_T > 20\) GeV and \(|\eta| < 2.5\) (--lepton-ptmin, --lepton-etamax); failing events are regenerated before any hydro. Further cuts (Z rapidity, mass window, \(p_T^Z\), jet \(\eta\)) are left to the analysis.
  • \(\hat p_T\) windows: 20–30, 30–35, 35–45, 45–55, 55–70 and 70–200 GeV, with each window's cross section stored.
  • The leptons pass through MATTER, LBT, the liquefier and the hadronization like photons, and end up with the jet hadrons.
  • Weights: every event has one Z while Z production scales with \(N_{\rm coll}\), so the events are weighted with their recorded \(N_{\rm coll}\).
  • Everything else (pair of MUSIC runs, liquefier, iSS, Colorless) is the Pb+Pb jet setup, which uses the Au+Au template's physics settings; they are not tuned at the LHC.

docs.title: 14. Hadrons from a stored hydro history
docs.text:
The pair files keep only \(e\) and \(\vec v\) on the output grid, without viscous fields: this is what an FNO learns and predicts. Hadrons can then only come from a surface found in that history, sampled without \(\delta f\). A dedicated study compares such hadrons with iSS on MUSIC's own surface for 100 Au+Au events (hydro_hist_vs_surface):

  • The surfaces agree to 2 % in volume.
  • \(dN_{\rm ch}/d\eta\) agrees (+0.2 %), but identified yields, \(\langle p_T\rangle\) and \(v_n\) are off by 5–30 %, almost entirely from the missing \(\delta f\): bulk \(\delta f\) sets the proton yield (−29 % without it) and \(\langle p_T\rangle\), shear \(\delta f\) the flow harmonics.
  • The jet wake keeps its shape but comes out about 10 % low.

The fast finite-volume solver FastHydro agrees with MUSIC to about 0.3 % (relative L2 of the energy density at freeze-out) on the same initial condition. It samples hadrons with ideal Cooper–Frye only.

docs.title: Approximations and limits
docs.text:
Keep these in mind when interpreting the output

  • No feedback of the wake on the jet: energy loss runs in the background medium.
  • No hadronic rescattering: iSS decays resonances, but nothing like SMASH runs after particlization.
  • No pre-equilibrium dynamics beyond the decelerating string sources.
  • One hard scattering per event: the event samples are hard-triggered; use the recorded \(N_{\rm coll}\) and the per-window cross sections as weights.
  • Centrality from \(b\), not from an event-activity class.
  • Pb+Pb and Z+jet use parameters tuned at 200 GeV.
  • Droplets after the jet leg's freeze-out are lost (recorded per event).
  • The stored hydro history has no viscous fields and is resampled onto a coarser grid (section 14).

docs.title: Python and machine learning
docs.text: X-SCAPE is a C++ framework. js-contrib opens it to Python, not as a wrapper that runs a finished binary, but down to the module level: Python can drive the event loop, read every intermediate result as numpy arrays, and replace any stage of the simulation with a class of its own. This page explains why that matters for heavy-ion physics and what you can do with it today; the Python section shows how.

docs.title: Why Python
docs.text:
Machine learning lives in Python. Neural networks are trained, evaluated and changed in PyTorch. A surrogate model that is only usable after it has been exported, frozen and re-linked into C++ is slow to iterate on. With js-contrib a PyTorch model can be a JETSCAPE module: it receives the initial condition from the framework, predicts the medium, and Matter, LBT and iSS run on its prediction as they would on MUSIC.

Hydro surrogates need hydro. A Fourier neural operator (FNO) learns the map from an initial condition to the full space-time evolution of the medium. In 2+1D it reproduces MUSIC orders of magnitude faster (Phys. Rev. C 113, 014904 (2026)). Training it, and the 3+1D and jet-deposition models that follow, takes many MUSIC evolutions in a format a training code reads directly. The productions write exactly that.

Jets in a medium need pairs. To learn how a jet changes the medium, a model needs the same event twice: once without the jet and once with its deposited energy, on an identical initial condition. Then arr - arr_bg is the jet's effect and nothing else. The two-stage productions (MUSIC, GPU) and FastHydro (a fast solver written in PyTorch) both write such pairs.

Physics modules are faster to prototype in Python. An idea for an energy-loss kernel or a hadronization model can be written as a Python class in an afternoon and run inside the full event, next to the C++ modules, without recompiling X-SCAPE. Once it works, it ports to C++ line by line, because the Python interface keeps the C++ names and argument order.

Analysis is in numpy, awkward and FastJet. Hadrons, partons and showers come out of an event, or out of the production files, as numpy arrays and nested awkward arrays with four-vector kinematics, ready for fastjet and histogramming.

docs.title: Why js-contrib
docs.text: X-SCAPE can simulate a heavy-ion collision from the initial state to the final hadrons, with jets that lose energy in a 3+1D viscous fluid and feed that energy back into it. A few such events are easy to make. Hundreds of thousands are not: MUSIC on a CPU takes minutes per event, the event record is written in formats meant for small samples, and the framework is driven from C++ and XML only. js-contrib closes that gap. It makes large, GPU-accelerated productions of the full chain possible, writes them in a form that both physics analyses and machine learning can use, gives access to all of it from Python, and shares the results openly. Read this page to see what the package adds and how it relates to the framework; the physics itself is on The physics.

docs.title: 1. Large-statistics productions with full 3+1D hydro
docs.text:
MUSIC, the 3+1D second-order viscous hydro of X-SCAPE, runs on the GPU through MUSIC4GPU: CUDA on NVIDIA cards and Metal on Apple Silicon. It is a direct port of MUSIC's CPU algorithms (no new physics) and is checked against the CPU build down to the final hadrons. Several production jobs share one GPU, so a single workstation produces large samples, and the same container runs on HPC clusters. Details and throughput per machine: GPU acceleration.

The productions are split into two stages:

  1. On the GPU: initial state, hard process, jet energy loss and hydro. Each job writes the hydro evolution and/or the input to hadronization (the freeze-out surfaces and the final partons) straight to HDF5.
  2. On CPUs, later: Cooper–Frye sampling and jet hadronization from those stored inputs, with as many oversamples as the analysis needs.

The split keeps the expensive GPU part from being repeated when the hadronization settings change, and lets cheap CPU nodes do the sampling. A one-job mode (--hadrons-only) does both stages at once when little oversampling is needed. How to run them: Run.

docs.title: 2. Jets and their wake: paired background/jet hydro
docs.text:
The medium's response to a jet (the wake) is a small perturbation on top of a fireball that fluctuates strongly from event to event. Subtracting a separate, average background leaves these fluctuations in. js-contrib's jet productions therefore evolve every event twice, on the same initial condition: once without the jet (the background leg) and once with the energy and momentum the jet deposits (the jet leg). Before the first deposit the two legs are bit-identical. The difference, jet leg minus background leg, is the jet's effect on the medium and nothing else, event by event.

The same idea carries over to the hadrons. Both legs' freeze-out surfaces are sampled with correlated random numbers, so that jet and background give the same hadrons where their surfaces agree. For Au+Au this makes jet − background about 8 times less noisy at \(|\eta| < 1\) at the same number of oversamples. The physics of the pair is explained in The physics.

docs.title: 3. Training data for machine-learned surrogates
docs.text:
Hydro is the most expensive part of the chain, and it is smooth enough to be learned. A Fourier neural operator (FNO) trained on MUSIC evolutions predicts the hydrodynamic evolution orders of magnitude faster (Stewart and Putschke, Phys. Rev. C 113, 014904 (2026)). js-contrib provides both sides of this:

  • Training data. The productions resample MUSIC's evolution (energy density and flow velocity, every 0.1 fm/c) onto a fixed output grid chosen in a YAML file, and store background/jet pairs, so a 3+1D surrogate can learn both the medium and the jet's wake. FastHydro, a fast 3+1D finite-volume solver running the same jet-deposition chain, produces such pairs cheaply.
  • Using a trained model in the chain. FnoHydro replaces MUSIC with an FNO in C++ (through LibTorch), and PyFNOHydro runs a PyTorch model live from Python. See Python and machine learning and Live PyTorch FNO hydro.

docs.title: 4. Python access to the whole framework
docs.text: PyJetscape exposes the X-SCAPE framework to Python (pyjetscape_core, built with pybind11), and the jetscape package adds a "Pythonic" layer on top. With it you can build and run the task list from Python, read the hydro, surfaces, partons and hadrons as numpy arrays, and write your own modules in Python (a hard process, energy loss, hadronization, an afterburner, a writer) without recompiling anything. The production drivers themselves are Python scripts built on it. See Python.

docs.title: 6. Open data on the OSDF
docs.text: Productions are shared on the Open Science Data Federation (OSDF) in the Pelican namespace osdf:///fno4hic. Reading it is public: no account, login or token is needed. Files can be downloaded with a provided tool or read in place over osdf://. Sharing the outputs means a campaign made once on GPUs serves many analyses and model trainings, and nobody needs a GPU just to analyse it. See Data on the OSDF.

docs.title: How it relates to JETSCAPE, X-SCAPE and C-SCAPE
docs.text:
• JETSCAPE is the modular, task-based framework for simulating all stages of a heavy-ion collision (The JETSCAPE framework).
  • X-SCAPE extends it, among other things, to small systems: the 3D MC-Glauber initial state with strings, initial-state radiation with iMATTER, and exact four-momentum conservation between the hard and soft sectors (arXiv:2308.02650, arXiv:2407.17443). js-contrib follows X-SCAPE's contrib branch.
  • C-SCAPE is in development; js-contrib is meant to serve it too.

js-contrib is to X-SCAPE what fastjet-contrib is to FastJet: contributions that live in their own repository, outside the framework's core, and plug into it. X-SCAPE fetches js-contrib into external_packages/js-contrib with external_packages/get_js_contrib.sh and builds it with -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON and a flag per contrib. The hydro (MUSIC4GPU), the Cooper–Frye sampler (iSS) and the initial state (3dMCGlauber) are X-SCAPE external packages, fetched by X-SCAPE's own get_*.sh scripts. The full list of components and repositories is in Contribs and repositories.

docs.title: Analyse
docs.text:
A production leaves behind HDF5 files: the hydro evolution of every event, the freeze-out surfaces and partons that hadronization starts from, and the hadrons themselves, plus ROOT copies of the hadrons if you made them. This section shows how to read each kind, how to combine many production files into one data set with the right statistics, and how to go from there to spectra, jets, the jet-induced wake and the O+O observables. Start here if you have production files in hand, your own or downloaded, and want physics out of them.

None of the analysis needs X-SCAPE, a GPU or the production container. Everything on these pages runs in a plain Python environment; ROOT is needed only for the C++ route.

flowchart LR
  P["production job<br/>(GPU)"] --> PAIR["stem.h5<br/>hydro pair"]
  P --> PART["stem_particlize.h5<br/>surfaces, partons"]
  PART --> HAD["hadronize.py<br/>(CPU)"]
  HAD --> H["stem_hadrons_{bulk_jet,bulk_bg,jet_frag}.h5"]
  H --> ROOT["run_h5toROOT.py"] --> R["stem_hadrons.root<br/>campaign_campaign.root"]

docs.text:
environment use it for set up the analysis venv (recommended) every HDF5 file, the ROOT files through uproot, FastJet in Python, the notebooks, run_h5toROOT.py Analysis environment the analysis venv + ROOT (conda) the above plus PyROOT, RDataFrame, the C++ macros and FastJet in C++ Analysis environment, and ROOT and C++ the Mac wheel (Apple Silicon) the same environment that runs X-SCAPE also analyses; on any other computer pyjetscape[analysis] installs the readers alone Mac (xscape wheel) the production container re-hadronizing stored surfaces (hadronize.py: more oversamples, other iSS settings), which needs X-SCAPE Production container

The venv installs PyJetscape's pure-Python readers (jetscape.hadrons_h5, jetscape.particlize_h5, ...), h5py with hdf5plugin (the files are Blosc-compressed), uproot, awkward, scikit-hep fastjet, matplotlib and Jupyter, and it sets MUSIC_EOS_TABLE for converting energy density to temperature.

Always import hdf5plugin

The production files are compressed with Blosc-zstd. h5py reads them only after import hdf5plugin; without it every dataset read fails with OSError: Can't synchronously read data. The PyJetscape readers import it for you.

docs.title: 2. Get the files
docs.text:
• Your own run: the job writes everything into its output directory, one set of files per job (<stem>.h5, <stem>_particlize.h5, ...); hadronize.py adds the hadron files next to them. See Au+Au jets, O+O with ISR and Z+jet and other systems.
  • Shared productions: campaigns are published on the OSDF under osdf:///fno4hic, public to read. js_osdf.py downloads a whole campaign or only the kind of file an analysis needs (--what h5 for the hadron analyses, --what root, --what pair), and small files can be read in place without downloading. See Data on the OSDF.

docs.title: 3. A first analysis
docs.text:
The charged-hadron pT spectrum of the background events of a whole campaign, at \(|\eta| < 0.5\), each event averaged over its oversamples:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronFileReader

edges = np.linspace(0, 4, 41)                                  # pT bins [GeV]
with HadronFileReader("/path/to/campaign") as r:               # the production files in there
    print(r.n_files, "files,", r.n_events, "events, tags", r.tags())
    mid = lambda ev, info: ev.charged & (np.abs(ev.eta) < 0.5)   # charged, |eta| < 0.5
    dn, err = r.hist("bulk_bg", "pt", edges, mask=mid, per_event=False)

pt, w = 0.5 * (edges[1:] + edges[:-1]), np.diff(edges)
plt.errorbar(pt, dn / w, err / w, fmt="o")                     # per event: d^2N/dpT deta
plt.yscale("log"); plt.xlabel(r"$p_T$ [GeV]"); plt.ylabel(r"$dN_{ch}/dp_T\,d\eta$")
plt.savefig("pt_spectrum.png")

hist returns, per bin, the count per event (each event first averaged over its own oversamples, then over the events) and its error. Replace "bulk_bg" with "bulk_jet" for the events with the jet's wake, or "jet_frag" for the jet's own hadrons. Hadrons explains all of it.
