docs.title: What a production writes
docs.text:
Every production job writes a small set of files that share one name, the stem (AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001, OO_isr_c1_0007, ...). This page describes each kind: what it holds, how it is laid out, and how big it is. It also says what one "event" means at hadron level, which settings must match before files are combined, and how to look inside any file. Read it once before your first analysis; the statistics of oversamples in particular affect every result.

Why HDF5, and why one file per job. The hydro evolution is a large 4D array per event; HDF5 stores it chunked (one chunk per event and τ frame) and compressed, so a single frame reads without the rest. Every file carries its provenance as attributes: the job's XML, the grid, the seed and the software build. Jobs are never merged: a campaign is a directory of production files, and the readers open them side by side as one data set.

docs.title: 1. The files at a glance
docs.text:
The Au+Au jet production (two hydro legs per event) writes, per job:

file made by holds size per event read with <stem>.h5, the pair file the production job both hydro legs on the output grid: arr (jet leg), arr_bg (background); the droplets, the showers, diagnostics ~170 MB with 15 jets per background, 285 MB with one h5py, FNO4d's loader, wake_observables.py <stem>_particlize.h5 the job, with --write-particlize both freeze-out surfaces (32 columns per cell), the final partons, the shower initiators, the event table ~90 MB (15 jets per background) ParticlizeFile <stem>_hadrons_bulk_jet.h5 hadronize.py iSS on the jet leg's surface: bulk + wake, N oversamples per event ~0.2 MB per oversample at full precision HadronFileReader <stem>_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5 hadronize.py iSS on the background's surface, once per background as above HadronFileReader <stem>_hadrons_jet_frag.h5 hadronize.py the fragmented surviving partons, M fragmentations per event small HadronFileReader <stem>_hadrons.root, <campaign>_campaign.root run_h5toROOT.py the three hadron tags as RNTuple or TTree, one entry per oversample; event table, cross sections, provenance 0.9 × the HDF5 hadron files uproot, RDataFrame, HadronFileReader.h <stem>.json, .xml, .log every job the job summary (seed, events, droplets, edge hits), the exact job XML, the log json, an editor

The sizes are for the Au+Au campaign setting (three pT̂ windows, five jets per window and background, partons at \(|y| < 0.6\)): pair + particlize file together 0.243 GB per event, 0.097 GB with --particlize-only (no pair file).

Other productions write a subset or a variant:

production files Au+Au hydro only (prod_AuAu_0_10) AuAu_0_10_*.h5 with arr only (~140 MB per event) Au+Au hadrons only (run_prod_jet.py --hadrons-only) the three hadron files and the undecayed _primary bulk files, written in the job; no pair and no particlize file; the event record sits in the jet files' units/ O+O with ISR (prod_OO_isr) one hydro per event (OO_isr_*.h5, ~17 MB), a particlize file (~10 MB), the jet hadrons and optionally the bulk hadrons made in the job; see O+O Z+jet (Pb+Pb) hadrons-only jobs, as above, with the Z and its leptons in the event record; see Z+jet and other systems

docs.title: Which files an analysis needs
docs.text:
analysis files hadron spectra, the wake at hadron level, jets the particlize file and the three hadron files of every production file (hadrons-only jobs: the hadron files); or the ROOT files alone the wake in the fluid, the energy balance, the deposit the pair files (and the particlize files) FNO training the pair files, or the hydro-only files more oversamples, other iSS settings the particlize files, and hadronize.py in the container on a CPU node

The particlize files are self-contained: a hadron analysis never needs the large pair files. With the OSDF downloader, --what h5 fetches exactly the particlize and hadron files (Data on the OSDF).

docs.title: 2. Hydro pair files
docs.text:
Why pairs. The jet production runs MUSIC twice on the same initial condition: once without the jet (the background, MUSIC_1), and once with the energy the jet deposits (the jet leg, MUSIC_2). Both legs are bit-identical until the first droplet arrives, so arr − arr_bg is the jet's effect on the medium and nothing else: no pairing of separate runs, no event-by-event fluctuations to subtract. How to use them: Hydro and hadrons together.

dataset shape content arr (nevents, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau) float32 the jet leg (MUSIC_2). Channels energy_density [GeV/fm³], vx, vy, vz (Cartesian lab velocities) arr_bg as arr the background (MUSIC_1) ntau_freezeout, ntau_freezeout_bg (nevents,) frames written per leg; every frame from there on is 0 tau_freezeout, tau_freezeout_bg (nevents,) when each leg's hydro ended [fm/c] source/droplets, source/offsets (M, 8), (nevents + 1,) the droplets MUSIC_2 received: tau, x, y, eta, E, px, py, pz; event i is rows offsets[i]:offsets[i+1] shower/ the shower graphs (partons, vertices, initiators), read with jetscape.showers diag/ (nevents,) each E_droplets, n_droplets, bg_id, frames_identical, boundary and edge flags, tau0_music, eloss_tstart, wall_s; with pT̂ windows pthat_bin, pthat, event_weight
  • The grid is in the attributes: x_min, dx, nx (and y_*, eta_*), tau_min, dtau. The production default (grid_fno.yaml) is 64 × 64 × 32 cells: x, y from −12.2 to 12.2 fm in steps of 0.3875 fm, η_s from −4.84 to 4.84 in steps of 0.3125, τ = 0.5 + k · 0.1 fm/c. MUSIC's own grid is recorded in the *_MUSIC attributes.
  • Read frame by frame. Each chunk is one event and one τ frame (~2 MB): f["arr"][i, ..., k] is fast, a single cell's whole history reads every chunk.
  • The legs freeze out at different times. The deposit reheats the jet leg, by 1–2 fm/c in 0–10 % Au+Au. After the background has frozen out, arr − arr_bg is the jet leg's whole medium, not a wake: compare only frames below both ntau_freezeout values.
  • Shared backgrounds. When several events share one background (--reuse, pT̂ windows), arr_bg is an HDF5 virtual dataset over arr_bg_store, so each background is stored once. Read arr_bg, never the store. Copy such files whole (cp, rsync, h5repack): copying only the arr_bg dataset into another file gives a view without its data, which reads as zeros.
  • No gridded source. There is no source/S: MUSIC evaluates the liquefier's kernel per cell and step, so only the droplets are stored.

docs.title: 3. Particlize files
docs.text:
The input to hadronization, stored instead of hadrons so that hadronization can run later, on CPUs, as often as needed (jetscape.particlize_h5):

group content surface/jet/cells MUSIC_2's freeze-out surface, (N, 32) float32, one unit per event: exactly the fields iSS reads surface/bg/cells MUSIC_1's, one unit per new background; events/bg_unit says which unit an event used partons/data the final partons the jet hadronization receives, (K, 14): shower, pid, pstat, E, px, py, pz, t, x, y, z, mass, col, acol initiators/data each event's shower-initiating partons, (J, 11): shower, pid, pstat, px, py, pz, E, x, y, z, t events/ per event: bg_id, bg_unit, bg_key, n_cells_jet, n_cells_bg, n_partons, droplet energies, MUSIC's τ₀, boundary flags; with windows pthat_bin, pthat attributes music_input (iSS reads the EoS from it), T_fo, pair_file, file_uuid, the provenance
  • Surface columns (SURFACE_COLUMNS): tau, x, y, eta, ds0..ds3, u0..u3, e, T, P, nB, nQ, nS, muB, muQ, muS, the 10 components of π^{μν} and Pi. Lossless: the framework's surface cells are float.
  • Parton status: 0 shower, 1 recoil, −1 hole, −11/−13/−17 went into the droplets (never hadronized), 22 photon. The jet hadronization takes 0, 1, 22 and −1.
  • A broken leg shows here: a background with far more or fewer cells than its jet leg did not freeze out (Hadrons, bad runs).

Reading one event:

from jetscape.particlize_h5 import ParticlizeFile, SURFACE_COLUMNS

with ParticlizeFile("AuAu_0_10_jet_c1_0001_particlize.h5") as pf:
    cells    = pf.surface("jet", 0)          # (N, 32) float32: MUSIC_2's surface, event 0
    cells_bg = pf.surface("bg", 0)           # the background event 0 used (events/bg_unit)
    partons  = pf.partons(0)                 # (K, 14)
    ini      = pf.initiators(0)              # (J, 11)
    n_cells  = pf.events("n_cells_jet")      # a column of the per-event table
    T_fo     = cells[:, SURFACE_COLUMNS.index("T")]

Particlize files from before the initiators were added have no initiators/ group; prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/add_initiators.py copies them in once from the pair files.

docs.title: 4. Hadron files
docs.text:
hadronize.py (or the job itself, in hadrons-only mode) writes one file per tag (jetscape.hadrons_h5, format xscape/hadrons):

tag from one unit is bulk_jet iSS on the jet leg's surface: bulk + wake an event bulk_bg iSS on the background's surface: bulk a background (shared by the events that reused it) jet_frag Colorless hadronization of the surviving partons (O+O: iColored, in the job) an event

Each file keeps every sample apart:

dataset content hadrons/pid, hadrons/pstat int32, one row per hadron hadrons/p float32 (n, 4): E, px, py, pz [GeV] hadrons/x float32 (n, 4): t, x, y, z [fm]; absent with --no-x hadrons/sample_offsets where each sample (oversample or fragmentation) starts hadrons/unit_offsets where each unit's samples start units/ per unit: unit, event, n_samples, seed, n_cells; hadrons-only and O+O jobs: the whole event record initiators/ bulk_jet, jet_frag: each event's shower initiators

Choices made at hadronization, recorded in the files. --keep-bits-p 12 --keep-bits-x 8 rounds the stored momenta and positions (58 % of the disk; the recommended campaign setting); --eta-max X, --charged and --no-x store only part of the hadrons. All three tags get the same selection, so jet − background stays complete inside it. They change only what is stored: the same seeds give the same hadrons, and hadronize.py --force without them recreates the full files from the particlize file. The attributes eta_max, charged_only, positions and each dataset's keep_mantissa_bits record them; HadronFileReader.precision(i), .eta_max() and .selection() read them back. Full option list: prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/README.md.

docs.title: What an event is
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  BG["background b<br/>(MUSIC_1 fluid)"] -->|"bulk_bg, unit b:<br/>samples 0..N_bg-1"| GB["G_b^k"]
  BG --> E1["jet event i<br/>(its own MUSIC_2 fluid)"]
  BG --> E2["jet event i' (same background)"]
  E1 -->|"bulk_jet, unit i:<br/>samples 0..N-1"| J["J_i^k: bulk + wake"]
  E1 -->|"jet_frag, unit i:<br/>fragmentations 0..M-1"| F["F_i^(k mod M)"]
  • A jet event at hadron level is oversample k of bulk_jet plus fragmentation k mod M of jet_frag. Its background is sample k of bulk_bg, unit events/bg_unit of that event.
  • Oversamples are not independent collisions. The N oversamples of an event are independent Cooper–Frye samplings of one fluid. Average each event over its samples first, then over events, and take errors per event. HadronFileReader does both.
  • Events that share a background (--reuse, pT̂ windows) are correlated through it. Per-window results and jet − background are fine; spectra stitched over windows have correlated errors.
  • Correlated sampling (hadronize.py --correlated): sample k of the jet leg and sample k of its background share most hadrons, so jet − background is ~8 times less noisy at \(|\eta| < 1\). Only the paired error (the spread of the per-sample differences) is then right; jet_minus_background uses it automatically.
  • An empty surface (MUSIC stopped at the grid boundary) gives a unit with no samples; the readers skip such events.

The ROOT files have the same structure, one entry per oversample: ROOT and C++.

docs.title: 5. Provenance: the job record
docs.text:
Every job keeps its exact inputs, so a file can always be traced and reproduced:

where what <stem>.json the job summary: seed, events written, droplets, edge hits, skipped events, cross sections <stem>.xml, attribute prod_user_xml the job's XML, verbatim prod_grid_yaml the output grid prod_seed, prod_reuse, prod_hard, prod_build, prod_host seed, background reuse, hard process, software build, machine pthat_bins, pthat_bin_sigma_gen, pthat_bin_sigma_err, pthat_bin_n_accepted, pthat_bin_seeds the pT̂ windows and each window's Pythia cross section [mb], written when the job ends music_input, hadronize_xml MUSIC's input and the hadronization settings file_uuid (particlize), source_uuid (hadron files) the link between a hadron file and the run it came from: HadronFileReader refuses a mismatch

The pair files and the particlize files carry the same prod_* attributes.

docs.title: 6. Settings to check before combining files
docs.text:
None of these shows in the data arrays. Files that differ in one of them belong in different data sets:

setting why it matters where it is recorded MUSIC's late time step (Δτ 0.02 → 0.05 fm/c from τ = 3 fm/c, on by default in current images) the stored frames stay at 0.1 fm/c, so the files look alike; but the medium differs at the 10⁻³ level, the cell-level wake by ~5 % below ~1 fm. Hadron observables agree within ±2 %. Don't mix late-step and constant-step files in one training set or comparison <late_delta_tau> in the job XML (prod_user_xml); absent or 0: constant step the image or build MUSIC on the GPU and on the CPU differ at 2 × 10⁻³: one image per campaign prod_build, prod_host; the campaign's notes the output grid 64 × 64 × 32 at ±12.2 fm, or the earlier 65 × 65 × 33 at ±10 fm: never in one training set prod_grid_yaml; nx, dx, ... hadron precision and selection --keep-bits-*, --eta-max, --charged, --no-x: one setting per campaign HadronFileReader.precision(i), .eta_max(), .selection(); the reader warns on a mix correlated sampling the errors of jet − background must be paired HadronFileReader.correlated pT̂ windows, parton rapidity cut, reuse each window has its own cross section; events sharing a background are correlated pthat_bins, pthat_bin_sigma_gen, parton_ymax, prod_reuse; events/bg_unit the liquefier normalisation and the LBT double counting older pair files gave MUSIC_2 the wrong droplet energy (only a rerun fixes the jet leg) or counted absorbed LBT partons twice (fix_lbt_double_counting.py repairs the partons) pair file: liquefier_normalize_on_hydro_grid = 1 for fixed files; lbt_double_count_fix on repaired ones

The settings of every production file of a campaign:

import glob, h5py, hdf5plugin, yaml              # hdf5plugin registers the Blosc filter
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

for path in sorted(glob.glob("/path/to/campaign/**/*_particlize.h5", recursive=True)):
    with h5py.File(path, "r") as f:
        A = f.attrs
        late = ET.fromstring(A["prod_user_xml"]).findtext(".//Hydro/MUSIC/late_delta_tau")
        grid = yaml.safe_load(A["prod_grid_yaml"])["grid"]
        print(path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1], "| seed", A["prod_seed"],
              "| late_delta_tau", late.strip() if late else "absent (constant step)",
              "| grid x", grid["x"], "| reuse", A.get("prod_reuse"))

The details behind the late time step: docs/REPORT_FINAL_OPTIM.md; the liquefier normalisation: docs/SOURCE_NORMALIZATION.md.

docs.title: 7. Looking inside any file: h5_inspect.py
docs.text:
utils/h5_inspect.py prints every group and dataset with its shape, dtype, storage and attributes. For the hydro files it adds a summary that decodes the conventions: the output and MUSIC grids, the axes, the per-event freeze-out, the ragged *offsets groups with their columns, the diag/ vectors, and it flags inconsistencies. It needs only h5py and numpy, and reads nothing from the large datasets unless asked:

python utils/h5_inspect.py AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5                  # tree + summary
python utils/h5_inspect.py AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5 --no-tree        # summary only
python utils/h5_inspect.py AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5 --attr prod_user_xml   # one attribute in full
python utils/h5_inspect.py AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5 --stats --event 0      # min/max/mean, NaN/inf of event 0
python utils/h5_inspect.py AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001_hadrons_bulk_jet.h5 --json > meta.json

For the HDF5 command-line tools (h5dump, h5ls) on Blosc data, point them at the plugin: export HDF5_PLUGIN_PATH=$(python -c "import hdf5plugin; print(hdf5plugin.PLUGIN_PATH)").

docs.title: Hadrons
docs.text:
This page shows how to read the hadron files of a whole campaign as one data set, fill histograms with the right per-event statistics, pull out single events, weight pT̂ windows by their cross sections, and spot bad runs. The tool for almost all of it is HadronFileReader from jetscape.hadrons_h5; lower-level readers and the Pythonic HadronArray are at the end, for when you need one file, one sample or awkward arrays. It applies to the Au+Au jet productions (two stages or hadrons-only jobs) and the Z+jet productions; O+O hadron files made in the job are read differently (O+O).

The file layout and what an event is: What a production writes.

docs.title: 1. Open a campaign
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronFileReader

r = HadronFileReader("/path/to/campaign")       # or: with HadronFileReader(...) as r:
print(r.n_files, "files,", r.n_events, "events, tags", r.tags())

source can be:

  • a directory: every production file in it, i.e. every *_particlize.h5, and every hadrons-only job (its *_hadrons_jet_frag.h5). Subdirectories are not searched.
  • a glob pattern (quoted, of particlize or hadron files): the way to read a campaign spread over subdirectories, e.g. the per-GPU output of a multi-GPU run: HadronFileReader("/data/zjet_c00/gpu*/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5").
  • a list of stems or particlize paths.

Events are numbered globally, in the sorted order of the files: r.locate(g) gives (file index, local event), r.global_event(file, local) the reverse, and r.stems lists the files.

What it checks on open:

  • a hadron file whose recorded source_uuid is not its particlize file's file_uuid (renamed, or from another run) is refused (check_uuid=False overrides);
  • mixed precisions, η cuts, charged-only or no-position files give warnings: results are then right only for what all files hold;
  • a background that appears in two production files (two campaigns over the same seeds) gives a warning; r.duplicate_backgrounds() lists them.

docs.title: 2. Histograms, totals and the wake
docs.text:
hist, total and jet_minus_background do the statistics for you. For every event, the samples of its unit are histogrammed and divided by that unit's number of samples; these per-event means are then averaged over events. So every event counts the same, even when files were hadronized with different --oversample, and the errors are per event (compound-Poisson per event, added over events).

def lead(info):
    """phi and pseudorapidity of the event's hardest shower-initiating parton."""
    ini = info.initiators()                     # (K, 11): shower, pid, pstat, px, py, pz, E, ...
    px, py, pz = ini[np.argmax(np.hypot(ini[:, 3], ini[:, 4])), 3:6]
    return np.arctan2(py, px), np.arcsinh(pz / np.hypot(px, py))

def dphi(ev, info):                             # azimuth relative to the leading parton
    return np.mod(ev.phi - lead(info)[0] + np.pi / 2, 2 * np.pi) - np.pi / 2

def soft_charged(ev, info):
    return ev.charged & (ev.pt > 0.2) & (ev.pt < 4) & (np.abs(ev.eta) < 1)

with HadronFileReader("/path/to/campaign") as r:
    # names of EventHadrons attributes: per-event sample means, averaged over events
    pt, pt_err = r.hist("bulk_bg", "pt", np.linspace(0, 3, 31), mask="charged")
    n_mid, n_err = r.total("bulk_jet", mask=lambda ev, info: ev.charged & (np.abs(ev.eta) < 1))

    # the wake: <jet leg> - <its own background>, event by event
    bins = np.linspace(-np.pi / 2, 3 * np.pi / 2, 17)
    wake, wake_err = r.jet_minus_background(dphi, bins, mask=soft_charged)
    full, _ = r.jet_minus_background(dphi, bins, mask=soft_charged, fragments=True)  # + jet_frag
  • values, mask, weights are either names (an attribute of EventHadrons: pid, pstat, p, x, E, px, py, pz, pt, eta, y, phi, charged, sample; for mask also "charged" or a species, "pi+", "K-", "p", "pbar", "pi", "K", "p+pbar"), or callables f(ev, info) returning one value per hadron. A tuple of names (or a callable returning a tuple) gives an N-dimensional histogram.
  • Callables get the event's info (EventInfo: event, stem, local_event, bg_unit, seed, pthat_bin, pthat, n_coll, z, initiators()), which jet-relative observables need: above, Δφ to the event's leading initiator.
  • Names are faster. With names only, a background shared by several events is binned once and counted for each of them. For a callable that does not use info, pass per_event=False for the same single pass; the result is identical.
  • events= restricts any of them to a subset, e.g. one pT̂ window.
  • jet_minus_background uses only events whose jet leg and background have samples, each against its own background. fragments=True adds the jet's own hadrons.

Which error

For files hadronized with --correlated, jet_minus_background takes its error from the spread of the per-sample differences (paired=True, chosen automatically: r.correlated), the only right error when the legs share hadrons. The default compound-Poisson error treats every hadron as independent; resonance daughters in one bin make it ~20 % too small for soft multiplicities, which paired=True also avoids for independent legs with equal sample counts.

docs.title: 3. A worked example: multiplicity and spectra
docs.text:
The charged dN/dη of the background and of the jet events, the identified spectra at \(|y| < 0.5\), and the wake's charged multiplicity, for one campaign:

import numpy as np
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronFileReader

eta_e = np.linspace(-5, 5, 41)
pt_e = np.linspace(0, 3, 31)
with HadronFileReader("/path/to/campaign") as r:
    # dN_ch/deta, per event (each event: the mean over its oversamples)
    bg, bg_err = r.hist("bulk_bg", "eta", eta_e, mask="charged")
    jet, jet_err = r.hist("bulk_jet", "eta", eta_e, mask="charged")
    dndeta_bg = bg / np.diff(eta_e)

    # identified dN/dpT at |y| < 0.5 (width 1 in y)
    spectra = {}
    for s in ("pi+", "K+", "p"):
        mid_y = lambda ev, info, s=s: ev.species(s) & (np.abs(ev.y) < 0.5)
        h, e = r.hist("bulk_bg", "pt", pt_e, mask=mid_y, per_event=False)
        spectra[s] = (h / np.diff(pt_e), e / np.diff(pt_e))

    # the wake's charged hadrons at |eta| < 1, and the jet's own
    mid = lambda ev, info: ev.charged & (np.abs(ev.eta) < 1)
    wake, wake_err = r.jet_minus_background(None, None, mask=mid, per_event=False)
    n_frag, n_frag_err = r.total("jet_frag", mask=mid, per_event=False)
print("dN_ch/deta at eta = 0:", dndeta_bg[len(dndeta_bg) // 2])
print("wake N_ch(|eta| < 1):", wake[0], "+-", wake_err[0], "| fragments:", n_frag)

With values=None, bins=None, jet_minus_background returns the difference of the totals as a one-bin array. For a 2D map in the jet frame, pass a callable returning a tuple, e.g. lambda ev, info: (ev.eta - lead(info)[1], dphi(ev, info)), and a tuple of bin edges.

docs.title: 4. Single events
docs.text:
with HadronFileReader("/path/to/campaign") as r:
    ev = r.jet_event(0, 17)          # global event 0, oversample 17 + its fragmentation
    ev["pid"], ev["p"], ev["x"]      # p = (E, px, py, pz); ev["origin"]: 0 bulk, 1 fragment
    bg = r.background_event(0, 17)   # oversample 17 of the background event 0 used
    info = r.event_info(0)           # stem, local_event, bg_unit, seed, pthat_bin, initiators()
    n, m = r.n_oversamples(0), r.n_frag(0)
    for ev in r.iter_jet_events(0):  # every oversample of event 0
        ...

jet_event(e, k) pairs oversample k with fragmentation k mod n_frag(e); frag_sample= picks another, fragments=False leaves them out. These are the inputs for jet finding (Jets with FastJet).

docs.title: 5. pT̂ windows and cross sections
docs.text:
Campaigns with several pT̂ windows per background (--pthat-bins) have one Pythia, and one cross section, per window. Each window's histogram is a per-event average, so the windows can have different event counts; multiply each by its cross section to stitch them:

with HadronFileReader("/path/to/campaign") as r:
    r.pthat_bins                                   # (K, 2): the windows
    edges = np.linspace(0, 40, 41)
    spec, var = np.zeros(40), np.zeros(40)
    for k in range(len(r.pthat_bins)):
        h, e = r.hist("jet_frag", "pt", edges, mask="charged", events=r.pthat_bin_events(k))
        sigma, _ = r.pthat_bin_sigma(k)            # mb, after the parton-y cut
        spec += sigma * h                          # each window: per-event mean x its sigma
        var += (sigma * e) ** 2                    # jet_frag: windows independent

spec is then dσ/dpT per bin [mb]. pthat_bin_sigma(k) combines the files' Pythia estimates, weighted by their accepted events; pthat_bin_acceptance(k) is the parton-rapidity cut's acceptance. The windows share their backgrounds, so for the bulk tags the errors of different windows are correlated: the simple sum of variances above is right for jet_frag only.

docs.title: 6. Bad runs
docs.text:
Two rare failures show up in the data, not in the logs. Check for them before an analysis:

  • A leg that never froze out. Its background has ~3 times the freeze-out cells and ~11 times the hadrons of its jet leg. Compare n_cells_bg / n_cells_jet (particlize file's events/): wake_hadrons.py, hadron_distributions.C and the C++ HadronFileReader.h drop events where it is off by more than 20 %. In the job logs, grep -l "Maximum allowed time reached" DIR/*.log finds such jobs.
  • A job whose jets lost almost no energy (once in ~250 campaign jobs): its droplets per event fall far below the campaign's. utils/check_deposition.py reads every job summary and flags it (exit code 1):
python utils/check_deposition.py /path/to/campaign              # every <stem>.json below it
python utils/check_deposition.py /data/c1/gpu0 /data/c1/gpu1    # one campaign, two directories

Move a flagged job's files away and rerun the campaign command, which redoes the job.

docs.title: 7. Lower-level readers
docs.text:
For one file, one sample, or a whole small file in memory:

from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronFile, JetEvents, Hadrons

with HadronFile("<stem>_hadrons_bulk_jet.h5") as hf:       # random access, nothing loaded
    one = hf.sample_event(0, 17)                            # unit (event) 0, sample 17: pid, pstat, p, x
    ini = hf.initiators(0)                                  # the event's shower initiators
with JetEvents.from_stem("<stem>") as je:                   # the three files + particlize of one job
    ev = je.jet_event(0, 17)                                # bulk_jet sample 17 + a fragmentation

h = Hadrons.from_h5("<stem>_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5")            # a whole file in memory
dn, err = h.hist(h.eta, np.linspace(-1, 1, 5), mask=h.charged)   # per sample

Hadrons carries pt, eta, y, phi, charged, sample, unit as arrays (in float64, about 2.4 times the file's memory) and hist / total averaged per sample. units= reads only some units.

docs.title: The Pythonic HadronArray
docs.text:
jetscape.HadronArray holds a hadron file as flat arrays with sample offsets, without derived columns, and turns it into awkward arrays of vector four-momenta on demand, for selections and FastJet's array interface:

import jetscape as js

bulk = js.HadronArray.from_h5("<stem>_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5")
had = bulk.to_awkward(by_unit=True)            # units x samples x hadrons, Momentum4D records
charged = had[js.select(had, "charged")]
mid = abs(charged.eta) < 0.5

It needs no X-SCAPE build and also reads file objects (e.g. a file streamed from the OSDF). More in The Pythonic interface.

docs.title: 8. Scripts and notebooks for hadrons
docs.text:
what analysis/tutorials/hadron_distributions.ipynb η, φ, pT of background, background + wake, fragments and the wake, in the lab and relative to the jet; checks the correlated-sampling flags (HADRON_DIR, MAX_EVENTS, PAIRED) analysis/wake_hadrons.py + wake_hadrons.ipynb one pass over a campaign: the wake per event in the jet frame, ΔR profiles, identified spectra, totals → wake_hadrons.h5; then the figures. See Hydro and hadrons together

Threads and memory. HadronFileReader is one Python process, reading one production file at a time and only the units it needs: the four events of two seed files with 500 and 100 oversamples (~11 M hadrons) take 2.7 s. A background of 2000 oversamples is ~14 M hadrons, ~1.5 GB with the derived kinematics. For more speed, split a campaign by events= over processes.

Reading in place from the OSDF. HadronFileReader takes local paths only; download the campaign first (Data on the OSDF). Single files can be read in place with h5py or HadronArray through fsspec.

docs.title: Hydro and hadrons together
docs.text: The Au+Au and Pb+Pb jet productions store each event twice in the fluid, with and without the jet, and both legs again at hadron level. This page shows how to use that: read a hydro pair and take the difference as the wake, follow the wake through a whole campaign, connect the hadron files to the pair's events, measure the wake in hadrons, walk through one event from energy density to hadrons with jet_wake.ipynb, and judge how well hadrons made from the stored hydro history (what an FNO prediction would give) reproduce MUSIC's own. You need the pair files (<stem>.h5) for the fluid side; the hadron side needs only the particlize and hadron files.

docs.title: 1. Why a pair, and what the difference is
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  IC["one initial condition<br/>(3D MC-Glauber strings)"] --> M1["MUSIC_1<br/>background"] --> BG["arr_bg"]
  M1 --> EL["Matter + LBT<br/>in MUSIC_1's medium"] --> LQ["liquefier<br/>droplets"]
  IC --> M2["MUSIC_2<br/>same strings + droplets"] --> J["arr"]
  LQ --> M2

The jet loses energy in the background's medium (MUSIC_1); the liquefier turns what it loses into droplets, and a second MUSIC run (MUSIC_2) gets the same initial condition plus those droplets. Both legs are bit-identical until the first droplet is deposited, so \(\Delta e = e_\text{jet} - e_\text{bg}\) is the jet's effect on the medium (the wake, with its excess and its depletion) and nothing else. There are no event-by-event fluctuations to subtract, and no pairing of separate runs. The physics behind it: The physics.

Two things to keep in mind:

  • The legs freeze out at different times. The deposit reheats the jet leg, by 1–2 fm/c in 0–10 % Au+Au. After the background has frozen out, arr − arr_bg is the jet leg's whole medium: use only frames below both ntau_freezeout values.
  • The jet leg ignores late droplets. Energy deposited after MUSIC_2 has stopped never enters the fluid (diag/E_droplets_late).

docs.title: 2. Reading a pair
docs.text:
import os
import h5py, hdf5plugin, numpy as np            # hdf5plugin: without it Blosc data won't read

with h5py.File("AuAu_0_10_jet_c1_0001.h5", "r") as f:
    A = f.attrs
    x   = A["x_min"]   + A["dx"]   * np.arange(A["nx"])      # cell centres [fm]
    y   = A["y_min"]   + A["dy"]   * np.arange(A["ny"])
    eta = A["eta_min"] + A["deta"] * np.arange(A["neta"])
    tau = A["tau_min"] + A["dtau"] * np.arange(f["arr"].shape[-1])   # 0.5, 0.6, ... fm/c

    i, k = 0, 40                                   # event 0, frame tau = 4.5 fm/c
    jet = f["arr"][i, :, :, :, :, k]               # (4, nx, ny, neta): e, vx, vy, vz
    bg  = f["arr_bg"][i, :, :, :, :, k]            # the same collision without the jet
    de  = jet[0] - bg[0]                           # the wake in e [GeV/fm^3]
    live = min(f["ntau_freezeout"][i], f["ntau_freezeout_bg"][i])   # frames where both legs live

    o = f["source/offsets"]
    droplets = f["source/droplets"][o[i]:o[i + 1]]   # tau, x, y, eta, E, px, py, pz
    E_dep = droplets[:, 4].sum()                   # = diag/E_droplets[i]

    # e -> T with MUSIC's hotQCD table (columns e, P, s, T); the venv sets MUSIC_EOS_TABLE
    tab = np.fromfile(os.environ["MUSIC_EOS_TABLE"], dtype="<f8").reshape(-1, 4)
    tab = tab[np.argsort(tab[:, 0])]
    T = np.interp(jet[0], tab[:, 0], tab[:, 3])    # GeV; T_fo = 0.15 at e = 0.234
  • Read frame by frame. Each chunk is one event and one τ frame; a frame is ~2 MB.
  • The grid (cell centres, steps) is in the attributes; the production grid is 64 × 64 × 32, ±12.2 fm in x and y, ±4.84 in η_s, every 0.1 fm/c from τ = 0.5 fm/c.
  • The showers that made the droplets are in shower/, read with jetscape.showers (fates, segments, to_milne).
  • A campaign to one τ length: python contribs/PyJetscape/python/jetscape/repad_h5.py FILES grows arr and arr_bg in place (a metadata resize), for loaders that need equal shapes.
  • FNO training: FNO4d's read_3d_data_hdf5(files, h5_key="arr"/"arr_bg", unique_bg=...) reads many pair files lazily; unique_bg drops the repeated backgrounds of a reuse campaign.

docs.title: FastHydro's PairBrowser (optional)
docs.text:
With FastHydro's readers installed (setup_analysis_env.sh --with-fasthydro), a pair file opens in a browser that checks the premise and answers the common questions:

from fasthydro.browse import PairBrowser

with PairBrowser("AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5") as p:
    print(p.summary(0))      # identical IC?, first differing frame, droplets, deposited E, freeze-out times
    de = p.diff(0, 20)       # arr - arr_bg, energy density, frame 20: (nx, ny, neta)

More about FastHydro and its notebooks: FastHydro. 3D views and movies of a pair file (wake_pyvista.py, hydro_jet_particles_pyvista.py): 3D visualization.

docs.title: 3. The wake in the fluid, for a whole campaign
docs.text:
analysis/wake_observables.py reads each pair file once and writes a small wake_observables.h5; the notebook makes the figures from it alone, so a new figure never needs another pass over the data:

cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis
python wake_observables.py /path/to/campaign -j 10 -o /path/to/campaign/wake_observables.h5
WAKE_OBS=/path/to/campaign/wake_observables.h5 jupyter lab wake_observables.ipynb
table content showers per initial parton: kinematics, vertex, heading in or out of the fireball, angle to the background's ψ₂, the energy bookkeeping from the shower graph, and the medium along its path (path length above T_c, ∫T², ∫T³, ...) droplets position, four-momentum, the shower it came from, background T and v at the deposit events pT̂ window and cross section, ψ₂ and ε₂, freeze-out times, energy totals evolution P^μ and S of both legs through every τ surface (ideal-fluid T^{μν} with MUSIC's EoS), and the cumulative droplet four-momentum jetframe the stacked wake about the leading-deposit leg's source, in (Δη, Δφ)

It takes ~1 min for 300 events at -j 10, with ~0.5 GB extra per process for reading ahead. It also flags legs that never froze out (the hottest cell of a leg's last frame above 1.5 e_fo) and leaves those events out of the figures.

How faithful is the stored wake? The output grid is coarser than MUSIC's (0.3875 fm against 0.3 fm, 0.3125 against 0.2 in η_s). A comparison on 6 events (pT̂ 50–70 GeV) of the same Δe on MUSIC's grid and on the output grids found: the wake's net energy within ~1 % of MUSIC's; its shape at scales of 0.5 fm and up within ~10 %; peaks at 0.76 of MUSIC's height; and a ~30 % point-by-point loss that every resampling has, even one at MUSIC's own spacing shifted by half a cell. The background is unaffected (0.2 %). Details: docs/Wake_grid_comparison.md.

docs.title: Matching hadron files to the pair's events
docs.text:
All files of one job share its stem and its event order. Event i of the pair file is event i of the particlize file, unit i of bulk_jet and of jet_frag; its background in bulk_bg is unit events/bg_unit[i] of the particlize file (backgrounds are stored once, so their numbering is not the events'). In the pair file arr_bg[i] already resolves a shared background. HadronFileReader numbers events over the whole campaign, and its event_info leads back to the job and the local event:

import h5py, hdf5plugin, numpy as np
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronFileReader
from jetscape.particlize_h5 import ParticlizeFile

with HadronFileReader("/path/to/campaign") as r:
    for g in r.events():
        info = r.event_info(g)                         # the job (stem) and the event in it
        i = info.local_event
        with h5py.File(f"{info.stem}.h5", "r") as f:   # the pair file of the same job
            live = min(f["ntau_freezeout"][i], f["ntau_freezeout_bg"][i])
            E_dep = f["diag/E_droplets"][i]            # energy handed to MUSIC_2 [GeV]
            k = live - 1                               # the last frame where both legs live
            de = f["arr"][i, 0, ..., k] - f["arr_bg"][i, 0, ..., k]
        with ParticlizeFile(f"{info.stem}_particlize.h5") as pf:
            cells = pf.events("n_cells_bg")[i] / pf.events("n_cells_jet")[i]   # ~1, else a bad leg
        # the same event at hadron level: the wake's energy at |eta| < 1
        dE, dE_err = r.jet_minus_background(None, None, mask=lambda ev, inf: np.abs(ev.eta) < 1,
                                            weights="E", events=[g])
        print(f"event {g}: {E_dep:.1f} GeV deposited, wake in hadrons {dE[0]:.1f} +- {dE_err[0]:.1f} GeV")

docs.title: Jet minus background, in hadrons
docs.text:
At hadron level the wake is \(\langle\)bulk_jet\(\rangle - \langle\)bulk_bg\(\rangle\): each event's oversample average of its jet leg minus that of its own background, then averaged over events. HadronFileReader.jet_minus_background does exactly that, with the right error for correlated sampling (Hadrons). The jet event is that plus the fragments (fragments=True). Jet-relative observables use the event's shower initiators (info.initiators()) as the jet axis.

For a campaign, analysis/wake_hadrons.py does the same in one pass and writes wake_hadrons.h5, which wake_hadrons.ipynb turns into figures together with wake_observables.h5:

cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis
python wake_hadrons.py /path/to/campaign -j 10 -o /path/to/campaign/wake_hadrons.h5
WAKE_HAD=/path/to/campaign/wake_hadrons.h5 WAKE_OBS=/path/to/campaign/wake_observables.h5 \
  jupyter lab wake_hadrons.ipynb
  • Per event and relative to the leading initiator: the (Δη, Δφ, pT) map of charged hadrons, ΔR profiles, identified spectra at \(|y| < 1\) near and away side, and totals (N, E, pT, ...) per \(|\eta|\) band; ~3.5 min for 300 events at -j 10.
  • Correlated files (--correlated, or --common-seeds): the events of one background are not independent, so it also stores the jet leg and the wake as means over --batches (default 10) aligned blocks of samples, and the notebook takes the errors from their spread. On a 1005-event campaign with 15 events per background this cut the wake's errors 4–8 times.
  • Bad runs are checked first, from the pair file, the hadron multiplicities and the logs; flagged events are not histogrammed unless --keep-flagged.
  • Stored hadrons: with files hadronized at --eta-max, every "all η" result is only within that cut; the script records and warns about it.

What it found on a 285-event 0–10 % Au+Au campaign at pT̂ 10–40 GeV: the wake's hadrons carry 1.01 ± 0.13 ± 0.18 of the energy MUSIC_2 received; fragments (minus beam remnants) plus wake give 1.006 of the initial partons' energy. The wake has thermal chemistry and a harder spectrum than the background (⟨pT⟩ 0.85 against 0.54 GeV), peaks along both jets with no significant depletion behind them, and brings back 20 % of the leading leg's deposit inside R = 0.4 and 70 % inside 1.5. Details: analysis/README.md.

Beam remnants in the fragments

Colorless hadronization closes colour-unpaired strings with remnant quarks of \(\sqrt{s}/6\) = 33 GeV along the beam. That energy is not the jet's, and the strings to a remnant spread hadrons across all Δη, so no rapidity cut removes them. wake_hadrons.ipynb takes them out of the energy balance.

docs.title: 5. One event, end to end: jet_wake.ipynb
docs.text:
prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/jet_wake.ipynb follows one pair from the energy density to the hadrons. It needs only numpy, h5py, matplotlib and scipy (and jetscape for the hadron section):

section shows 1–3 the data, a check that both legs start identical, the dijet: several showers, several sources, each droplet assigned to a leg 4–5 Δe in the transverse plane and in (η, φ), re-centred on the jet 6–7 how big, how much, how wide; whether the front sits where a Mach cone would 8 freeze-out: the jet extends the medium's lifetime 10 the same event at hadron level: bulk_jet − bulk_bg in (Δη, Δφ) about the leading leg, the energy at ( 11 the energy balance: initial partons = surviving partons + deposited energy 
cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
WAKE_H5=/path/to/AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5 jupyter lab jet_wake.ipynb

WAKE_H5 names the pair file; the hadron section looks for <stem>_particlize.h5 and the three hadron files next to it and prints the commands that make them if they are missing. MUSIC_EOS_TABLE gives the EoS for c_s². The shipped example (seed 1) shows a Mach-cone-like pattern behind the source, a wake whose hadrons return the deposited energy within errors (18.1 ± 2.7 GeV at \(|\eta| < 1\), 24.6 ± 5.6 GeV at \(|\eta| < 2\), for 25.0 GeV deposited), and a medium lifetime extended by 1.1 fm/c. One event shows the shape and the mechanism, not an average.

docs.title: 6. Hadrons from the stored hydro history
docs.text:
The pair files keep only e, vx, vy, vz on the output grid, with no viscous fields. That is all a neural operator (FNO) trained on them would predict. Such a history can only be hadronized through a freeze-out surface found in it, sampled without viscous corrections. The study in hydro_hist_vs_surface/ measures how far those hadrons are from the correct ones: iSS on MUSIC's own surface, with π^{μν} and Π. Same events, same hadronize.py settings, same seeds; only the surface changes:

variant surface viscous corrections isolates ref MUSIC's shear + bulk δf the correct answer ref_no_shear MUSIC's, π^{μν} = 0 bulk only shear δf ref_no_bulk MUSIC's, Π = 0 shear only bulk δf ref_ideal MUSIC's, π^{μν} = Π = 0 none all of δf hist Cornelius on the stored history, T from MUSIC's EoS none + the coarse history

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
It needs an X-SCAPE build with iSS and PyJetscape (as for hadronize.py; see Source build), and a production directory made with run_prod_jet.py --write-particlize both plus its reference hadrons:

cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/hydro_hist_vs_surface
PYTHON=$(which python) ./run_study.sh /path/to/production       # all variants, resumable
HVS_SUMMARY=/path/to/production/hist_vs_surface/summary.npz jupyter lab hydro_hist_vs_surface.ipynb

run_study.sh [DATA [OUT]] builds each variant's particlize files (make_surfaces.py), hadronizes them (run_hadronize.py) and summarizes everything into one small summary.npz (analyze.py). The hadronization settings must be the reference's: pass them as HADRONIZE_OPTS if they differ from the default --oversample 100 --n-frag 50 --correlated --keep-bits-p 12 --keep-bits-x 8. Other knobs: HADRONIZE_J, VARIANTS. On the GB10 (20 cores) 4 files × 25 events took 2 h 12 min and 51 GB, most of it the surface search in the history (~31 s per leg). Because the variants keep the reference's seeds and the sampling is correlated, variant − reference is far less noisy than either.

docs.title: What it found
docs.text:
(0–10 % Au+Au, pT̂ 50–70 GeV, 100 events; shifts relative to ref, mid-rapidity.)

  • The surfaces agree to 2 %: 0.981 of MUSIC's freeze-out volume, same position and timing, but less of the fastest fluid.
  • For the bulk, the missing viscous corrections dominate, not the coarse history:
observable all δf off (ref_ideal) history on top total (hist − ref) dN_ch/dη, ( \eta <0.5) −0.4 % dN/dy p + p̄ −29.3 % +1.0 % −28.6 % ⟨pT⟩ π +13.5 % −1.2 % +12.1 % v₂{2} +6.5 % −3.0 % +3.3 % v₃{2} +21.4 % −4.9 % +15.4 %

Bulk δf sets the yields and spectral shapes, shear δf the flow harmonics. - The jet wake: δf cancels, the history loses about 10 %. ΔE at \(|\eta| < 1\) is 24.0 ± 1.2 GeV with ref and 21.5 ± 1.1 GeV with hist; the deficit is a scale, not a change of shape (per-event correlation 0.97, same Δφ shape), and is already in the surfaces. - So: dN/dη and the wake's shape can be taken from a history as it is (the wake's size ~10 % low); spectra, identified yields, ⟨pT⟩ and v_n cannot (5–30 % off, almost all of it missing δf). A single weight table w(species, pT) corrects yields and ⟨pT⟩ to within 0.3 %, one scale fixes the wake and v₂, but v₃ per event needs δf restored at the surface.

The study also lists its limits (the output grid ends at \(|\eta_s|\) = 5, where the medium is still above T_sw, so forward hadrons are missing) and next steps. Full write-up: hydro_hist_vs_surface/README.md.

docs.title: Jets with FastJet
docs.text:
This page shows how to find jets in the production hadrons with FastJet from Python: the conventions the notebooks and analyses share, the classic (SWIG) interface with jet areas and ρA background subtraction, embedding a jet into a background it never touched, charged and full jets, and the array (awkward) interface. It ends with the Z+jet, Z+hadron and dijet Δη analyses as worked examples of a complete campaign analysis. Use it once you can read hadrons (Hadrons).

What you need. scikit-hep fastjet from PyPI, which is in the analysis venv: it ships the FastJet library itself and offers both interfaces. For FastJet in C++ (ROOT macros, fjcontrib), see ROOT and C++.

docs.title: 1. Why the model's events are good for jets
docs.text:
Every Au+Au and Pb+Pb jet event comes with its twin without the jet: the background leg, the same fluid without the jet's energy (see What a production writes). Per oversample k there are three events to cluster:

event hadrons tests bkg bulk_bg sample k ρ, random cones, combinatorial (fake) jets bkg + jet bulk_bg sample k + jet_frag sample k mod n_frag embedding: the jet on a background it did not touch, ⟨δpT⟩ = 0 bkg + wake + jet bulk_jet sample k + the same jet_frag sample (r.jet_event(e, k)) the full event, with the medium response

Comparing the last two isolates what the medium response does to a jet; comparing the reconstructed jets with the fragments alone measures the subtraction.

docs.title: 2. Conventions
docs.text:
The notebooks and the snippets below use one set of choices; change them deliberately:

  • Particles: \(|\eta| < 1.5\), pT > 0.15 GeV, charged by default, clustered as massless (E = |p|), so that rapidity equals pseudorapidity and the ghosts cover the acceptance exactly.
  • Jets: anti-kT, R = 0.4, \(|\eta_\text{jet}| < 1.5 - R\); active areas with explicit ghosts (ghost area 0.005).
  • ρ: the median of pT/A of the kT jets (R = 0.4) in \(|\eta| < 1.5 - R\), without the two hardest, with set_use_area_4vector(False): the scalar area that pT − ρA uses. Without it FastJet 3 divides by the 4-vector area's transverse part, which gives a ρ about 1 GeV larger.
  • user_index tags each particle with its row in the sample; offsetting the fragment rows tells a jet's fragment content exactly.
  • Weights: every event counts once, so each oversample of an event weighs 1/(n · N_events) with n its oversamples; multiply by σ_k/N_k for cross sections (Hadrons).

Ghost positions are random

The Python bindings cannot set FastJet's ghost seed, so the ghosts get new random jitter at every clustering: areas and ρ change slightly from run to run. jet_fastjet.ipynb §4 measures by how much.

docs.title: 3. The classic interface, with ρA subtraction
docs.text:
The whole jet event of every oversample, clustered with areas, ρ from the kT jets, and the subtracted spectrum per event:

import numpy as np
import fastjet as fj
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import CHARGED, HadronFileReader

ETA_MAX, R = 1.5, 0.4
JET_DEF  = fj.JetDefinition(fj.antikt_algorithm, R)
KT_DEF   = fj.JetDefinition(fj.kt_algorithm, R)
AREA_DEF = fj.AreaDefinition(fj.active_area_explicit_ghosts, fj.GhostedAreaSpec(ETA_MAX, 1, 0.005))
RHO_SEL  = (~fj.SelectorNHardest(2)) * fj.SelectorAbsRapMax(ETA_MAX - R)
JET_SEL  = fj.SelectorAbsRapMax(ETA_MAX - R) * fj.SelectorPtMin(10.0)
CHARGED_PID = np.array(CHARGED)

def pseudojets(ev, charged=True, pt_min=0.15):
    """Massless PseudoJets of one sample; user_index = the hadron's row in the sample."""
    E, px, py, pz = np.asarray(ev["p"], dtype=np.float64).T
    pt = np.hypot(px, py)
    eta = np.arcsinh(pz / np.maximum(pt, 1e-12))
    keep = (np.abs(eta) < ETA_MAX) & (pt > pt_min)
    if charged:
        keep &= np.isin(np.abs(ev["pid"]), CHARGED_PID)
    out = []
    for i in np.flatnonzero(keep):
        pj = fj.PseudoJet(px[i], py[i], pz[i], np.hypot(pt[i], pz[i]))
        pj.set_user_index(int(i))
        out.append(pj)
    return out

r = HadronFileReader("/path/to/campaign")
pt_sub, weight = [], []
for e in r.events():
    n = r.n_oversamples(e)
    for k in range(n):
        parts = pseudojets(r.jet_event(e, k))               # bkg + wake + jet
        cs = fj.ClusterSequenceArea(parts, JET_DEF, AREA_DEF)
        bge = fj.JetMedianBackgroundEstimator(RHO_SEL, KT_DEF, AREA_DEF)
        bge.set_use_area_4vector(False)
        bge.set_particles(parts)
        rho = bge.rho()
        for jet in fj.sorted_by_pt(JET_SEL(cs.inclusive_jets())):
            pt_sub.append(jet.pt() - rho * jet.area())
            weight.append(1.0 / (n * r.n_events))           # per event: mean over its samples
spectrum, edges = np.histogram(pt_sub, np.arange(-20, 104, 4.0), weights=weight)

A raw R = 0.4 jet in a 0–10 % Au+Au event carries ρπR² of background, 25–30 GeV for charged hadrons, so the subtraction is not optional. Cost: 20 oversamples of ~7,000 hadrons (the charged ones at \(|\eta| < 1.5\) clustered), anti-kT with areas and ρ, take 0.4 s.

Charged or full jets. pseudojets(ev, charged=False) keeps neutral hadrons too: full jets need every hadron, which hadronizing with --charged would have dropped (check r.selection()). The notebooks switch with PARTICLES=charged or PARTICLES=full.

docs.title: 4. Embedding: a jet on a background it did not touch
docs.text:
Cluster the background sample plus the event's fragments, and keep track of which constituents are fragments through user_index (continuing the block above):

def embedded(r, e, k):
    """bulk_bg sample k of event e's background + the event's fragments (no wake)."""
    bg = r.background_event(e, k)
    full = r.jet_event(e, k)
    frag = full["origin"] == 1                              # 0 bulk, 1 fragment
    return {"pid": np.concatenate([bg["pid"], full["pid"][frag]]),
            "p": np.concatenate([bg["p"], full["p"][frag]])}, len(bg["pid"])

ev, n_bg = embedded(r, 0, 0)
parts = pseudojets(ev)
cs = fj.ClusterSequenceArea(parts, JET_DEF, AREA_DEF)
for jet in fj.sorted_by_pt(JET_SEL(cs.inclusive_jets())):
    frag_pt = sum(c.pt() for c in jet.constituents() if c.user_index() >= n_bg)

The reference is the jet of the fragments alone: match the embedded jet to it, and pT,emb − pT,ref is the subtraction's offset and resolution (δpT). Repeating the same with r.jet_event(e, k), the full event with the wake, shows what the medium response adds inside the cone. Random cones in r.background_event(e, k) give the background's fluctuations.

docs.title: 5. The array interface (awkward)
docs.text:
One ClusterSequence call clusters all samples of a unit in C++, with no Python loop (continuing the first block: np, CHARGED_PID, r):

import awkward as ak, vector, fastjet as fj
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronFile
vector.register_awkward()

def samples(path, unit, n=None):
    """The samples of one unit as samples * var * Momentum4D (massless)."""
    with HadronFile(path) as hf:
        u = hf.unit_index(unit)
        s0, s1 = int(hf.unit_offsets[u]), int(hf.unit_offsets[u + 1])
        s1 = s1 if n is None else min(s1, s0 + n)
        so = hf.sample_offsets[s0:s1 + 1]
        p = hf.f["hadrons/p"][so[0]:so[-1]].astype(np.float64)
        pid = hf.f["hadrons/pid"][so[0]:so[-1]]
    rec = ak.zip({"px": p[:, 1], "py": p[:, 2], "pz": p[:, 3],
                  "E": np.linalg.norm(p[:, 1:], axis=1),
                  "charged": np.isin(np.abs(pid), CHARGED_PID)}, with_name="Momentum4D")
    return ak.unflatten(rec, np.diff(so))

info = r.event_info(0)
ev = samples(f"{info.stem}_hadrons_jet_frag.h5", info.local_event)      # the jet hadrons alone
ev = ak.to_packed(ev[(abs(ev.eta) < 1.5) & (ev.pt > 0.15) & ev.charged])
cs = fj.ClusterSequence(ev, fj.JetDefinition(fj.antikt_algorithm, 0.4))  # all samples at once
jets = cs.inclusive_jets(min_pt=10.0)                                     # samples * jets
cons = cs.constituent_index(min_pt=10.0)                                  # indices into ev

jetscape.HadronArray.from_h5(path).to_awkward(by_unit=True) gives the same jagged arrays without writing samples() yourself (Hadrons).

supported yes inclusive and exclusive jets, constituents and their indices (constituent_index stands in for user_index), fjcontrib's SoftDrop, Lund declusterings, energy correlators and N-subjettiness no areas, background estimators, Selectors, user_index

So the array interface is ideal for the jet hadrons alone, for pp, and for substructure; in the heavy-ion background, use the classic interface for the subtraction, or add explicit ghosts as particles by hand, which jet_fastjet_awkward.ipynb §6 does. A batch with explicit ghosts is large: cluster it in chunks. 100 samples cluster in 0.2 s.

docs.title: 6. The notebooks
docs.text:
notebook what jet_fastjet.ipynb classic interface: the spectrum and fragmentation function of the jet hadrons alone; is the area right (tiling, πR², ghost size); ρ with and without the two hardest kT jets, random cones; the spectrum with and without ρA; embedding δpT for bkg + jet and bkg + wake + jet jet_fastjet_awkward.ipynb the same with the array interface, plus exclusive jets, SoftDrop, Lund planes, energy correlators, N-subjettiness, and areas with hand-made ghosts

Both read HADRON_DIR, MAX_EVENTS, MAX_OVERSAMPLES and PARTICLES (charged or full) from the environment:

HADRON_DIR=/path/to/campaign MAX_EVENTS=200 MAX_OVERSAMPLES=100 \
  jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis/tutorials/jet_fastjet.ipynb

docs.title: 7. Worked examples: the Z+jet campaign analyses
docs.text:
The Pb+Pb Z+jet campaigns (0–30 % Pb+Pb at 5.02 TeV, hadrons-only jobs with the Z in the event record, a pp reference from run_prod_vacuum.py) are analysed against three CMS measurements. Each is written up step by step, from the downloaded files to the figures, in Python on the HDF5 files (route A) and with C++ map steps on the ROOT files (route B, see ROOT and C++). They share a design worth copying for any campaign analysis:

  • A map step, then a final stage. The map step reads every production file once and writes a small per-file summary (a "pool" of per-event histograms, or a tree of jets); the final stage computes everything else from those summaries in seconds to minutes. A new figure never needs another pass over the hadrons.
  • A ladder of steps from the model-only ideal (using the event's twin without the jet) to an emulation of the experiment's procedure. The difference between two steps is what the added ingredient costs.
  • Jackknife errors over blocks of hydro backgrounds: events that share a background are correlated, so the blocks are backgrounds, not events.
  • Weights: the window cross section over its events, times N_coll in Pb+Pb.

Reading multi-GPU output

A campaign run on two GPUs sits in gpu0/ and gpu1/. The readers do not search subdirectories: give Python a quoted glob, "$DATA/gpu*/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5", and convert both directories into one ROOT directory for C++.

docs.title: Z+jet: CMS 1702.01060
docs.text:
Δφ_jZ, x_jZ = pT,jet/pT,Z, ⟨x_jZ⟩ and R_jZ (jet partners per Z) with anti-kT R = 0.3 jets, pT > 30 GeV, \(|\eta| < 1.6\). S are the Z–jet pairs of the Z's own event; B, the fake jets from background fluctuations, is subtracted:

step jets of the Z event (S) subtracted (B) 1 the fragments alone, smeared with CMS's resolution: the reference, a model quantity none 2 the whole event, ρA-subtracted the jets of the Z's own background (bulk_bg, sample k against sample k) 3 the whole event, ρA-subtracted the jets of 40 bulk_bg samples of the 20 other backgrounds closest in N_coll: CMS's minimum-bias mixing

Steps 2 and 3 are the model's version of the measured observable. Step 2 repeated on the embedded event (the same fragments in bulk_bg sample k, no wake) gives "what the wake does to the jets" with very small errors, since both share everything else. In short (route A):

DATA=/data/zjet_c00     # the campaign: gpu0/, gpu1/ with <stem>_hadrons_*.h5
PP=/data/zjet_pp        # the pp reference of run_prod_vacuum.py
ANA=/data/ana_c00       # the outputs (private)
cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis/zjet
./get_hepdata.sh                                                    # CMS's HEPData, once
python zjet_jets_map.py "$DATA/gpu*/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5" $ANA/jets_py/pbpb --files 0:13   # map, in slices
python zjet_jets_map.py "$PP/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5" $ANA/jets_py/pp
python zjet_jets_qa.py --pbpb $ANA/jets_py/pbpb --pp $ANA/jets_py/pp --outdir $ANA/figures --tag _c00
python zjet_jets.py --pbpb $ANA/jets_py/pbpb --pp $ANA/jets_py/pp --outdir $ANA/figures --tag _c00 --blocks 100

The map step clusters every oversample (anti-kT, explicit ghosts on a fixed grid, ρ per jet from the kT jets in a strip \(|y - y_\text{jet}| < 1\)), embeds the fragments into bulk_bg, throws random cones and clusters every background sample. On the 9,600-event campaign (2 × RTX 3090 box) it took ~0.37 s per Pb+Pb oversample in one process. Read the jet QA first (subtraction, areas, response, geometry, fakes), then pp against CMS's pp, then steps 1 to 3. Full walk-through: ANA_Zjet.md.

docs.title: Z–hadron correlations: CMS 2507.09307
docs.text:
Charged hadrons around the Z in Δφ and Δy, per Z: S (the Z with the tracks of its own event) minus B (the Z with the tracks of other Z events, 10 per Z in CMS). What remains is the Z-correlated yield: the jet's fragments at Δφ ≈ π and the medium response, including the wake's depletion near the Z. Here the model's twin makes the exact answer available:

step mode S − B 1 factorized (bulk_jet − bulk_bg) + fragments, sample by sample: the reference, compared with data directly 2 all the full event against the pooled density of all events: the closure test of the mixing method on the model 3 cms10 10 partner events from 10 other backgrounds: CMS's procedure 4 strict one Z per background, one oversample: an experiment's statistics, to compare the errors 
cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis/zjet          # DATA, PP, ANA as in the Z+jet block
python qa.py map "$DATA/gpu*/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5" $ANA/qa_py/pbpb --jobs 8      # QA, both analyses
python qa.py map "$PP/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5" $ANA/qa_py/pp
python qa.py plot --pbpb $ANA/qa_py/pbpb --pp $ANA/qa_py/pp --outdir $ANA/figures --tag _c00
python mix.py --pbpb "$DATA/gpu*/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5" --vacuum "$PP/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5" \
    --pools $ANA/pools --hists '' --jobs 8 --outdir $ANA/figures --tag _c00   # all four steps

One mix.py run writes the pools (once) and computes all four steps, the checks and the jackknife. Two details matter in the model: every hydro background has its event plane near φ = 0 (the impact parameter is always along x), so mix.py rotates each background by its own random angle (an exact symmetry; --no-rotate keeps them as produced); and steps 3 and 4 never take a partner from the Z's own background, which shares its fluid. Full walk-through: ANA_Zhadron.md; every mode written out: MIXING_MODES.md; every cut of the paper and its setting in production and analysis: README_zjet_2507.09307.md.

docs.title: The η-separated dijet wake: CMS HIN-25-012
docs.text:
CMS compared dijet–hadron correlations for dijets with a large rapidity gap (R_asym) and a small one (R_sym) to see the diffusion wake. The same analysis runs on the Z+jet campaigns with the Z as jet1 (\(|y_Z| < 1\), pT,Z > 60 GeV) and the leading R = 0.4 jet above 30 GeV as jet2. It builds on the Z–hadron pools and the jets at R = 0.4, and its final stage is dijet/deta.py:

RUNS=contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis/runs    # data/ and figures/ per campaign (git-ignored)
OPT="--pools $RUNS/zjet_c00/data/mix/pbpb --vacuum-pools $RUNS/zjet_pp/data/mix/vacuum \
   --jets $RUNS/zjet_c00/data/jets_r04 --pp-jets $RUNS/zjet_pp/data/jets_r04 --run zjet_c00"
python contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis/dijet/deta.py $OPT --tag _c00

It reports the model's truth (wake + fragments), the wake alone, the experiment-like full event, and closure contents that must come out flat, next to CMS's HEPData. With the Z as jet1 the comparison with CMS is a shape reference, not like for like. Full walk-through, including the map steps at R = 0.4: ANA_Deta.md.

Results not public yet

The Z+jet and dijet results are not public: write their outputs (--outdir, runs/) outside the repository or in its git-ignored runs/ directory.

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text: Every notebook sits next to the code or the production it belongs to; this page is the index. Each one reads its inputs from environment variables (the defaults are in its first code cell), so the same notebook runs on the shipped example files, on your own run or on a downloaded campaign. Most are committed with their outputs, so they can be read on GitHub before running anything.

docs.title: Running a notebook
docs.text:
Set the notebook's variables, then open it in Jupyter or run it headless:

source ~/.venvs/js_analysis/bin/activate                  # the analysis venv
HADRON_DIR=/path/to/campaign jupyter lab contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis/tutorials/hadron_distributions.ipynb
HADRON_DIR=/path/to/campaign jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace \
    contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis/tutorials/hadron_distributions.ipynb

The notebooks name the kernel they were saved with; in the venv choose Python 3 (ipykernel), or the kernel registered with setup_analysis_env.sh --kernel NAME (for VS Code or another JupyterLab). On the Mac, the xscape environment runs them too, from your copy of the examples (Mac (xscape wheel)).

Environments in the tables: venv = the analysis environment (no X-SCAPE, no ROOT); venv + ROOT = the same with ROOT ≥ 6.34 (ROOT and C++); X-SCAPE = an environment that runs X-SCAPE: the Mac wheel or a source build.
