docs.title: O+O
docs.text: This page is for the analysis of O+O collisions at 200 GeV with initial-state radiation, from the prod_OO_isr production: what one event is, what its per-event record holds, how to load a campaign, how to weight it (pT̂-window cross sections, N_coll), the checks to run, and recipes for multiplicity, centrality, flow from the oversamples and jets. O+O differs from the Au+Au jet production in ways that change the analysis: there is no background twin, every event is hard-triggered, and the hadrons are usually made in the job. Running the production: O+O with ISR.

docs.title: 1. What an O+O event is
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  IS["3dMCGlauber<br/>O16 positions"] --> H["PythiaIsrGun<br/>hard scattering at one binary collision"]
  H --> ISR["ISR (iMATTER),<br/>backward in time"]
  ISR --> S["strings from what<br/>the hard pair left"]
  S --> M["MUSIC<br/>one hydro per event"]
  M --> E["Matter + LBT<br/>in MUSIC's medium"]
  E --> JH["iColored:<br/>jet hadrons"]
  M --> SP["iSS:<br/>bulk hadrons"]

What matters for an analysis:

  • One MUSIC run per event, no background leg. The medium response to the jet is part of the bulk and cannot be separated from it: there is no jet − background.
  • Every event is hard-triggered: exactly one hard scattering, at a binary collision drawn uniformly. The geometry is sampled as in minimum-bias collisions within the b range, but in nature the hard-process rate grows with N_coll: weight with N_coll for the geometry of hard events (§6).
  • The hard partons' momentum is taken from the strings (the default): the bulk loses what the hard pair and its remnants carry. That biases a multiplicity-based centrality towards peripheral, more so at small N_part.
  • The jet hadrons are the whole hard nucleon pair: the dijet showered by Matter + LBT, the ISR emissions, Pythia's MPI partons and the pair's beam remnants, hadronized together by iColored. Their pstat is mostly 1000 (the gun's mark, which the shower's daughters keep); that does not mean "unshowered".
  • Events without a medium: when the hard collision is the only one, no string is made: no evolution, Matter showers in vacuum, the bulk unit is empty (has_medium 0). In 0–80 % (b < 5.6 fm) that is ~5 % of the events, mostly with N_coll = 1.
  • Centrality comes from b. For O+O at 200 GeV with this Glauber setup, the b percentiles are 10 % 1.91, 20 % 2.71, 40 % 3.84, 60 % 4.71, 80 % 5.59 fm; the production's default b < 3 fm is about 0–24 %.

docs.title: 2. The files
docs.text:
Each job writes, next to each other (stem OO_isr_<campaign>_NNNN or OO_isr_seedNNNN):

file holds when size per event <stem>_hadrons_jet_frag.h5 the jet hadrons, one sample per event; units/ with the whole event record (§3); initiators/ always (unless --no-jet-hadrons) small <stem>_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5 the bulk (iSS), N oversamples per event --bulk-hadrons N in the job, or later hadronize.py --tags bulk_bg ~13 kB per oversample <stem>_particlize.h5 MUSIC's freeze-out surface (one unit per event), the final partons, the initiators default; not with --no-particlize ~10 MB <stem>.h5 MUSIC's evolution (e, vx, vy, vz) on grid_oo.yaml, diag/ default; not with --no-hydro-file ~17 MB <stem>.json, .xml, .log the job summary (cross sections, skipped events), the job XML, the log always

The usual production setting is hadron files only (--bulk-hadrons 10 --no-particlize --no-hydro-file), 0.13 MB per event; the bulk can then not be resampled later. Download a campaign with js_osdf.py download <campaign> --what h5 (Data on the OSDF).

Unit i is event i, and HadronFileReader does not apply

Unit i of the jet file and unit i of the bulk file are the same event. Hadron files made in the job have no source_uuid, so HadronFileReader and run_h5toROOT.py, made for the Au+Au pairs, refuse them. Read them as in §5 (or with Hadrons / HadronFile / HadronArray), and convert them to ROOT as in §13.

docs.title: 3. The per-event record
docs.text:
units/ of the jet file (and of an in-job bulk file), diag/ of the hydro file and events/ of the particlize file carry the same columns:

column meaning unit, event the unit (row), the event's number in the job (skipped events leave gaps in event) pthat, pthat_bin the hard scattering's pT̂ and its window sigma_gen, sigma_err Pythia's running cross-section estimate at that event [mb]; use the per-window file attributes instead (§6) glauber_b, glauber_npart, glauber_ncoll, glauber_nstrings the geometry has_medium, hydro_row 1 if the event has a medium; its row in <stem>.h5 (−1: none) isr_sub_{E,px,py,pz}_{proj,targ}, isr_sub_E_total what the ISR handed over for subtraction from the projectile (+z) and target (−z) nucleon remnant_E_{proj,targ}, remnant_pz_{proj,targ} the hard pair's remnants, which go to the jet hadronization strings_E_total, strings_pz_net what MUSIC's strings carry (NaN without a medium) parton_y_lead, parton_pt_lead, parton_y_sub, parton_pt_sub the two hardest partons of the hard process after the ISR tau0_music MUSIC's start time n_samples, seed, n_cells per file: the unit's samples, its seed, the surface cells (bulk file)

Per event, exactly: strings_E_total + isr_sub_E_total + remnant_E_proj + remnant_E_targ = Npart √s_NN / 2.

docs.title: 4. Settings to check before combining files
docs.text:
setting why where subtract_hard_momentum 1 (default) or 0 (--no-subtraction, a reference that counts the hard pair's energy twice) attribute of every file; .json the b range, √s e.g. O+O 200 GeV, b in [0.0, 3.0] fm the system attribute MUSIC's late time step the freeze-out surface is 0.20 % larger and the bulk +0.05 % against a constant step: one setting per campaign <late_delta_tau> in the job XML (<stem>.xml, or prod_user_xml of the hydro/particlize file) energy loss Matter + LBT (current default) or Matter alone (--matter-only, and older campaigns) the eloss attribute (absent: Matter alone) jet colour handling the jet hadrons differ between campaigns with and without colour tags in the energy loss; <colour_closure> must be the same across a campaign units/colour_partons present or not; the jet_hadronization_xml attribute pT̂ windows, parton rapidity cut the cross section per window pthat_bins, pthat_bin_sigma_gen, pthat_bin_acceptance, parton_ymax bulk oversamples, hadron selection --eta-max, --charged, --no-x, --keep-bits-* n_samples, eta_max, charged_only, positions skipped events a few per campaign in older builds events_skipped in the attributes and the .json 
# the settings of every job of a campaign
import glob, h5py, hdf5plugin
for p in sorted(glob.glob("/path/to/OO_c1/**/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5", recursive=True)):
    with h5py.File(p, "r") as f:
        A = f.attrs
        windows = A["pthat_bins"].tolist() if "pthat_bins" in A else "none"
        print(p.rsplit("/", 1)[-1], "|", A["system"], "| subtraction", A["subtract_hard_momentum"],
              "| skipped", A.get("events_skipped"), "| windows", windows)

The late step is recorded only in the job XML, which hadron-only jobs keep next to the files: grep late_delta_tau OO_c1/*.xml.

docs.title: 5. Reading a campaign
docs.text:
The hadron files are small, so a whole campaign fits in memory as flat arrays: one event table, and one array per hadron quantity with the global event index and the sample of each hadron:

import glob
import h5py, hdf5plugin, numpy as np
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import CHARGED, pseudorapidity

def read(path):
    """units/ and the hadrons of one file; 'event' = the unit's position, 'sample' within it."""
    with h5py.File(path, "r") as f:
        units = {k: f["units"][k][:] for k in f["units"]}
        attrs = dict(f.attrs)
        so, uo = f["hadrons/sample_offsets"][:], f["hadrons/unit_offsets"][:]
        p, pid = f["hadrons/p"][:].astype(np.float64), f["hadrons/pid"][:]
    n_had = np.diff(so)
    unit_of_sample = np.repeat(np.arange(len(uo) - 1), np.diff(uo))
    h = {"event": np.repeat(unit_of_sample, n_had),
         "sample": np.repeat(np.arange(len(n_had)) - uo[:-1][unit_of_sample], n_had),
         "pid": pid, "E": p[:, 0], "px": p[:, 1], "py": p[:, 2], "pz": p[:, 3]}
    return units, attrs, h

def load(campaign):
    """Every finished job (its .json) of a campaign: one event table, bulk and jet hadrons."""
    stems = sorted(p[:-5] for p in glob.glob(f"{campaign}/**/*.json", recursive=True))
    ev, bulk, jet, n0 = [], [], [], 0
    for i, stem in enumerate(stems):
        u, attrs, hj = read(f"{stem}_hadrons_jet_frag.h5")      # the event record: always here
        ub, _, hb = read(f"{stem}_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5")          # in the job or hadronize.py
        assert len(ub["unit"]) == len(u["unit"])                # unit i = event i in both
        u["n_samples_jet"] = u.pop("n_samples")
        u["n_samples_bg"] = ub["n_samples"]                     # 0: no medium
        u["file"] = np.full(len(u["unit"]), i)
        for k in ("pthat_bin_sigma_gen", "pthat_bin_n_accepted"):   # per window, this file
            u[k] = np.tile(np.atleast_1d(attrs.get(k, np.nan)), (len(u["unit"]), 1))
        hj["event"] += n0
        hb["event"] += n0
        ev.append(u), jet.append(hj), bulk.append(hb)
        n0 += len(u["unit"])
    cat = lambda parts: {k: np.concatenate([x[k] for x in parts]) for k in parts[0]}
    ev, bulk, jet = cat(ev), cat(bulk), cat(jet)
    for h in (bulk, jet):
        h["pt"] = np.hypot(h["px"], h["py"])
        h["eta"] = pseudorapidity(np.stack([h["E"], h["px"], h["py"], h["pz"]], axis=1))
        h["phi"] = np.arctan2(h["py"], h["px"])
        h["charged"] = np.isin(np.abs(h["pid"]), CHARGED)
    return ev, bulk, jet

ev, bulk, jet = load("/path/to/OO_c1")
n_ev = len(ev["unit"])

On a test campaign (2,991 events, 10 bulk oversamples) this loads 5.5 M bulk and 0.35 M jet hadrons in ~1 s. Only finished jobs (with a .json) are read, so it also works while a campaign runs.

The Pythonic alternative: jetscape.HadronArray.from_h5(path).to_awkward(by_unit=True) gives events × oversamples × hadrons as awkward arrays; the notebook pythonic/oo_analysis.ipynb does an O+O analysis that way, streaming the files of a public test run from the OSDF (The Pythonic interface).

docs.title: 6. Weights and statistics
docs.text:
Cross sections. Each pT̂ window is its own Pythia; each file records per window pthat_bin_sigma_gen [mb] (after the parton-rapidity cut) and pthat_bin_n_accepted. Combine the files weighted by their accepted events:

first = np.unique(ev["file"], return_index=True)[1]          # one row per file
sig, n_acc = ev["pthat_bin_sigma_gen"][first], ev["pthat_bin_n_accepted"][first]
sigma_k = (n_acc * sig).sum(0) / n_acc.sum(0)                 # mb per window
k = ev["pthat_bin"]
N_k = np.bincount(k, minlength=len(sigma_k))                  # events per window

w_hard = sigma_k[k] / N_k[k]             # sum over events = sigma of the hard process [mb]
SIGMA_NN = 42.0                          # mb, inelastic NN at 200 GeV
w_coll = ev["glauber_ncoll"] * sigma_k[k] / SIGMA_NN / N_k[k]   # per O+O collision in the b range
weight normalises to use none (per event, per window) per hard event of that window shapes and ratios within a window w_hard dσ/dX of the hard process [mb], summed over windows spectra stitched over windows w_coll the yield per O+O collision in the b range, assuming the hard rate ∝ N_coll σ_k/σ_NN comparisons with measured per-event yields; ratios to a p+p reference ev["glauber_ncoll"] alone the geometry of hard events ⟨N_part⟩, multiplicities "for events with a jet"

The N_coll weight matters because the events are hard-triggered with one hard scattering whatever the geometry: unweighted, peripheral events are over-represented. In the 0–80 % test campaign it moves the bulk's dN_ch/dη at \(|\eta| < 0.5\) from 28.3 (unweighted) to 36.7 (N_coll-weighted).

Statistics.

  • Events are independent: there is no shared background. Different windows are independent samples.
  • The bulk oversamples of one event sample one fluid: average each event over its samples (n_samples_bg), then over events, and take errors from the spread of the per-event values.
  • The jet hadrons are one sample per event. Combining them with each bulk oversample makes N correlated copies of the event: weight each by 1/N.
  • n_samples_bg is 0 for events without a medium: their bulk is empty, not missing. Keep them unless the analysis needs a medium.

docs.title: 7. Checks
docs.text:
E_beam = ev["glauber_npart"] * 200.0 / 2                     # Npart sqrt(s_NN) / 2
E_sum = (ev["strings_E_total"] + ev["isr_sub_E_total"]
         + ev["remnant_E_proj"] + ev["remnant_E_targ"])
med = ev["has_medium"] == 1                                  # no medium: strings_E_total is NaN
print(np.max(np.abs(E_sum[med] - E_beam[med]) / E_beam[med]))   # test campaign: 3e-9
print("without a medium:", 1 - med.mean())                   # 4.9 % in 0-80 %
  • Skipped events: events_skipped in every file's attributes and the .json (with the error).
  • The b range: glauber_b must stay inside the system attribute's range.
  • Windows: np.bincount(ev["pthat_bin"]) should be about equal (event i uses window i mod K).

docs.title: 8. Multiplicity and spectra
docs.text:
Per event: the bulk's sample mean plus the event's jet hadrons:

n_samp = ev["n_samples_bg"]
mid_b = bulk["charged"] & (np.abs(bulk["eta"]) < 0.5)
mid_j = jet["charged"] & (np.abs(jet["eta"]) < 0.5)
dn_bulk = np.bincount(bulk["event"][mid_b], minlength=n_ev) / np.maximum(n_samp, 1)
dn_jet = np.bincount(jet["event"][mid_j], minlength=n_ev)
dndeta = dn_bulk + dn_jet                                    # |eta| < 0.5: width 1
w = ev["glauber_ncoll"]
mean = np.average(dndeta, weights=w)                         # test campaign: 36.7
err = np.sqrt(np.sum(w**2 * (dndeta - mean)**2)) / w.sum()

A pT spectrum is the same with np.histogram(..., weights=1/n_samp[event]) per hadron and the event weights on top; hard_sub_compare.ipynb has a complete, weighted version with errors from the per-event spread.

docs.title: 9. Centrality
docs.text: An experiment classifies events by a multiplicity, not by b. hard_sub_compare.ipynb §2 shows how: an estimator from charged hadrons at \(3.1 < |\eta| < 3.9\) (like RHIC's beam-beam counters), from one bulk sample (one collision's fluctuations) plus the jet hadrons; class boundaries from a reference without a hard scattering's effect; then each event classified by what an experiment would count. The hard-momentum subtraction makes events with a hard scattering look more peripheral, the more so at small N_part: compare classes defined this way, not by b, with data.

docs.title: 10. Flow from the oversamples
docs.text:
Pairs of hadrons from different oversamples of one event correlate only through the fluid (its flow and geometry): no resonance-decay or momentum-conservation pairs within one sample. That gives v_n{2} of the events' own fluids, without that non-flow:

def vn2(h, n, n_samples, mask):
    """v_n{2} from pairs of hadrons in different oversamples of the same event."""
    m = mask & (n_samples[h["event"]] >= 2)
    e, s, q = h["event"][m], h["sample"][m], np.exp(1j * n * h["phi"][m])
    key = e * 100000 + s                                     # (event, sample)
    uk, inv = np.unique(key, return_inverse=True)
    Qs = np.bincount(inv, weights=q.real) + 1j * np.bincount(inv, weights=q.imag)
    Ms = np.bincount(inv).astype(float)
    ev_of = uk // 100000
    Q = np.bincount(ev_of, weights=Qs.real) + 1j * np.bincount(ev_of, weights=Qs.imag)
    M = np.bincount(ev_of, weights=Ms)
    num = np.abs(Q)**2 - np.bincount(ev_of, weights=np.abs(Qs)**2)   # sum over a != b of Q_a Q_b*
    den = M**2 - np.bincount(ev_of, weights=Ms**2)                    # number of such pairs
    ok = den > 0
    return np.sqrt(num[ok].sum() / den[ok].sum())

sel = bulk["charged"] & (np.abs(bulk["eta"]) < 1) & (bulk["pt"] > 0.2) & (bulk["pt"] < 3)
v2 = vn2(bulk, 2, ev["n_samples_bg"], sel)       # test campaign (0-80 %, unweighted): 0.031
  • The pairs are weighted by their number; for an N_coll-weighted average, weight num and den per event.
  • Ten oversamples give ~45 sample pairs per event, enough for v₂; v₃ needs more oversamples.
  • A pseudorapidity gap between the two hadrons (as in data) is a mask on each sample's Q.

docs.title: 11. Jets
docs.text:
The full event at hadron level is one bulk oversample plus the jet hadrons. Clustering bulk sample 0 with them:

import fastjet as fj
JET_DEF = fj.JetDefinition(fj.antikt_algorithm, 0.4)

def pseudojets(h, idx):        # massless, as on the FastJet page
    return [fj.PseudoJet(px, py, pz, np.hypot(pt, pz))
            for px, py, pz, pt in zip(h["px"][idx], h["py"][idx], h["pz"][idx], h["pt"][idx])]

acc_b = bulk["charged"] & (np.abs(bulk["eta"]) < 1.5) & (bulk["pt"] > 0.15) & (bulk["sample"] == 0)
acc_j = jet["charged"] & (np.abs(jet["eta"]) < 1.5) & (jet["pt"] > 0.15)
by_b = np.split(np.flatnonzero(acc_b), np.searchsorted(bulk["event"][acc_b], np.arange(1, n_ev)))
by_j = np.split(np.flatnonzero(acc_j), np.searchsorted(jet["event"][acc_j], np.arange(1, n_ev)))
lead_pt = np.zeros(n_ev)
for e in range(n_ev):
    parts = pseudojets(bulk, by_b[e]) + pseudojets(jet, by_j[e])
    jets = fj.sorted_by_pt(fj.SelectorAbsRapMax(1.1)(
        fj.ClusterSequence(parts, JET_DEF).inclusive_jets(5.0)))
    lead_pt[e] = jets[0].pt() if jets else 0.0
  • Background: the O+O bulk is small; ρA subtraction works as in Jets with FastJet (areas with explicit ghosts, ρ from kT jets).
  • All oversamples: cluster bulk sample k plus the jet hadrons for every k and weight each by 1/N: the jet hadrons are the same in all of them.
  • Relative to the hard partons: the initiators of event (file i, unit u) are in the jet file, HadronFile(path).initiators(u) → (K, 11), columns shower, pid, pstat, px, py, pz, E, x, y, z, t; the two hardest partons after the ISR are also in parton_{y,pt}_{lead,sub}.
  • A p+p reference with the same chain (ISR, Matter in vacuum, iColored) is not part of the production.

docs.title: 12. The hydro and particlize files
docs.text:
With the default outputs:

  • <stem>.h5: arr (nevents, 4, 64, 64, 32, ntau) on grid_oo.yaml (x, y ±9.84 fm and η_s ±4.84 in steps of 0.3125), τ = 0.5 + k · 0.1 fm/c, diag/ with the record of §3. Only events with a medium have a row: an event's row is its hydro_row. Read it as the Au+Au pair files (Hydro and hadrons together), without arr_bg.
  • <stem>_particlize.h5: surface/bg (one unit per event), the final partons and the initiators; ParticlizeFile reads it. It is the input for more bulk hadrons later, in the container or an X-SCAPE build:
contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/run_hadronize.py /work/OO_c1 -j 8 --tags bulk_bg --oversample 100

hadronize.py refuses jet_frag on these files: the O+O jet hadrons are made in the job.

docs.title: 13. ROOT
docs.text:
run_h5toROOT.py and HadronFileReader.h expect the Au+Au layout (they stop on O+O with KeyError: 'seed'). For O+O, convert each tag with the single-file converter and write the event record next to it:

import glob, subprocess, sys
import h5py, hdf5plugin, numpy as np, uproot

CONV = "contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/root_export/hadrons_to_root.py"
for jf in sorted(glob.glob("/path/to/OO_c1/**/*_hadrons_jet_frag.h5", recursive=True)):
    stem = jf[: -len("_hadrons_jet_frag.h5")]
    for tag in ("bulk_bg", "jet_frag"):                     # one ntuple per tag, one entry per sample
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, CONV, f"{stem}_hadrons_{tag}.h5",
                        "-o", f"{stem}_{tag}.root", "--no-x"], check=True)
    with h5py.File(jf, "r") as f:                           # the event record (jet file)
        ev = {k: f["units"][k][:] for k in f["units"]}
        win = {k: np.atleast_1d(f.attrs[k]) for k in ("pthat_bin_sigma_gen", "pthat_bin_n_accepted")
               if k in f.attrs}
    with h5py.File(f"{stem}_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5", "r") as f:  # unit i = event i in both files
        ev["n_samples_bg"] = f["units/n_samples"][:]
    ev["n_samples_jet"] = ev.pop("n_samples")
    with uproot.recreate(f"{stem}_events.root") as out:
        out["events"] = {k: v.astype(np.float64 if v.dtype.kind == "f" else np.int64)
                         for k, v in ev.items()}
        if win:
            out["windows"] = {k: v.astype(np.float64) for k, v in win.items()}

It writes, per job, <stem>_bulk_bg.root and <stem>_jet_frag.root (one entry per sample: event, unit, sample, pid[n], pstat[n], E/px/py/pz[n]) next to the inputs, and <stem>_events.root (events, one entry per unit; windows). An RDataFrame macro for the N_coll-weighted bulk dN_ch/dη on these files is docs/analysis_snippets/oo_dndeta.C: root -l -b -q 'oo_dndeta.C+("/path/OO_c1/OO_isr_c1_0001")'. More on ROOT: ROOT and C++.

notebook what prod_OO_isr/oo_isr_overview.ipynb one job: the medium at three τ with the freeze-out contour and the dijet; η, φ, pT and Δφ to the leading parton of bulk and jet hadrons (OO_STEM, XSCAPE_BUILD for the EoS) prod_OO_isr/hard_sub_compare/hard_sub_compare.ipynb two campaigns with and without the hard-momentum subtraction: the centrality bias, dN/dη, dE/dη and spectra of bulk and jet hadrons, energy against the parton pT; N_coll-weighted (HSC_DIR) pythonic/oo_analysis.ipynb the O+O hadron files of a public test run, streamed from the OSDF: event record, awkward views, spectra, jets with FastJet (OO_DIR for local copies)

docs.title: ROOT and C++
docs.text: Most analyses in the field are written in ROOT. This page shows how to turn a hadronized campaign into ROOT files, read them with or without ROOT (uproot, RDataFrame), loop over events in C++ with the header-only HadronFileReader.h, cluster jets with FastJet's C++ library, and run the C++ map steps of the Z+jet analyses. The ROOT files hold the hadrons and the event information only; the hydro stays in HDF5 (read it with h5py, also from PyROOT).

docs.title: 1. Set up
docs.text:
need environment converting (run_h5toROOT.py), reading with uproot the analysis venv; it writes with uproot, or with ROOT when PyROOT imports RDataFrame, the macros, HadronFileReader.h, PyROOT ROOT ≥ 6.34 (RNTuple) next to the venv FastJet in C++ conda-forge fastjet-cxx (FastJet, fastjet-config) and fastjet-contrib (fjcontrib) in the ROOT env

conda gives ROOT and its Python, and the venv is made from that Python:

conda create -n root -c conda-forge "root>=6.34"           # RNTuple needs ROOT >= 6.34
conda activate root
conda install -c conda-forge fastjet-cxx fastjet-contrib   # only for FastJet in C++
./utils/analysis_env/setup_analysis_env.sh ~/.venvs/js_analysis_root --system-site-packages

Then source ~/.venvs/js_analysis_root/bin/activate has PyROOT. For the root prompt and compiled macros, conda activate root first: without it ACLiC does not find the system headers ('assert.h' file not found). Details: Analysis environment.

docs.title: 2. Convert a campaign: run_h5toROOT.py
docs.text:
run_h5toROOT.py turns every hadronized production file into one ROOT file, plus one campaign file:

cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
python run_h5toROOT.py /path/to/campaign -j 4                        # RNTuple, next to the inputs
python run_h5toROOT.py /path/to/campaign -j 4 --format ttree         # TTree, for ROOT < 6.34
python run_h5toROOT.py /path/to/campaign -j 4 --out-dir root --no-x --charged --eta-max 1
python run_h5toROOT.py /path/to/campaign --dry-run                   # the plan only
python run_h5toROOT.py /data/c00/gpu0 /data/c00/gpu1 -j 8 --out-dir /data/root/c00   # several directories into one
option -j N files in parallel; ~80 B per hadron of the largest tag each (~3.5 GB for a 15-event file at 400 oversamples) --format {rntuple,ttree} RNTuple (default): 0.9 × the HDF5 size, ~1.8 times faster to read than a TTree; needs ROOT ≥ 6.34 to read --writer {auto,root,uproot} auto: ROOT if PyROOT imports (16–24 % smaller files), else uproot --out-dir DIR where the ROOT files go (default: next to the inputs) --no-x, --charged, --eta-max X leave out positions (40 % of the bytes), neutral hadrons, ( --tags a subset of bulk_jet,bulk_bg,jet_frag --campaign-file NAME / none the campaign file's name, or none --force redo files already converted

A file is converted once its particlize file and every tag's hadron file are complete (hadrons-only jobs: their hadron files). Outputs are written to .part and renamed, so rerunning finishes an interrupted pass and skips what is done. The 20-file test campaign took 2 min 40 s at -j 4.

Check a conversion against the HDF5 files, every hadron bit for bit, the event record, the windows and the cross sections (exit 1 on a difference):

python root_export/check_h5_vs_root.py /path/to/campaign /path/to/root --campaign /path/to/root/c1_campaign.root

docs.title: What is in the files
docs.text:
Per production file, <stem>_hadrons.root:

object one entry per content bulk_jet, bulk_bg, jet_frag oversample event, unit, sample, bg_unit, n, pid[n], pstat[n], E/px/py/pz[n] (GeV), t/x/y/z[n] (fm; not with --no-x) events event the particlize file's events/, sigma_file_mb, n_samples_*, seed_*, the initiators ini_*[...] windows pT̂ window pthat_lo/hi, this file's sigma_mb, sigma_err_mb, acceptance, counts provenance – JSON: every setting, seed, XML and EoS behind the file

<campaign>_campaign.root: windows with the campaign's sigma_mb, sigma_err_mb, acceptance, n_events and weight_mb = sigma_mb / n_events; files with event_offset per file (global event = event_offset[file] + event, the numbering of the Python HadronFileReader); provenance.

Why one entry per oversample: one entry per event would hold ~2.8 M hadrons at 400 oversamples, and one entry per hadron loses the event. One entry per oversample reads like an MC event. Remember that the oversamples of an event are samplings of one fluid, not independent events (What a production writes).

One file at a time. root_export/hadrons_to_root.py <stem>_hadrons_<tag>.h5 -o out.root converts a single hadron file (the same --format, --writer, --no-x, --eta-max, --charged options); the O+O files are converted that way (O+O). The format study behind the defaults: root_export/README.md.

docs.title: 3. Reading without ROOT: uproot
docs.text:
import uproot, awkward as ak, numpy as np

f = uproot.open("AuAu_0_10_jet_c1_0001_hadrons.root")
jet = f["bulk_jet"].arrays(["event", "sample", "pid", "px", "py", "pz"], entry_stop=100)
pt = np.hypot(jet.px, jet.py)                     # jagged: samples * hadrons
ev = f["events"].arrays()                         # awkward: the ini_* columns are jagged
ini_pt = np.hypot(ev.ini_px, ev.ini_py)
c = uproot.open("pth10-40_c1_campaign.root")
if "windows" in c:                                # pT-hat-window campaigns only
    w = c["windows"].arrays(["sigma_mb", "weight_mb"])
  • Read events as awkward (the default): library="np" fails on the jagged initiator columns.
  • np.isin does not take jagged arrays; flatten and unflatten for a species mask:
CHARGED = [211, 321, 2212, 3222, 3112, 3312, 3334, 11, 13]        # jetscape.hadrons_h5.CHARGED
b = f["bulk_jet"].arrays(["event", "pid", "px", "py", "pz"])
eta = np.arcsinh(b.pz / np.hypot(b.px, b.py))
charged = ak.unflatten(np.isin(np.abs(ak.flatten(b.pid)), CHARGED), ak.num(b.pid))
n_mid = ak.sum(charged & (abs(eta) < 1), axis=1)  # charged at |eta| < 1, per oversample
  • In the venv, uproot also reads files in place over osdf://, e.g. uproot.open("osdf:///fno4hic/<campaign>/<file>.root") (Data on the OSDF).

docs.title: RDataFrame
docs.text:
A cross-section-weighted spectrum of the jet leg, every event the mean over its oversamples:

ROOT::RDataFrame w("windows", "pth10-40_c1_campaign.root");
auto wt = *w.Take<double>("weight_mb");             // per window
ROOT::RDataFrame ev("events", "RUN_0001_hadrons.root");
auto nsamp = *ev.Take<int>("n_samples_jet");        // per event
auto bin   = *ev.Take<int>("pthat_bin");
ROOT::RDataFrame jet("bulk_jet", "RUN_0001_hadrons.root");
auto h = jet.Define("w", [&](int e) { return wt[bin[e]] / nsamp[e]; }, {"event"})
            .Define("pt", "sqrt(px*px + py*py)")
            .Histo1D({"pt", "", 100, 0, 5}, "pt", "w");

TTree and RNTuple read the same way. ROOT::EnableImplicitMT(n) runs it on n threads.

docs.title: HadronFileReader.h
docs.text:
analysis_root/HadronFileReader.h is the header-only C++ counterpart of the Python reader. It finds an event's entries in the three ntuples and returns their hadrons as std::vector<Hadron>:

call the hadrons of r.bkg(e, k) the background (MUSIC_1): sample k of the background event e used r.bkg_dep(e, k) the jet leg (MUSIC_2): background + deposition r.bkg_dep_frag(e, k) the whole jet event: bkg_dep(e, k) + fragmentation k mod n_frag(e) r.frag(e, j) fragmentation j of the surviving partons 
#include "HadronFileReader.h"
using namespace hadrons_root;

HadronFileReader r("/path/to/campaign");    // every *_hadrons.root, + its *_campaign.root
r.set_charged_eta(1.0);                     // optional filter while reading
for (long e : r.select_events()) {          // hadronized events, flagged ones left out
  const EventInfo &info = r.info(e);        // pthat_bin, bg_unit, initiators, leading(), weight_mb
  const int n = r.n_oversamples(e);
  for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k)
    for (const Hadron &h : r.bkg_dep_frag(e, k)) { /* h.pt(), h.eta(), h.phi(), h.p4(), h.origin */ }
}
  • Source: a directory (without its subdirectories) or one *_hadrons.root file, or a std::vector<std::string> of files. For multi-GPU output, convert all subdirectories into one directory with --out-dir.
  • EventInfo: pthat_bin, pthat, bg_unit, sample and cell counts, weight_mb, the initiators and leading(), n_coll, the trigger Z (z), and flagged(): the background has more than 20 % more or fewer freeze-out cells than the jet leg, so one surface is not a freeze-out surface. select_events() leaves those out.
  • Normalisation: a hadron of bkg_dep or bkg_dep_frag weighs w_e / n_oversamples(e), of bkg w_e / n_bg_samples(e), of frag w_e / n_frag(e), with w_e = 1/N per event or σ_k / N_k for the cross section. Errors per event, not per sample; for --correlated files pair bkg_dep(e, k) with bkg(e, k).
  • Cross sections: sigma_mb(k), weight_mb(k) come from the campaign file, or are combined from the files' windows tables when there is none.
  • PyROOT: ROOT.gInterpreter.Declare('#include "/path/HadronFileReader.h"'), then ROOT.hadrons_root.HadronFileReader(...).
  • Speed: the whole jet event of every oversample of one event with 500 oversamples (3.5 M hadrons) takes 0.24 s compiled. It gives the same hadrons as the Python reader on the HDF5 files, event by event.

docs.title: The macros
docs.text:
cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis_root
root -l -b -q 'read_hadrons.C+("/path/to/campaign")'                       # per event
root -l -b -q 'read_hadrons.C+("/path/to/campaign", -1, true)'             # dsigma/dX [mb]
root -l -b -q 'hadron_distributions.C+("/path/to/campaign", -1, false, true, 1.0, "out.root", 8)'
macro what read_hadrons.C the reader by example: pT spectra and Δφ to the leading initiator, per source (bkg, bkgdep, full, frag) and for the wake (bkgdep − bkg). Arguments: dir, window = -1, xsec = false, eta_cut = 1.0, out, max_samples = -1 read_hadrons.ipynb the same, one step per cell, in ROOT's C++ notebook kernel (HADRON_DIR, HADRON_OUT, MAX_SAMPLES); needs pip install metakernel in the env hadron_distributions.C η, φ, pT of every source and of the wake, with RDataFrame, multithreaded. Arguments: dir, window = -1, xsec = false, charged = true, eta_cut = 1.0, out, threads = 1, keep_flagged = false

hadron_distributions.C reproduces HadronFileReader.hist / jet_minus_background on the HDF5 files bin for bin: a 285-event campaign takes 21 s with 8 threads, against ~6 min in Python. Its errors are those of independent sampling; for the paired error of correlated files use the Python jet_minus_background. Full reference: analysis_root/README.md.

docs.title: 5. FastJet in C++
docs.text:
With FastJet's C++ library next to ROOT, HadronFileReader.h hands the hadrons straight to FastJet. This macro clusters the whole jet event of every oversample with the conventions of Jets with FastJet and fills the raw and ρA-subtracted spectrum:

// jets_fastjet.C: anti-kT jets with rho*A subtraction on the ROOT files of run_h5toROOT.py
#include "HadronFileReader.h"

#include <fastjet/ClusterSequenceArea.hh>
#include <fastjet/Selector.hh>
#include <fastjet/tools/JetMedianBackgroundEstimator.hh>

#include <TFile.h>
#include <TH1D.h>

void jets_fastjet(const char *dir = "out_root", double eta_max = 1.5, double R = 0.4,
                  int max_samples = 20) {
  using namespace hadrons_root;
  HadronFileReader r(dir);
  r.set_charged_eta(eta_max);                    // charged hadrons at |eta| < eta_max only

  const fastjet::JetDefinition jet_def(fastjet::antikt_algorithm, R);
  const fastjet::JetDefinition kt_def(fastjet::kt_algorithm, R);
  const fastjet::AreaDefinition area_def(fastjet::active_area_explicit_ghosts,
                                         fastjet::GhostedAreaSpec(eta_max, 1, 0.005));
  const fastjet::Selector rho_sel =
      (!fastjet::SelectorNHardest(2)) * fastjet::SelectorAbsRapMax(eta_max - R);
  const fastjet::Selector jet_sel =
      fastjet::SelectorAbsRapMax(eta_max - R) * fastjet::SelectorPtMin(5.0);

  TH1D h_raw("h_raw", ";p_{T,jet} (GeV);dN_{jet}/dp_{T} per event", 60, -20, 100);
  TH1D h_sub("h_sub", ";p_{T,jet} - #rho A (GeV);dN_{jet}/dp_{T} per event", 60, -20, 100);

  const std::vector<long> events = r.select_events();      // hadronized, flagged ones out
  for (long e : events) {
    const int n = std::min(r.n_oversamples(e), max_samples);
    const double w = 1.0 / (double(events.size()) * n);    // per event: mean over its samples
    for (int k = 0; k < n; ++k) {
      std::vector<fastjet::PseudoJet> parts;
      for (const Hadron &h : r.bkg_dep_frag(e, k))           // bulk (bkg + wake) + fragments
        if (h.pt() > 0.15) parts.emplace_back(h.px, h.py, h.pz, h.p());   // massless
      fastjet::ClusterSequenceArea cs(parts, jet_def, area_def);
      fastjet::JetMedianBackgroundEstimator bge(rho_sel, kt_def, area_def);
      bge.set_use_area_4vector(false);                       // rho = median of pT / A
      bge.set_particles(parts);
      const double rho = bge.rho();
      for (const fastjet::PseudoJet &jet : jet_sel(cs.inclusive_jets())) {
        h_raw.Fill(jet.pt(), w);
        h_sub.Fill(jet.pt() - rho * jet.area(), w);
      }
    }
  }
  h_raw.Scale(1.0, "width");
  h_sub.Scale(1.0, "width");
  TFile out("jets_fastjet.root", "RECREATE");
  h_raw.Write();
  h_sub.Write();
}

The file is in docs/analysis_snippets/, with jets_main.cxx, a main that calls it.

ACLiCg++ 
conda activate root                         # the env with ROOT and fastjet-cxx
AR=/path/to/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis_root
root -l -b -q \
  -e "gSystem->AddIncludePath(\"-I$AR -I$CONDA_PREFIX/include\"); gSystem->Load(\"libfastjet\"); gSystem->Load(\"libfastjettools\")" \
  'jets_fastjet.C+("/path/to/campaign")'

cd docs/analysis_snippets                   # jets_main.cxx includes jets_fastjet.C; AR as in the ACLiC tab
g++ -O2 -std=c++17 -I$AR jets_main.cxx $(root-config --cflags --libs) \
    $(fastjet-config --cxxflags) $(fastjet-config --libs) -lROOTNTuple -o jets
./jets /path/to/campaign
  • fastjet-config takes one query at a time: --cxxflags and --libs separately.
  • fjcontrib: add -lfastjetcontribfragile (conda-forge fastjet-contrib) and include e.g. <fastjet/contrib/SoftDrop.hh> or ConstituentSubtractor.hh; in a macro, gSystem->Load("libfastjetcontribfragile").
  • Cross sections: replace w with info.weight_mb / n (or r.sigma_mb(k) / N_k / n for a subset of events, as read_hadrons.C does).
  • Embedding: cluster r.bkg(e, k) plus r.frag(e, k % r.n_frag(e)) for the jet on a background it did not touch; the fragments have Hadron::origin == kFrag, which can go into the PseudoJets' user_index.
  • One event with 20 oversamples of ~7,000 hadrons took 21 s, ACLiC compilation included, on the GB10.

docs.title: 6. The Z+jet analyses in C++
docs.text:
analysis_root/zjet/ holds the C++ map steps of the Z+jet analyses (Jets with FastJet). Each has a Python twin and agrees with it value for value; the final stage is the same Python for both:

program map step output per production file zqa the QA: a table per Z event and per-source hadron histograms <stem>_qa.root, drawn by qa.py plot zhadron_pools the Z–hadron pool (CMS 2507.09307) <stem>_pool.root, read by mix.py --pbpb-pools zjets every oversample clustered with FastJet, ρA-subtracted, with embedding and random cones (CMS 1702.01060) <stem>_jets.root, read by zjet_jets.py 
# DATA (the campaign), PP (the pp reference) and ANA (the outputs) as on the FastJet page
cd contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis_root/zjet && make     # root-config and fastjet-config on PATH
P=../../prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
python $P/run_h5toROOT.py $DATA/gpu0 $DATA/gpu1 -j 8 --out-dir $ANA/root/pbpb \
    --campaign-file $ANA/root/pbpb/zjet_c00_campaign.root
python $P/run_h5toROOT.py $PP --out-dir $ANA/root/pp --campaign-file $ANA/root/pp/zjet_pp_campaign.root
./zjets $ANA/root/pbpb $ANA/jets_cxx/pbpb --files 0:13        # in slices, in parallel
./zjets $ANA/root/pp $ANA/jets_cxx/pp
cd ../../analysis/zjet
python zjet_jets.py --pbpb $ANA/jets_cxx/pbpb --pp $ANA/jets_cxx/pp --outdir $ANA/figures --tag _c00_cxx
python check_cxx.py jets $ANA/jets_py/pbpb $ANA/jets_cxx/pbpb | tail -1      # against the Python map step

zjets took 0.12 s per Pb+Pb oversample on the test set, at ~0.35 GB per process. make FASTJET_PY=<the fastjet wheel's package directory> builds against the pip fastjet wheel instead of a system FastJet, so both routes use the same FastJet. Options and details: analysis_root/zjet/README.md.

docs.title: Choose your setup
docs.text: There are four ways to get js-contrib running. Two of them come ready-made, with X-SCAPE, MUSIC4GPU, iSS, 3dMCGlauber and the Python bindings already compiled: the production container for Linux machines with an NVIDIA GPU, and the xscape wheel for Apple Silicon Macs. The third, the analysis environment, only reads and analyses the files a production writes, on any computer. The fourth, the source build, is for changing the code itself. Pick by your hardware and by what you want to do; you can have more than one side by side.

docs.title: Which one?
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[What do you want to do?] -->|change C++ code, the bindings<br/>or the jetscape package,<br/>FnoHydro with LibTorch, ROOT output| S[Source build<br/>js_fno conda env]
    A -->|run simulations,<br/>your own scripts and notebooks| B{Which machine?}
    A -->|only read and analyse<br/>production files| N[Analysis environment<br/>Python venv]
    B -->|Linux with an NVIDIA GPU,<br/>an HPC cluster| C[Production container<br/>Docker / Apptainer]
    B -->|Apple Silicon Mac,<br/>macOS 26 or later| M[xscape wheel<br/>installed with uv]
    B -->|no supported GPU| N
Production container xscape wheel Analysis environment Source build runs on Linux with an NVIDIA GPU (Docker); HPC clusters (Apptainer); without a GPU for analysis and hadronization Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later), macOS 26 or later any computer with Python 3.10 or later Linux (x86_64, aarch64), Apple Silicon Mac hydro on the NVIDIA GPU (CUDA) the Mac's GPU (Metal) no simulation CUDA, Metal, or MUSIC on the CPU you need Docker with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, or Apptainer uv (one command) a js-contrib checkout, or one pip install conda, compilers (the env brings them), CUDA toolkit or Xcode with its Metal toolchain productions yes yes no yes your own scripts, notebooks, Python modules yes yes reading files only yes analysis (HDF5, uproot, FastJet, Jupyter) yes yes yes yes ROOT / PyROOT no (uproot reads ROOT files) no (uproot reads ROOT files) optional, next to it yes change C++, bindings, jetscape no no no yes FNO hydro with PyTorch no PyTorch in the image no PyTorch in the environment no yes page Production container Mac (xscape wheel) Analysis environment Source build

Precompiled still means extensible

The container and the wheel come compiled, so they need no compiler. You can still write your own physics modules in Python (a hard process, energy loss, hadronization, an afterburner, a writer) and run them inside X-SCAPE's event loop next to the C++ modules: see Writing modules in Python. Only changes to the C++ code, the bindings or the jetscape package itself need the source build.

docs.title: The four setups in one paragraph each
docs.text:
Production container (jhputschke/xscape-prod). One image holds X-SCAPE with MUSIC on the GPU, iSS, 3dMCGlauber, Matter, LBT, iColored and Pythia, PyJetscape and its Pythonic layer, and the analysis packages with JupyterLab. It runs the productions, your own scripts and notebooks, and the analysis. The same image runs on CPU-only nodes for the second (hadronization) stage and for analysis. It can't use a Mac's GPU: Docker on macOS runs containers in a Linux VM without Metal.

xscape wheel (Apple Silicon). The same software as the container, installed natively from a lock file with uv, with MUSIC on the Mac's GPU through Metal. There is no compiler, Xcode, Homebrew, conda or Docker to install. It does not include ROOT or PyTorch, and it can't rebuild X-SCAPE. Intel Macs are not supported.

Analysis environment. A plain Python venv with the HDF5 readers, uproot, awkward, FastJet, the notebooks and pelicanfs for files on the OSDF. It needs no GPU, no X-SCAPE build and no conda. It can't run X-SCAPE, so no productions and no re-hadronization. ROOT can be added next to it from conda.

Source build (the js_fno conda environment). X-SCAPE (branch contrib) and its external packages built from source, with js-contrib in the tree. This is the setup for changing C++ (X-SCAPE modules, MUSIC4GPU, iSS, 3dMCGlauber), the PyJetscape bindings or the jetscape package, for the C++ FNO hydro (FnoHydro, through LibTorch), the live PyTorch FNO hydro, and ROOT output. On Linux with an NVIDIA GPU, the dev container jhputschke/xscape-fno4d-dev provides the same build environment.

Keep them apart

The wheel and a source build can share a Mac, and the container and a source build can share a Linux machine. Use them in separate terminals: a source build sets PYTHONPATH, XSCAPE or JETSCAPE_BUILD, and those variables point the ready-made setups at the wrong tree.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Install one of the four setups: container, Mac, analysis environment, source build.
  • Then run your first event.

docs.title: Analysis environment
docs.text:
The analysis environment is a plain Python venv for reading and analysing the files a production writes, on any computer with Python 3.10 or later. It needs no GPU, no X-SCAPE build, no compiled pyjetscape_core, no conda and no ROOT. Use it when someone else runs the productions and you get the files (from a disk or from the OSDF), or when you analyse on a laptop and simulate elsewhere. It holds the HDF5 readers of the jetscape package, uproot and awkward, FastJet, vector, particle, hist, mplhep, scipy, pandas, Jupyter, pyvista for the 3D visualization, and pelicanfs for osdf:// files.

You may already have one

The production container (run without --gpus) and the xscape wheel on a Mac carry the same analysis packages. This page is for computers that have neither.

docs.title: What works in it, and what doesn't
docs.text:
works doesn't every HDF5 file of a production: pair, particlize and hadron files (jetscape.hadrons_h5, jetscape.particlize_h5, jetscape.showers) anything that runs X-SCAPE: run_prod_jet.py, run_jobs.sh run_h5toROOT.py (hadron files → ROOT ntuples, written with uproot) and reading ROOT files with uproot re-hadronization (hadronize.py, run_hadronize.py): iSS and Pythia live in the compiled core the analysis scripts and notebooks (analysis/, jet_wake.ipynb, the FastJet tutorials) the ROOT macros and the C++ reader, unless ROOT is added (below) the visualization of stored files (wake_pyvista.py, hydro_jet_particles_pyvista.py --file) the visualization of a live event

jetscape.HAS_CORE is False in this venv. That is expected: every reader works without the compiled core.

docs.title: 1. Make the venv
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib.git
cd js-contrib
./utils/analysis_env/setup_analysis_env.sh           # venv in ~/.venvs/js_analysis

The script

  1. creates the venv (default ~/.venvs/js_analysis; give another directory as the first argument). Re-running it on an existing venv updates it;
  2. installs the analysis packages from utils/analysis_env/requirements.txt, plus pyvista/vtk and pelicanfs (both on by default), about 1.6 GB in total;
  3. installs PyJetscape from your checkout in editable mode, so import jetscape works from anywhere and follows git pull;
  4. downloads MUSIC's hotQCD EoS table (3.2 MB, md5-checked) into the venv and sets MUSIC_EOS_TABLE in its activate script. The pair files store the energy density, not the temperature; jet_wake.ipynb, analysis/wake_*.py and the visualization use the table to convert e → T;
  5. runs check_env.py.

Nothing outside the venv directory is written, except a Jupyter kernel spec if you ask for one.

docs.title: 2. Activate and check
docs.text:
source ~/.venvs/js_analysis/bin/activate
python utils/analysis_env/check_env.py /path/to/out    # opens every file of a production directory

check_env.py checks the packages, the Blosc filter (the HDF5 files are Blosc-compressed and don't open without hdf5plugin), PyROOT if present, the EoS table and off-screen rendering. With a directory it opens its pair, hadron and ROOT files. Two flags:

flag does --no-render skips the off-screen rendering test --remote-test also reads one public object over gs:// and osdf://

docs.title: 3. Options
docs.text:
./utils/analysis_env/setup_analysis_env.sh [VENV_DIR] [options]
option --uv create the venv and install with uv: much faster (uv must be on PATH) --python PY the interpreter for the venv (default python3; 3.10 or later) --no-viz leave out pyvista/vtk/ffmpeg (about 0.6 GB of the 1.6 GB) --with-fasthydro also install FastHydro, for FastHydro's own files and readers; not needed for the production files. Its solver also needs pip install torch --system-site-packages let the venv see the packages of the Python it is made from, e.g. PyROOT of a conda env (§4); on an existing venv it switches this on --with-gcs add Google Cloud Storage (gcsfs, google-cloud-storage): gs:// URLs for fsspec, h5py and uproot --no-pelican leave out pelicanfs, which is installed by default: osdf:// and pelican:// URLs --eos-table PATH copy the EoS table from PATH (an EOS/hotQCD directory of a MUSIC or X-SCAPE build, or the .dat file) instead of downloading it --no-eos neither download nor copy it --kernel NAME register a Jupyter kernel NAME for the venv (for VS Code or a JupyterLab elsewhere) --check DIR at the end, open the production files in DIR

Full description: utils/analysis_env/README.md and ./utils/analysis_env/setup_analysis_env.sh --help.

docs.title: 4. ROOT next to it
docs.text:
ROOT isn't needed: run_h5toROOT.py falls back to uproot, and the ntuples hold the same hadrons. You want ROOT for PyROOT and RDataFrame, the root prompt and browser, the ROOT macros and the C++ reader, or the --bits-p/--bits-x options of run_h5toROOT.py. A venv sees ROOT only when it is made from the Python that ROOT was built for, with --system-site-packages.

conda with ROOT + the venv (tested)one conda env with everything (untested) 
# 1. conda, once (skip if you have it): Miniforge, conda-forge by default
curl -fLO "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
bash "Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh" -b -p ~/miniforge3
source ~/miniforge3/bin/activate

# 2. an env with ROOT (ROOT >= 6.34 reads the RNTuple files run_h5toROOT.py writes)
conda create -n root -c conda-forge "root>=6.34"
conda activate root

# 3. the venv, from this env's Python
cd js-contrib
./utils/analysis_env/setup_analysis_env.sh ~/.venvs/js_analysis_root --system-site-packages

check_env.py then prints ok PyROOT 6.xx ... writes with ROOT. Afterwards PyROOT works from the venv alone; for the root prompt and compiled macros, conda activate root (without it ACLiC doesn't find the system headers: 'assert.h' file not found):

source ~/.venvs/js_analysis_root/bin/activate
python contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/run_h5toROOT.py /path/to/out -j 4

conda activate root
root -l -b -q 'contribs/PyJetscape/example/analysis_root/hadron_distributions.C+("/path/to/out")'

The same works with any other ROOT that has PyROOT (LCG/CVMFS, Homebrew, a source build): make the venv from the python3 in which import ROOT works, with --python "$(which python3)" --system-site-packages.

cd js-contrib
conda env create -f utils/analysis_env/environment.yml    # env "js_analysis"
conda activate js_analysis
python utils/analysis_env/check_env.py /path/to/out

Everything comes from conda-forge except the scikit-hep fastjet and PyJetscape (editable). The EoS table is not part of it; add it with

mkdir -p "$CONDA_PREFIX/share/music_eos/hotQCD"
curl -fL -o "$CONDA_PREFIX/share/music_eos/hotQCD/hrg_hotqcd_eos_binary.dat" \
  https://api.bitbucket.org/2.0/repositories/wayne_state_nuclear_theory/hotqcd/src/main/hrg_hotqcd_eos_binary.dat
conda env config vars set MUSIC_EOS_TABLE="$CONDA_PREFIX/share/music_eos/hotQCD/hrg_hotqcd_eos_binary.dat"
conda activate js_analysis                               # again, to pick up the variable

More on ROOT, RDataFrame and the C++ reader: ROOT and C++.

docs.title: 5. FastJet
docs.text:
Python C++ (ROOT macros, programs) package scikit-hep fastjet (the FastJet library is in the wheel): the classic SWIG interface and the array (awkward) interface conda-forge fastjet-cxx (FastJet, fastjet-config) and fastjet-contrib (fjcontrib as one library, libfastjetcontribfragile) install already in the venv conda install -c conda-forge fastjet-cxx fastjet-contrib in the ROOT env fjcontrib only SoftDrop, Lund declusterings, energy correlators and N-subjettiness, through the array interface all of it (#include <fastjet/contrib/SoftDrop.hh>, ...; link -lfastjetcontribfragile)

Jet finding on the hadron files: Jets with FastJet.

docs.title: 6. Files on the OSDF or in Google Cloud Storage
docs.text: pelicanfs (default) and gcsfs (--with-gcs) are fsspec file systems, so osdf:// and gs:// URLs work wherever fsspec does: uproot takes the URL directly, and h5py takes the file object fsspec opens (with hdf5plugin imported). Only the chunks you read travel over the network. Reading the public osdf:///fno4hic namespace needs no login or token. How to find, download and read the published productions: Data on the OSDF.

docs.title: 7. Jupyter
docs.text:
source ~/.venvs/js_analysis/bin/activate
cd js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet
jupyter notebook jet_wake.ipynb

The notebooks name the kernel they were saved with. If Jupyter asks, choose "Python 3 (ipykernel)": started from the activated venv, that is the venv. For a Jupyter elsewhere (VS Code, a JupyterLab of another env), register the venv with --kernel js_analysis and choose that kernel. The notebooks read out/ by default; point them elsewhere with WAKE_H5=/path/to/<stem>.h5 (jet_wake.ipynb) or HADRON_DIR=/path/to/out (the analysis/ notebooks).

Headless machines: the visualization renders off-screen and check_env.py tests that it works. If it fails on a machine without a display, run under xvfb-run (Linux, apt install xvfb).

docs.title: Without a checkout: the pyjetscape wheel
docs.text:
The jetscape package with the same analysis packages also comes as a pure-Python wheel, part of every xscape-macos release. It installs on any platform, in any Python 3.10+ environment:

uv pip install "pyjetscape[analysis] @ https://github.com/jhputschke/xscape-macos/releases/download/v0.1.0/pyjetscape-1.3-py3-none-any.whl"

Quote the argument: zsh treats [...] as a pattern. The readers, HadronArray, the awkward views and the notebooks work with it; running X-SCAPE does not. Unlike the setup script, it installs neither pyvista nor pelicanfs (add pelicanfs with uv pip install pelicanfs for the OSDF), and it does not fetch the EoS table: download hrg_hotqcd_eos_binary.dat as in the conda tab above and point MUSIC_EOS_TABLE at it.

docs.title: Threads and memory
docs.text:
The analysis tools are mostly single-threaded Python. Parallelise over files with processes, and keep processes × threads at or below the number of cores.

tool parallel with memory HadronFileReader one process; split a campaign by events= over processes the units it reads: a background of 2000 oversamples is ~14 M hadrons, ~1.5 GB with the derived kinematics (estimate) wake_observables.py -j N, wake_hadrons.py -j N N processes over files about +0.5 GB per process for the read-ahead (wake_observables.py) run_h5toROOT.py -j N N processes ~80 B per hadron of the largest tag: ~3.5 GB for a 15-event file at 400 oversamples hadron_distributions.C (RDataFrame) its threads argument numpy (OpenBLAS) OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS set it to 1 when running with -j, or the processes oversubscribe the cores Blosc decompression (h5py) BLOSC_NTHREADS helps little; leave it unset with -j

Measured times and more: docs/README_analysis.md.

docs.title: Next: start analysing
docs.text: Analyse walks through what a production writes and how to read it: hadrons, jets with FastJet, hydro and hadrons together, O+O, and ROOT.

docs.title: Production container
docs.text:
The production image jhputschke/xscape-prod is the ready-made setup for Linux machines with an NVIDIA GPU: workstations, cloud VMs (Docker) and HPC clusters (Apptainer). It holds X-SCAPE with MUSIC on the GPU (MUSIC4GPU, CUDA), iSS, 3dMCGlauber, Matter, LBT, iColored and Pythia, all compiled, together with PyJetscape and its Pythonic layer and the analysis packages (awkward, vector, fastjet, particle, hist, mplhep, matplotlib, scipy, pandas, uproot, JupyterLab). Nothing is compiled on your machine. One image serves three uses:

use GPU you bring the production scripts (run_prod_jet.py, run_prod_oo_isr.py, run_jobs.sh, run_hadronize.py, ...) yes; stage 2 (hadronization) no an output directory your own scripts and notebooks (the O+O workflow, the examples, Python modules of your own) yes your scripts, notebooks and XMLs in a directory analysis only (hadron and pair files, FastJet, plots, notebooks) no the files, or OSDF paths

On a Mac

Containers on macOS can't reach the GPU: Docker runs them in a Linux VM without Metal. Use the xscape wheel there; the scripts, notebooks and outputs are the same.

docs.title: 1. Requirements
docs.text:
• For simulations: an NVIDIA GPU with a driver recent enough for the image's CUDA version (table below), and either
    • Docker with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (workstation, cloud VM), or
    • Apptainer (or Singularity) on an HPC cluster; it needs no extra toolkit.
  • For analysis and hadronization only: any Linux machine with Docker or Apptainer; no GPU.
  • Disk: the full image is about 5.4 GB (5.36 GB for cu130 on arm64); the -slim variant is 0.6 GB smaller.

Pick the tag by the CUDA version your driver supports. nvidia-smi on the host prints it in the top right corner ("CUDA Version").

tag CUDA GPUs host driver CPU architectures cu126 12.6 V100, RTX 20xx–40xx, A100, A40, L4, H100, GH200 supports CUDA 12.6 or later (R560+) amd64, arm64 cu130 13.2 GH200, B200/GB200, RTX 50xx / RTX PRO Blackwell, GB10; no V100 supports CUDA 13.2 or later (R580+) amd64, arm64 cu124 12.4 as cu126 older drivers (R550) amd64 only

Each tag is a multi-architecture manifest: docker pull and apptainer pull take the image for the machine's CPU (x86_64 or ARM, e.g. GH200 and GB10). There is no performance difference to expect between cu124 and cu126.

For a campaign, pin the image

cu126 is a moving tag: it always points at the latest build. For a production campaign take a fixed, dated tag, cu126-<YYYYMMDD>-<xscape commit>, or the image digest, and use the same one on every machine. Physics fixes change results, so don't mix images of different builds in one campaign, and record which image you used: the output files don't say. The image's /opt/X-SCAPE/BUILD_INFO.txt lists the commits it was built from.

docs.title: 2. Pull the image and check it
docs.text:
DockerApptainer 
docker pull jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126
docker run --rm --gpus all jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 nvidia-smi       # the GPU is seen
docker run --rm jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 \
  python /opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/utils/container/image_check.py --analysis

apptainer pull xscape_prod.sif docker://jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126
apptainer exec --nv xscape_prod.sif nvidia-smi
apptainer exec xscape_prod.sif \
  python /opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/utils/container/image_check.py --analysis

image_check.py ends with image_check: all ok. To confirm that the bindings were built against the GPU MUSIC:

docker run --rm jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 \
  python -c "import jetscape as js; print(js.HAS_CORE, js.pyjetscape_core.MUSIC_BACKEND)"
# -> True music4gpu-cuda

docs.title: 3. The rules of the container
docs.text:
Everything else on this page follows from four rules.

  1. The image is read-only; your files live in /work. The X-SCAPE tree is /opt/X-SCAPE (read-only in Apptainer, owned by root in Docker). Mount a directory of yours at /work (Docker -v "$PWD/work:/work", Apptainer --bind "$PWD/work:/work") and write every output there. A file written anywhere else is gone when the container ends.
  2. Run as yourself. With Docker, pass --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)", or the outputs belong to root. Apptainer runs as you anyway.
  3. GPU access is explicit. Docker --gpus all (or --gpus device=1), Apptainer --nv. Without it MUSIC falls back to its CPU path: about 10× slower, and its numbers are not the GPU's.
  4. Everything finds the tree by itself. import jetscape works everywhere; scripts and notebooks find the build through $XSCAPE=/opt/X-SCAPE (jetscape.paths), and each job runs in a private working directory under its output directory, so jobs never share files and nothing writes into the image. Leave XSCAPE and JETSCAPE_BUILD as the image sets them.

Where things are inside the container:

path X-SCAPE tree, build /opt/X-SCAPE, /opt/X-SCAPE/build_gpu js-contrib /opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib examples and production scripts /opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example start directory Docker: .../example/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet; Apptainer: the directory you start it from your files /work (you mount it) X-SCAPE's default parameters /opt/X-SCAPE/config/jetscape_main.xml

docs.title: 4. Your first event
docs.text:
xscape-examples copies every example into a writable directory (the examples write next to themselves, so they can't run inside the read-only image). Then one O+O event runs through the whole chain: 3dMCGlauber, Pythia with initial-state radiation, MUSIC on the GPU, Matter + LBT, iColored + iSS. It takes under a minute on a GPU and leaves two hadron files in ./work/out_oo/.

DockerApptainer 
mkdir -p work
docker run --rm --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/work:/work" -w /work \
  jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 bash -c \
  'xscape-examples /work/examples && cd /work/examples/pythonic &&
   python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir /work/out_oo'

W=$SCRATCH/xscape; mkdir -p $W
apptainer exec --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif xscape-examples /work/examples
apptainer exec --nv --pwd /work/examples/pythonic --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif \
  python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir /work/out_oo

work/examples/ now holds the production scripts, the Pythonic examples (pythonic/), the toy Python modules (python_modules/), the analysis notebooks and their XMLs, editable on the host with your own editor. xscape-examples never overwrites: for a fresh copy, give it a new directory. What the event does and what the files contain: Your first event.

docs.title: 5. Running the productions
docs.text:
The production scripts run from the image's own copy, with their outputs in /work. Docker starts in prod_AuAu_0_10_jet; for O+O, change the directory with -w.

IMG=jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126
mkdir -p prod

# Au+Au 0-10 % with a jet: 2 events
docker run --rm --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/prod:/work" $IMG \
  python run_prod_jet.py --events 2 --seed 1 --write-particlize both --outdir /work/out

# stage 2 (hadronization) needs no GPU
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/prod:/work" $IMG \
  python run_hadronize.py /work/out -j 4 --oversample 500 --n-frag 50

# O+O with initial-state radiation
docker run --rm --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/prod:/work" \
  -w /opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/prod_OO_isr $IMG \
  python run_prod_oo_isr.py --events 2 --seed 5 --outdir /work/out_oo

Put OUTDIR one level inside /work

Use /work/out, not /work: every job records its seed in OUTDIR/../seeds_used.tsv, so the parent of OUTDIR must be writable too.

Your own physics settings go in a user XML that you mount and pass: -v "$PWD/xml:/xml:ro" and --user-xml /xml/PbPb_0_10.xml. Campaigns, several jobs per GPU, SLURM arrays and the two stages are explained in Au+Au jets (two stages), O+O with ISR, Z+jet and other systems and Clusters, GPUs and monitoring.

docs.title: A script of your own
docs.text:
Put the script and its user XML in work/ (start from a copy of examples/pythonic/oo_workflow.py and oo_workflow.xml). Every such script has the same skeleton:

# work/my_job.py
import jetscape as js
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronH5Writer

with js.JobDir("/work/out_mine", "/work/my_job.xml") as job:      # private working directory
    with js.per_event(job.main_xml, job.user_xml) as driver, \
         HadronH5Writer("/work/out_mine/my_job_hadrons.h5", tag="jet_frag", n_samples=1) as out:
        for i in driver.events():                                 # one iteration per event
            jets = driver.hadronization_manager.hadron_array()
            out.append_unit(jets.to_dict(), unit=i, event=i)
            print(i, len(jets), "jet hadrons")

docker run --rm --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/work:/work" -w /work \
  jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 python my_job.py

js.JobDir(out_dir, user_xml) copies your XML to out_dir/, makes its relative paths (such as iSS's tables) absolute for the image's build, runs the job in a private directory out_dir/work/<name> and removes that directory after a successful run. Inside the with block the current directory is that working directory, so use absolute output paths. The interface (driver.events(), hadron_array(), the hadron files) is described in The Pythonic interface; writing physics modules in Python in Writing modules in Python.

docs.title: Python packages that are not in the image
docs.text:
Install them once into /work and put that directory on the path:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/work:/work" jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 \
  pip install --target /work/pylib seaborn
docker run ... -e PYTHONPATH=/work/pylib:/opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/python ...

Don't upgrade numpy or h5py this way: pyjetscape_core is compiled against the image's numpy. For a group, a small Dockerfile of your own is cleaner: FROM jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126-<date>-<commit> plus RUN pip install --no-cache-dir seaborn.

docs.title: Changing js-contrib's Python code
docs.text:
The image uses its own jetscape package unless yours comes first on the path. For changes to pure Python, mount your js-contrib checkout and put its package in front:

docker run ... -v "$HOME/js-contrib:/src/js-contrib:ro" \
  -e PYTHONPATH=/src/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/python ...

This works only if your checkout is close to the image's js-contrib commit (BUILD_INFO.txt), and the compiled pyjetscape_core*.so must come from the image (copy it from the image's python/jetscape/ into your checkout's). Changes to C++ need the source build.

docs.title: 7. Analysis without a GPU
docs.text:
Without --gpus (Docker) or --nv (Apptainer) the image is an analysis environment. It also runs stage 2 (hadronization) on CPU-only nodes, unchanged.

# a script of yours on your files
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/work:/work" -w /work \
  jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 python my_analysis.py /work/data

# open every file of a production directory
docker run --rm -v "$PWD/prod:/work:ro" jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 \
  python /opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/utils/analysis_env/check_env.py /work/out --no-render

pelicanfs reads osdf:// paths in place; public namespaces need no token, a protected one takes -e BEARER_TOKEN_FILE=/work/token. Notebooks to start from (in the xscape-examples copy):

notebook reads pythonic/oo_analysis.ipynb the O+O hadron files, streamed from the OSDF pythonic/oo_workflow.ipynb (sections 4–6) the hadron files of your own run analysis/tutorials/hadron_distributions.ipynb, jet_fastjet*.ipynb a production directory prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/jet_wake.ipynb a pair file and its hadron files prod_OO_isr/oo_isr_overview.ipynb an O+O production

How to read the files: Analyse.

docs.title: 8. Jupyter
docs.text:
xscape-jupyter [DIR] starts JupyterLab on port 8888 with DIR (default /work) as its root and prints the URL with its access token.

docker run --rm -it --gpus all --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -p 8888:8888 \
  -v "$PWD/work:/work" jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 xscape-jupyter

Open the http://127.0.0.1:8888/lab?token=... line it prints. Notebooks run with the image's Python ("Python 3 (ipykernel)"), and simulations in a notebook use the GPU as scripts do. Stop it with Ctrl-C twice.

  • Another port: -p 8890:8888, then open 127.0.0.1:8890.
  • On a remote GPU server: start it there as above, then on your laptop run ssh -N -L 8888:localhost:8888 user@server and open the URL locally.
  • Keep Jupyter's settings and history: $HOME is a temporary directory with --user; add -e HOME=/work/.home.
  • Analysis only: the same command without --gpus all.

docs.title: 9. HPC clusters with Apptainer
docs.text:
Apptainer runs the same image as you, with your home directory mounted and the host's network. It differs from Docker in three ways: --nv for the GPU, --bind for /work, and it starts in the current directory, not the image's start directory, so pass --pwd or full paths.

apptainer pull xscape_prod.sif docker://jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126-<date>-<commit>
W=$SCRATCH/xscape; mkdir -p $W
EX=/opt/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example

# a production
apptainer exec --nv --pwd $EX/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif \
  python run_prod_jet.py --events 2 --seed 1 --outdir /work/out

# a script of your own
apptainer exec --nv --pwd /work/examples/pythonic --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif \
  python oo_workflow.py --events 3 --outdir /work/out_oo

# analysis, no GPU
apptainer exec --pwd /work --bind $W:/work xscape_prod.sif python my_analysis.py

In a SLURM batch script these lines run as they are (after #SBATCH --gpus=1 or your site's equivalent). Job arrays, several GPUs and the LBT table cache: Clusters, GPUs and monitoring.

  • Mixed clusters: a .sif file holds one CPU architecture. Where the login nodes are x86 but the GPU nodes are ARM (GH200), pull with apptainer pull --arch arm64, or pull on a compute node.
  • Home directory: Apptainer mounts it, but write outputs to /work on scratch, not to ~.

Jupyter on a compute node:

salloc --gpus=1 --time=2:00:00                  # your site's options; you land on a node
apptainer exec --nv --bind $SCRATCH/xscape:/work xscape_prod.sif xscape-jupyter

In Apptainer, xscape-jupyter listens on 127.0.0.1 only, since the node is shared. Tunnel from your laptop through the login node to the compute node:

ssh -N -L 8888:localhost:8888 -J user@login.cluster user@<node>   # if nodes accept ssh
ssh -N -L 8888:<node>:8888 user@login.cluster                     # otherwise, with JUPYTER_IP=0.0.0.0

For the second form start Jupyter with apptainer exec --env JUPYTER_IP=0.0.0.0 ...; the token still protects it.

docs.title: 10. Image variants
docs.text:
Each CUDA tag comes in flavours, marked by a suffix; suffixes combine (cu126-slim-gcs).

suffix what changes for (none) the full image: productions, analysis packages, JupyterLab, the helpers everything on this page -slim no analysis packages and no Jupyter; 0.6 GB smaller production runs only -viz adds pyvista/vtk with off-screen rendering 3D visualization -gcs adds Google Cloud Storage for Python (gcsfs, google-cloud-storage) reading and writing gs://

Which variants are published at a given time is visible on Docker Hub. Every image has Pelican/OSDF support (pelicanfs and the pelican command-line tool). The images contain neither ROOT nor PyTorch.

Images built before 2026-10-28 (the date is in the dated tag) lack the analysis packages, the helpers (xscape-examples, xscape-jupyter) and the preset PYTHONPATH; they only run the production scripts.

docs.title: 11. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
symptom cause and fix Permission denied or Read-only file system when writing writing into the image, or into /work itself where OUTDIR's parent must be writable: write to /work/<something>; with Docker use --user and a directory you own outputs owned by root Docker without --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"; fix once with sudo chown -R $USER work/ No CUDA device found ... falling back to CPU no --gpus all / --nv, or the driver is older than the image's CUDA: check nvidia-smi; take cu124 for R550 drivers docker: could not select device driver "" with capabilities: [[gpu]] the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is not installed on the host no kernel image is available for execution on the device the image has no code for this GPU (e.g. V100 with cu130): take cu126 or cu124; discard files written by such a run python: can't open file 'run_prod_jet.py' Apptainer: add --pwd $EX/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet or use the full path xscape-examples: ... exists and is not empty it never overwrites: give another directory JobDir: not found: .../music_input JETSCAPE_BUILD or XSCAPE set to something else; in the image leave them as they are ModuleNotFoundError: awkward (fastjet, Jupyter, ...) a -slim image, or an image built before 2026-10-28 Jupyter page does not load Docker: -p 8888:8888 missing; Apptainer: tunnel to the compute node, not the login node Matter warnings Second instance ... el_vector for ISR partons harmless: an ISR parton before t = 0 outside the light cone, where there is no medium

Full reference (helpers, environment variables, the image build): utils/README_Container_Usage.md, utils/BuildContainerProd.md.

docs.title: Next: run your first event
docs.text: You ran one event above; Your first event explains what it did, what the output files hold and where to go from there.

docs.title: Mac (xscape wheel)
docs.text:
On an Apple Silicon Mac, X-SCAPE runs natively with MUSIC on the Mac's own GPU through Metal. It comes as a Python wheel, xscape, installed with uv from a lock file. There is no compiler and no container involved. Docker on a Mac can't reach the GPU, so on a Mac the wheel takes the place of the production container; the scripts, notebooks and outputs are the same. The environment holds X-SCAPE with MUSIC (MUSIC4GPU, Metal), iSS, 3dMCGlauber, Matter, LBT, iColored and Pythia, PyJetscape and its Pythonic layer, and the analysis packages (awkward, vector, fastjet, particle, hist, mplhep, matplotlib, scipy, pandas, uproot, JupyterLab).

What it can't do: rebuild X-SCAPE or the bindings (that needs the source build), ROOT/PyROOT (uproot, included, reads ROOT files), and PyTorch (not in the environment). Intel Macs are not supported.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• A Mac with Apple Silicon (M1 or later) on macOS 26 or later (Apple menu → About This Mac).
  • About 3 GB of disk, 1 GB of it uv's download cache (uv cache clean frees it).
  • Internet access during the installation.

You do not need Xcode, Homebrew, conda, Docker, git or an Apple developer account.

Releases

The wheels are published on the Releases page of jhputschke/xscape-macos. The current release is v0.1.0; check that page for the latest. Each release is a set of three files: the xscape wheel (X-SCAPE, 175 MB), the pyjetscape wheel (the Python package), and a lock file xscape-<version>-cp313.lock.txt, which names every package of the environment with its exact version and checksum. You install from the lock file, so every Mac gets exactly the same software.

docs.title: Step 1: install uv
docs.text:
uv is Astral's Python package manager: a single program in ~/.local/bin.

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Then open a new Terminal window (or run source ~/.local/bin/env) so that uv is found. With Homebrew, brew install uv works too.

docs.title: Step 2: create the environment from the lock file
docs.text:
VER=0.1.0                     # the latest: github.com/jhputschke/xscape-macos/releases
mkdir -p ~/xscape && cd ~/xscape
curl -LO https://github.com/jhputschke/xscape-macos/releases/download/v$VER/xscape-$VER-cp313.lock.txt
uv venv --managed-python ~/.venvs/xscape-$VER --python 3.13
source ~/.venvs/xscape-$VER/bin/activate
uv pip sync xscape-$VER-cp313.lock.txt

uv downloads Python 3.13 and about 200 MB of packages, which takes seconds to a few minutes depending on the connection.

  • --managed-python makes uv use its own Python, never one from Homebrew, conda or python.org that happens to be installed, so nothing outside the environment is used.
  • uv pip sync installs exactly what the lock lists, hash-checked, and removes anything else.
  • source ~/.venvs/xscape-$VER/bin/activate is needed in every new Terminal window where you use X-SCAPE. Your prompt then starts with (xscape-0.1.0).

docs.title: Step 3: fetch the LBT tables
docs.text:
LBT, the jet energy-loss module, needs its scattering tables: a 240 MB download, 1.1 GB on disk. They are kept in ~/Library/Caches/xscape and shared by all your environments.

xscape-fetch-data lbt

It checks every file against the release's checksums and ends with xscape-fetch-data: LBT tables ... (checked) -> .... If you already have the tables on disk, xscape-fetch-data lbt --from DIR uses them instead of downloading.

docs.title: Step 4: check that the Metal GPU is used
docs.text:
python -c "import jetscape as js; print(js.HAS_CORE, js.pyjetscape_core.MUSIC_BACKEND)"
# -> True music4gpu-metal

True means the compiled bindings load; music4gpu-metal means they were built with the Metal MUSIC. The first import after the installation takes a little longer, because matplotlib builds its font cache once.

When an event runs, MUSIC prints the GPU it uses when it starts: [MUSIC-GPU] Metal device: <your chip>. There is nothing to switch on. If instead you see [MUSIC-GPU] Metal init failed, falling back to CPU., MUSIC runs on the CPU; that happens inside a virtual machine or a container, so run natively in Terminal.

docs.title: Step 5: copy the examples and run one event
docs.text:
xscape-examples ~/xscape/examples
cd ~/xscape/examples/pythonic
python oo_workflow.py --events 1 --outdir ~/xscape/out_oo

xscape-examples copies every example into a directory of yours: the production scripts, the Pythonic examples (pythonic/), the toy Python modules (python_modules/), the analysis notebooks and their XMLs. The examples write next to themselves, so they run from this copy. It never overwrites: for a fresh copy, give it a new directory.

The event is one O+O collision through the whole chain: 3dMCGlauber, Pythia with initial-state radiation, MUSIC on the GPU, Matter + LBT, iColored + iSS. It takes under a minute (27 s on an M3 Max) and writes two hadron files to ~/xscape/out_oo/. What it did: Your first event.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
1. Your files live in your own directories (e.g. ~/xscape). The installed X-SCAPE inside ~/.venvs/... is not edited; the examples run from your copy.
  2. Activate the environment in every new Terminal window: source ~/.venvs/xscape-VER/bin/activate.
  3. One environment per release. A release fixes all the software. For a campaign, keep to one release, and don't mix files of two releases, since physics fixes change results. The commits a release was built from: cat "$(python -c 'import xscape; print(xscape.TREE)')/BUILD_INFO.txt".
  4. Everything finds the installed X-SCAPE by itself (jetscape.paths). Leave XSCAPE, JETSCAPE_BUILD, PYTHONPATH and DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH unset in this environment: they belong to a source build and would point it elsewhere.
  5. Results agree statistically, not bit for bit, across Macs and macOS versions.
where the environment ~/.venvs/xscape-VER the installed X-SCAPE (data, config/, BUILD_INFO.txt) python -c "import xscape; print(xscape.TREE)" X-SCAPE's default parameters config/jetscape_main.xml in that tree the examples your copy, e.g. ~/xscape/examples the LBT tables ~/Library/Caches/xscape/LBT-tables-<commit>

docs.title: Running the productions
docs.text:
The productions run from your copy of the examples, with the same options as on a GPU server or in the container.

cd ~/xscape/examples/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet

# Au+Au 0-10 % with a jet: 2 events (about 40 s on an M3 Max)
python run_prod_jet.py --events 2 --seed 1 --write-particlize both --outdir ~/xscape/prod/out

# a campaign: 20 jobs x 25 events, unique seeds, 3 jobs at a time on the GPU
OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive KMP_BLOCKTIME=0 \
  ./run_jobs.sh -j 3 --campaign test 20 25 0 ~/xscape/prod/out

# stage 2 (hadronization) on the CPU
python run_hadronize.py ~/xscape/prod/out -j 4 --oversample 500 --n-frag 50

# O+O with initial-state radiation
cd ~/xscape/examples/prod_OO_isr
python run_prod_oo_isr.py --events 2 --seed 5 --outdir ~/xscape/prod/out_oo
  • Put OUTDIR one level inside a directory of yours (~/xscape/prod/out): every job records its seed in OUTDIR/../seeds_used.tsv.
  • Your own physics settings: copy a user XML from ~/xscape/examples/config/, edit it and pass it with --user-xml my.xml.
  • Several jobs at once: on an M3 Max, -j 3 with OMP_NUM_THREADS=5 and OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive gave the most events per hour; aim for -j × threads ≈ the number of performance cores. Without passive, idle OpenMP threads spin and slow the other jobs down.
  • Long campaigns: keep the Mac awake, e.g. caffeinate -i ./run_jobs.sh ....
  • ROOT output (run_h5toROOT.py with ROOT) needs PyROOT, which this environment does not have; uproot writes and reads the ROOT files instead.

The productions themselves: Au+Au jets (two stages), O+O with ISR, Z+jet and other systems.

docs.title: Your own scripts and Python modules
docs.text:
Put your script and its user XML in a directory of yours, starting from a copy of examples/pythonic/oo_workflow.py and oo_workflow.xml (oo_workflow.py takes any user XML with --xml). The skeleton every such script has:

# ~/xscape/mine/my_job.py
import os
import jetscape as js
from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronH5Writer

out = os.path.expanduser("~/xscape/out_mine")
with js.JobDir(out, os.path.expanduser("~/xscape/mine/my_job.xml")) as job:  # private working dir
    with js.per_event(job.main_xml, job.user_xml) as driver, \
         HadronH5Writer(f"{out}/my_job_hadrons.h5", tag="jet_frag", n_samples=1) as h5:
        for i in driver.events():                                         # one iteration per event
            jets = driver.hadronization_manager.hadron_array()
            h5.append_unit(jets.to_dict(), unit=i, event=i)
            print(i, len(jets), "jet hadrons")
