js.JobDir(out_dir, user_xml) copies your XML to out_dir/, points it at the installed X-SCAPE's tables, runs the job in a private directory out_dir/work/<name> and removes it after a successful run. Inside the with block the current directory is that working directory, so use absolute output paths. Details: The Pythonic interface.

Physics modules in Python (a hard process, energy loss, hadronization, an afterburner, a writer) run inside X-SCAPE's event loop with this environment as it is, next to the C++ modules. Start from examples/python_modules/ (python run_by_hand_pythonic.py --style new) and read Writing modules in Python.

More Python packages: uv pip install seaborn. A later uv pip sync (of the same or a new lock) removes them again, so keep your additions in a file and run uv pip install -r my_packages.txt after each sync. Don't change numpy or h5py this way.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
The same environment is an analysis environment; analysis needs no GPU. Notebooks to start from, in your copy of the examples:

notebook reads pythonic/oo_workflow.ipynb (sections 4–6) the hadron files of your own run pythonic/oo_analysis.ipynb the O+O hadron files streamed from the OSDF (first uv pip install pelicanfs) analysis/tutorials/hadron_distributions.ipynb, jet_fastjet*.ipynb a production directory prod_AuAu_0_10_jet/jet_wake.ipynb a pair file and its hadron files prod_OO_isr/oo_isr_overview.ipynb an O+O production

To analyse on another computer (Linux, an Intel Mac, a cluster) you need only the Python package, not X-SCAPE: see the analysis environment.

docs.title: Jupyter and VS Code
docs.text:
source ~/.venvs/xscape-VER/bin/activate
cd ~/xscape/examples
jupyter lab

JupyterLab opens in your browser. Notebooks run with the environment's Python ("Python 3 (ipykernel)"), and simulations in a notebook use the GPU as scripts do. Stop it with Ctrl-C twice in the Terminal.

VS Code: open ~/xscape/examples, then "Python: Select Interpreter" (for notebooks also "Select Kernel") and choose ~/.venvs/xscape-VER/bin/python.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
In the activated environment:

command does xscape-fetch-data lbt [--from DIR] the LBT tables into ~/Library/Caches/xscape (or $XSCAPE_CACHE), checked and linked into this environment xscape-examples [DEST] copies the examples to DEST (default ./examples); never overwrites xscape-run -w RUN_DIR -u USER_XML X-SCAPE's runJetscape on a user XML, in a directory of its own runJetscape USER_XML X-SCAPE's executable with this environment's data, in the current directory

For example, two proton-proton events with X-SCAPE's default user XML:

xscape-run -w ~/xscape/runs/pp -u "$(python -c 'import xscape; print(xscape.TREE)')/config/jetscape_user.xml"

docs.title: Updating and removing
docs.text:
A new release goes into a new environment next to the old one, so a running campaign keeps its software:

VER=<new version>
cd ~/xscape
curl -LO https://github.com/jhputschke/xscape-macos/releases/download/v$VER/xscape-$VER-cp313.lock.txt
uv venv --managed-python ~/.venvs/xscape-$VER --python 3.13 && source ~/.venvs/xscape-$VER/bin/activate
uv pip sync xscape-$VER-cp313.lock.txt
xscape-fetch-data lbt                    # reuses the cached tables when they match
xscape-examples ~/xscape/examples-$VER   # the examples of this release

Removing:

rm -rf ~/.venvs/xscape-VER               # one environment
rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/xscape           # the LBT tables
uv cache clean                           # uv's downloads
rm ~/.local/bin/uv ~/.local/bin/uvx      # uv itself

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
symptom cause and fix zsh: command not found: uv open a new Terminal window, or source ~/.local/bin/env ... has no wheels with a matching platform tag macOS older than 26, or an Intel Mac: update macOS; Intel Macs are not supported zsh: no matches found: pyjetscape[analysis]... quote the argument: "pyjetscape[analysis] @ ..." ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'jetscape' the environment is not active: source ~/.venvs/xscape-VER/bin/activate import jetscape picks up a source checkout, or JobDir: not found: .../music_input PYTHONPATH, XSCAPE or JETSCAPE_BUILD set (e.g. in ~/.zshrc): unset PYTHONPATH XSCAPE JETSCAPE_BUILD LBT: cannot open ... LBT-tables step 3 not done for this environment: xscape-fetch-data lbt xscape-fetch-data: ... file(s) missing or different an interrupted download: rm -rf ~/Library/Caches/xscape/LBT-tables-* and run it again xscape-examples: ... exists and is not empty it never overwrites: give another directory python: can't open file 'run_prod_jet.py' run it from your copy, ~/xscape/examples/prod_AuAu_0_10_jet MUSIC slow, no GPU inside a virtual machine or a container there is no Metal GPU: run natively in Terminal ModuleNotFoundError: ROOT ROOT is not part of this environment; uproot reads ROOT files

The same guide, with every detail: utils/README_Mac_Usage.md (also the README of jhputschke/xscape-macos).

docs.title: Next: run your first event
docs.text: You ran one event in step 5; Your first event explains what it did, what the output files hold and where to go from there.

docs.title: Source build (conda)
docs.text:
The source build compiles X-SCAPE (branch contrib) with its external packages and js-contrib inside the tree, in the js_fno conda environment. You need it to change C++ (X-SCAPE modules, MUSIC4GPU, iSS, 3dMCGlauber), the PyJetscape bindings or the jetscape package, to use the C++ FNO hydro (FnoHydro, through LibTorch) or the live PyTorch FNO hydro, and for ROOT output. If you only want to run productions, write scripts and Python modules, or analyse, the container or the Mac wheel gets you there without compiling.

Why conda. One conda prefix holds every C++ dependency (Boost, Pythia8, HDF5, GSL, HepMC3, FastJet, ROOT) next to Python, PyTorch, pybind11 and the analysis packages, so CMake finds them all without system packages. That matters most on Apple Silicon (native ARM builds, PyTorch with MPS) and on Linux aarch64 (AWS Graviton, ARM servers, GB10), where several JETSCAPE dependencies are missing from the usual package managers; conda-forge has native builds of all of them.

The order of the steps: get the sources, make the environment, fetch the external packages, configure and build, make jetscape importable, run the tests.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
LinuxmacOS
  • x86_64 or aarch64.
  • For MUSIC on the GPU: an NVIDIA GPU with its driver and the CUDA toolkit (nvcc). Without them, MUSIC builds and runs on the CPU.
  • git, and conda (the install script offers to install Miniconda if conda isn't found).
  • On a machine with an NVIDIA GPU, the dev container is an alternative to steps 2 to 4's environment.
  • An Apple Silicon Mac. PyTorch from PyPI (the latest release) and MLX need macOS 14 or later.
  • Xcode with its Metal toolchain, for MUSIC on the GPU (-DUSE_METAL=ON).
  • git, and conda (the install script offers to install Miniconda if conda isn't found).

The Mac wheel and a source build on one Mac

They can coexist, but use them in separate Terminal windows: the source build's conda environment and variables (PYTHONPATH, XSCAPE, ...) must not be active where the wheel's environment runs.

docs.title: 1. Get X-SCAPE and js-contrib
docs.text:
js-contrib is built inside X-SCAPE's tree, from external_packages/js-contrib. X-SCAPE must be on its contrib branch: get_js_contrib.sh, the USE_JS_* options and the hooks the bindings use exist only there, not on main or in the original JETSCAPE.

git clone -b contrib https://github.com/JETSCAPE/X-SCAPE.git
cd X-SCAPE/external_packages
./get_js_contrib.sh            # clones https://github.com/jhputschke/js-contrib into js-contrib/

docs.title: 2. Create the js_fno environment
docs.text:
Run the scripts from the js-contrib checkout inside the tree: they finish with an editable pip install -e of PyJetscape and FastHydro from that checkout, so the jetscape package you import is the one you build.

cd X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib
bash utils/conda_install/test_js_fno_build_env.sh          # dry run: is every package reachable?
LinuxmacOS 
bash utils/conda_install/install_js_fno_build_minimal.sh        # CUDA detected from nvcc / nvidia-smi
# bash utils/conda_install/install_js_fno_build_minimal.sh 12.4 # or force a CUDA version
conda activate js_fno

bash utils/conda_install/install_js_fno_build_minimal.sh none   # CPU/MPS PyTorch from PyPI
conda activate js_fno

The dry run prints [PASS]/[FAIL]/[WARN] per package and ends with All checks passed — safe to run install_js_fno_build_minimal.sh. It takes the same CUDA argument (none on a Mac). The install script then creates the environment (Python 3.11) with:

layer packages C++ build cmake, make, compilers, boost-cpp, zlib, hdf5, pythia8, hepmc3, fastjet, gsl, openmpi ROOT root>=6.34,<6.38 from conda-forge PyTorch torch, torchvision: CUDA wheels from download.pytorch.org, or CPU/MPS wheels with none analysis and tests numpy, scipy, matplotlib, h5py, hdf5plugin, pandas, JupyterLab, ipykernel, vector, pybind11, pytest, ...; with pip: neuraloperator, uproot, awkward, pyvista, imageio MLX Apple Silicon only js-contrib pip install -e of PyJetscape and FastHydro

Arguments and settings, the same for all install scripts:

1st argument the CUDA version for the PyTorch wheels (12.4, 13.0, ...), or none; omitted: detected 2nd argument where to install Miniconda if conda isn't found (default ~/miniconda3) JS_FNO_ENV_NAME=<name> another environment name, e.g. a new install next to a working js_fno JS_FNO_FORCE=1 replace an existing environment of that name (otherwise the script stops) JS_FNO_NO_EDITABLE=1 skip the final editable install of PyJetscape and FastHydro JS_FNO_NO_MLX=1 skip MLX on Apple Silicon

For exact reproducibility there are pinned variants in utils/conda_install/pinned/ (install_js_fno_build_pinned.sh, Python 3.11.9, torch 2.4.1, ROOT 6.36.14, ...). Details: utils/conda_install/README.md.

docs.title: 3. Fetch the external packages
docs.text:
Each external package has a download script in X-SCAPE/external_packages/, pinned to a tested commit.

cd X-SCAPE/external_packages
./get_music4gpu.sh      # MUSIC with GPU backends (CUDA, Metal), + its hotQCD EoS tables
./get_iSS.sh            # iSS particlization, + its EoS and delta-f tables
./get_3dglauber.sh      # 3dMCGlauber initial state, + LHAPDF
./get_lbtTab.sh         # LBT's scattering tables (1.2 GB), needed at run time
script for CMake flag get_music4gpu.sh MUSIC on the GPU (MUSIC4GPU, branch XSCAPE) -DUSE_MUSIC=ON with -DUSE_CUDA=ON or -DUSE_METAL=ON get_music.sh MUSIC on the CPU only (the upstream package) -DUSE_MUSIC=ON alone get_iSS.sh iSS (hadronization of the stored surfaces) -DUSE_ISS=ON get_3dglauber.sh 3dMCGlauber (also needed for iColored and iMATTER) -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON get_lbtTab.sh LBT tables none; run it before configuring, so CMake links them into the build directory get_js_contrib.sh js-contrib (step 1) -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON

After git pull of X-SCAPE

The get_*.sh scripts carry the pinned commit of each package. When a pull changes a pin (git diff on external_packages/get_*.sh), bring that package to the new commit (or fetch it again) and rebuild; a pull alone doesn't update the packages already in external_packages/.

docs.title: 4. Configure and build
docs.text:
Build into a directory called build_gpu at the top of the X-SCAPE tree: the production scripts (--build) and jetscape.paths look there by default. With another name, pass --build to the scripts or set JETSCAPE_BUILD.

Linux, NVIDIA GPUmacOS, MetalCPU only 
conda activate js_fno
cd X-SCAPE
cmake -S . -B build_gpu -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DUSE_MUSIC=ON -DUSE_CUDA=ON -DUSE_ISS=ON -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON \
  -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON -DUSE_JS_PYJETSCAPE=ON
cmake --build build_gpu -j"$(nproc)"

MUSIC4GPU compiles for the GPU it finds at configure time (CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES defaults to native). On a node without a GPU, give the architectures explicitly, e.g. -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=80 for an A100. If nvcc fails to find the CUDA headers with conda's compilers, use the system GCC as nvcc's host compiler, export CUDAHOSTCXX=/usr/bin/g++, as the container builds do.

conda activate js_fno
cd X-SCAPE
cmake -S . -B build_gpu -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DUSE_MUSIC=ON -DUSE_METAL=ON -DUSE_ISS=ON -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON \
  -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON -DUSE_JS_PYJETSCAPE=ON
cmake --build build_gpu -j"$(sysctl -n hw.ncpu)"

conda activate js_fno
cd X-SCAPE
cmake -S . -B build_gpu -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DUSE_MUSIC=ON -DUSE_ISS=ON -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON \
  -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON -DUSE_JS_PYJETSCAPE=ON
cmake --build build_gpu -j"$(nproc)"

MUSIC without a GPU flag is the CPU MUSIC from get_music.sh. Its results differ systematically from the GPU path, so don't mix CPU and GPU events in one campaign.

The flags:

flag what it does -DUSE_MUSIC=ON builds MUSIC; required for the bindings, which include MUSIC's wrapper -DUSE_CUDA=ON / -DUSE_METAL=ON MUSIC from MUSIC4GPU on an NVIDIA GPU / on Apple Silicon (mutually exclusive; Metal only on macOS) -DUSE_ISS=ON iSS; needed for hadronization (hadronize.py, run_hadronize.py) -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON 3dMCGlauber; required for the bindings: without it iColoredHadronization and iMATTER are not compiled and pyjetscape_core fails to load (undefined symbol ... iColoredHadronization) -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON builds js-contrib from external_packages/js-contrib -DUSE_JS_PYJETSCAPE=ON the Python bindings pyjetscape_core -DUSE_JS_FNO_HYDRO=ON the C++ FnoHydro module (LibTorch, about 2 GB, and ROOT); see below -DJS_PIP_INSTALL_PYJETSCAPE=ON runs pip install -e of PyJetscape on every build ROOT used when the environment has it (js_fno does): adds the FastRootBulkWriter binding (jetscape.HAS_ROOT). Without ROOT everything else builds and HAS_ROOT is False

CMake finds Boost, Pythia8, HDF5, ROOT and the rest in the active conda environment by itself. After a change to the bindings only, rebuild just them: cmake --build build_gpu --target pyjetscape_core.

FnoHydro (C++ FNO hydro). Add -DUSE_JS_FNO_HYDRO=ON and PyTorch's CMake files to the prefix path:

cmake -S . -B build_gpu ... -DUSE_JS_FNO_HYDRO=ON \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$CONDA_PREFIX;$(python -c 'import torch; print(torch.utils.cmake_prefix_path)')"

The live PyTorch FNO hydro (PyFNOHydro) needs no extra flag, only PyTorch in the Python environment, which js_fno has: Live PyTorch FNO hydro.

docs.title: 5. Make jetscape importable
docs.text:
The build writes the compiled extension pyjetscape_core*.so into external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/python/jetscape/. The install script of step 2 already installed that package in editable mode, so with conda activate js_fno it imports from anywhere:

python -c "import jetscape as js; print(js.HAS_CORE, js.pyjetscape_core.MUSIC_BACKEND)"
# -> True music4gpu-cuda      (Linux)    or    True music4gpu-metal   (macOS)

HAS_CORE is True once the compiled extension loads; MUSIC_BACKEND names the MUSIC it was built against (music for the CPU build). In another environment, make the package importable in one of two ways:

# editable install (recommended, e.g. for Jupyter)
pip install -e X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape
# or, without installing
export PYTHONPATH="/path/to/X-SCAPE/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/python:$PYTHONPATH"

The compiled core must match that environment's Python version (the one it was built with).

  • PYTHIA8DATA: the compiled core needs it, and conda activate js_fno sets it. Without it import jetscape aborts with Assertion 'InternalHelperPythia.particleData.isParticle(id)' failed.
  • Import order with PyTorch and ROOT: both ship their own libomp. Import torch before jetscape and ROOT (on macOS, import jetscape does this for you); if you see a segfault at import, check the order first.

docs.title: 6. Run the tests
docs.text:
cd X-SCAPE
pytest external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/tests -q

Most of the Python tooling is tested without a build; the tests that need the compiled core are skipped when it doesn't load. FastHydro and Visualization have their own suites in contribs/FastHydro/tests and contribs/Visualization/tests.

docs.title: The dev container (Linux, NVIDIA)
docs.text:
On Linux with an NVIDIA GPU, the dev image jhputschke/xscape-fno4d-dev holds the same build environment as js_fno, ready-made: CUDA, a conda environment (xscape, already on PATH), PyTorch and the C++ dependencies, but no sources. Mount your X-SCAPE checkout (with its external packages fetched, steps 1 and 3) and build inside it with the commands of step 4.

tag GPUs cu126 GH200, H100, A100, RTX 20/30/40xx cu132 the above plus Blackwell (GB200, GB10) 
docker pull jhputschke/xscape-fno4d-dev:cu126
docker run --rm -it --gpus all -v "$PWD/X-SCAPE:/workspace/X-SCAPE" \
  jhputschke/xscape-fno4d-dev:cu126
# inside: cd /workspace/X-SCAPE, then step 4

The image starts in /workspace and sets CUDAHOSTCXX for nvcc. It is published for amd64 and arm64, but has not been tested on aarch64 yet; there, use the conda environment. Image details: utils/BuildContainerDev.md.

docs.title: Linux aarch64
docs.text: On ARM servers (AWS Graviton, GH200, GB10) the conda environment is the tested way to build: conda-forge has native aarch64 builds of every C++ dependency, and the CUDA 12.x PyTorch wheels run on a CUDA 13 driver. To run productions without building, the production container has arm64 images (cu126, cu130).

docs.title: Other ways to build js-contrib
docs.text: js-contrib can also be built standalone against an X-SCAPE build tree or an installed X-SCAPE prefix (Paths B and C of the js-contrib README); for the Python bindings that route does not work at present, so use the in-tree build above. For X-SCAPE checkouts older than the contrib integration there is a manual patch recipe (Path A′ of the same README), kept for legacy checkouts.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
symptom cause and fix conda: command not found after the install the installer doesn't edit your shell config: run the printed init command, e.g. ~/miniconda3/bin/conda init zsh, and open a new terminal Environment 'js_fno' exists already remove it (conda env remove -n js_fno), replace it with JS_FNO_FORCE=1, or install next to it with JS_FNO_ENV_NAME=js_fno_new CMake doesn't find ROOT on macOS activate the environment before cmake; if it still fails, add -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="${CONDA_PREFIX}" pyjetscape_core fails to load: undefined symbol ... iColoredHadronization configure with -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON Assertion 'InternalHelperPythia.particleData.isParticle(id)' failed on import jetscape PYTHIA8DATA not set: conda activate js_fno MPS: False for PyTorch on Apple Silicon the environment was made without none, or Python runs under Rosetta: python -c "import platform; print(platform.machine())" must print arm64 JobDir: not found: .../music_input the build directory is not build_gpu: set JETSCAPE_BUILD or pass --build

Step-by-step reference for the environment and the workflows it covers: contribs/README.md; the bindings: contribs/PyJetscape/README.md.

docs.title: Next: run your first event
docs.text: With build_gpu built and jetscape importing, run your first event.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: js-contrib's Python interface, PyJetscape, lets you run X-SCAPE events from Python, read what every module produced as numpy arrays while the event is still in memory, and put modules of your own, written in Python, into the chain. Use it when the productions' command-line scripts are not enough: for a study of your own, for a notebook, for machine learning, or to try a new physics module without touching C++. Why this matters for ML is on Python and machine learning.

docs.title: The three layers
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["Your script or notebook"] --> B["Pythonic layer<br/>per_event, final_parton_array(), HadronArray,<br/>to_awkward, select, @js.module"]
    B --> C["jetscape package (pure Python)<br/>drivers, HDF5 writers and readers,<br/>PyFNOHydro, utils"]
    C --> D["pyjetscape_core (pybind11)<br/>X-SCAPE's C++ classes with their C++ names"]
    D --> E["X-SCAPE + MUSIC4GPU, iSS, Pythia, ..."]
  • pyjetscape_core is the compiled extension: pybind11 bindings of X-SCAPE's classes (JetScape, JetScapePerEvent, Parton, FourVector, PartonShower, the module base classes, MUSIC, iSS access, ...) with their C++ names and argument order, so C++ code ports line by line. Every module base class has a trampoline: a Python subclass runs as a real JETSCAPE module.
  • The jetscape package is pure Python around it: event-loop drivers (jetscape.run_jetscape), the HDF5 writers and readers of the productions, PyFNOHydro, conversion helpers (jetscape.utils), and jetscape.paths / JobDir, which find the X-SCAPE tree and give each run a working directory. The HDF5 readers work without the compiled extension; jetscape.HAS_CORE says whether it is there.
  • The Pythonic layer is installed onto the bound classes by import jetscape: numpy record arrays instead of column indices, hadrons as one array per field, awkward views with vector kinematics, an event loop that is a context manager, and modules that declare their XML parameters. It only adds names, so code written against the bare bindings keeps working.

In code, import jetscape as js gives the package and the Pythonic layer; the bound classes themselves are in jetscape.pyjetscape_core:

import jetscape as js                         # package + Pythonic layer
from jetscape import pyjetscape_core as core  # the bound C++ classes: core.JetEnergyLoss, core.FourVector, ...

PyTorch: import it first

torch and the compiled extension each bring an OpenMP runtime; the one loaded second can crash the process. When you use PyTorch, import torch before import jetscape. On macOS import jetscape does this for you if PyTorch is installed.

docs.title: Where you get it
docs.text:
ContainerMac (xscape wheel)Source build

The production image jhputschke/xscape-prod has pyjetscape_core and the jetscape package on PYTHONPATH, plus the analysis packages (awkward, vector, FastJet, Jupyter). PyTorch is not included. Copy the examples out of the read-only image once:

mkdir -p work
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD/work:/work" jhputschke/xscape-prod:cu126 \
  xscape-examples /work/examples

Details: Production container.

The xscape wheel (X-SCAPE with MUSIC4GPU for Metal, and the compiled pyjetscape_core) and the pyjetscape wheel (the jetscape package) install into one Python environment; import jetscape finds the compiled core there. PyTorch is not included. Copy the examples with

xscape-examples ~/xscape/examples

Details: Mac (xscape wheel).

Build X-SCAPE (branch contrib) with js-contrib and the bindings. -DUSE_MUSIC=ON and -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON are required (the bindings use MUSIC's wrapper, iColoredHadronization and iMATTER):

cmake .. -DUSE_MUSIC=ON -DUSE_ISS=ON -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON \
         -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON -DUSE_JS_PYJETSCAPE=ON
make -j pyjetscape_core
pip install -e ../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape   # or "...PyJetscape[fno,root]"
python -c "import jetscape; print(jetscape.HAS_CORE)"               # True

The extension must be built for the Python you run it with. Details: Source build (conda).

With only the analysis environment (no X-SCAPE build) you can read and analyse every production file, but not run events.

docs.title: A first event from Python
docs.text:
This runs one O+O event through the whole chain (3D MC-Glauber, Pythia with initial-state radiation, MUSIC, Matter + LBT, hadronization) with the user XML of the Pythonic example, pythonic/oo_workflow.xml in the copied examples, and prints what the jet left behind:

import numpy as np
import jetscape as js

with js.JobDir("out_first", "oo_workflow.xml") as job:          # a private working directory
    with js.per_event(job.main_xml, job.user_xml, n_events=1) as driver:
        for i in driver.events():                                # results are in memory here
            partons = driver.energy_loss_manager.final_parton_array()   # numpy records
            jet = driver.hadronization_manager.hadron_array()          # HadronArray
            print(f"event {i}: {len(partons)} final partons,",
                  f"leading parton pT {np.hypot(partons['px'], partons['py']).max():.1f} GeV,",
                  f"{len(jet)} jet hadrons")

On an M3 Max (Metal) this takes about 16 s and prints a line like event 0: 17 final partons, leading parton pT 9.2 GeV, 116 jet hadrons.

  • js.JobDir(out_dir, user_xml) copies the XML to out_dir/, points its relative paths at the X-SCAPE build, and runs inside out_dir/work/<name>, because MUSIC, 3dMCGlauber and iSS read and write files in the current directory. Write your own outputs to absolute paths.
  • js.per_event(...) as a context manager runs Init() on entry and Finish() on exit; driver.events() yields once per event, after the event ran and before its memory is freed.

A longer version that writes the hadrons to files is pythonic/oo_workflow.py (python oo_workflow.py --events 3 --seed 7 --outdir out_oo).

docs.title: Three ways to drive a run
docs.text:
how modules come from event loop A, from the XML jetscape.run_jetscape.run_automatic(main_xml, user_xml) the XML (C++ factory, plus registered Python modules) C++ B, by hand run_manual(main_xml, user_xml, modules=[...]) a Python list; the user XML sets <enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination>false C++ C, per event js.per_event(main_xml, user_xml, tasks=None) the XML, or tasks=[...] as in B Python

Mode C is the one to use for analysis and for anything that reads results: only there is each event's data still in memory when your code runs.

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• The Pythonic interface: running events, the result arrays, hadrons, awkward, FastJet, showers.
  • Writing modules in Python: your own hard process, energy loss, hadronization, afterburner or writer, with a worked example.
  • Live PyTorch FNO hydro: a PyTorch Fourier neural operator as the hydro module.
  • FastHydro: MC-Glauber and a 3+1D hydro solver in PyTorch, with jet-deposition pairs.
  • 3D visualization: the medium and the parton shower in PyVista.

The full reference of the bindings and the package is contribs/PyJetscape/README.md; all examples are listed in contribs/PyJetscape/example/README.md.

docs.title: FastHydro
docs.text:
FastHydro runs X-SCAPE's real jet energy-loss chain, Matter + LBT → CausalLiquefier → droplets, on top of a fast 3+1D finite-volume hydro solver in Milne coordinates written in PyTorch, with an MC-Glauber initial state. For each event it gives back a pair: the medium without the jet and the medium with the jet's lost energy deposited, both from the identical initial condition. That pair is what jet-deposition FNO studies and wake analyses need, and the cost per event makes large samples practical on a CPU, a CUDA GPU or Apple's MPS. On the same initial condition the solver agrees with MUSIC to about 0.3 % (relative L2 of the energy density at freeze-out). For production-grade pairs with MUSIC itself, use the two-stage Au+Au production; FastHydro writes the same file layout.

The solver and the initial state are FNO4d's fast_data, vendored unchanged under python/fast_data/. FastHydro itself is the glue that makes them X-SCAPE modules.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An X-SCAPE build (branch contrib) with PyJetscape: -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON -DUSE_JS_PYJETSCAPE=ON (source build). FastHydro is pure Python: it compiles nothing and needs no CMake option of its own.
  • The Python that pyjetscape_core was built with, with numpy, scipy, h5py, hdf5plugin, pyyaml, and PyTorch ≥ 2.0 for the solver. The js_fno conda environment has all of them and installs FastHydro as an editable package. PyTorch is not in the production container.
pip install -e external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FastHydro          # from the X-SCAPE root
# or without installing:
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FastHydro/python:$PYTHONPATH

The example scripts find their own paths, so they also run from a checkout without the install.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    IS["FastGlauberInitialState"] --> H["PythiaGun or PGun"] --> P["NullPreDynamics"]
    P --> BG["FastHydro('bg')<br/>background leg, no source"]
    BG --> E["JetEnergyLossManager: Matter, LBT<br/>+ CausalLiquefier"]
    E --> D["DropletBridge<br/>droplets -> the jet leg's source"]
    D --> JET["FastHydro('jet')<br/>same initial condition, with the source"]

This is X-SCAPE's two-stage hydro (config/jetscape_user_twostagehydro.xml, examples/custom_examples/TwoStagesHydro.cc) with FastHydro in place of MUSIC. Four things in it are fixed:

  • NullPreDynamics is mandatory. X-SCAPE requires a pre-equilibrium stage for every hydro except MUSIC and Brick. (The log then shows a harmless Unrecognized hydro module id warning.)
  • Matter before LBT. Matter hands over to LBT at Q0; <Eloss><mutex>ON</mutex> arbitrates.
  • The background leg comes first. X-SCAPE registers only the first FluidDynamics as the hydro, so Matter, LBT and the liquefier see the background and the jet leg is invisible to them. That is the two-stage semantics: the shower is quenched by the undisturbed medium, and its deposit goes into the second leg. The coupling is one-way.
  • The deposit is computed in Python. FastHydro deposits the droplets with fast_data's CausalLiquefierSource; the C++ CausalLiquefier is used only as the droplet container. There is no double counting.

docs.title: Configuration: an XML and a YAML
docs.text:
Two files, for two readers:

file read by holds config/jetscape_user_fasthydro.xml X-SCAPE (C++) <IS>, <Preequilibrium>, <Hard>, <Eloss>, <Liquefier> config/fasthydro_twostage.yaml, top level the solver (fast_data) grid, EoS, transport, τ axis, deposit scheme, device, dtype the same YAML, section fasthydro: FastHydro's adapters hard-scattering vertices, shower storage, bulk_info storage

The solver settings cannot go into the XML: X-SCAPE stops on any user-XML tag that jetscape_main.xml lacks. Three quantities appear in both files, and build_two_stage() refuses to run if they disagree:

quantity XML YAML rule grid <IS><grid_max_*>, <grid_step_*> grid: must agree (grid_max = n·d/2) hydro start <Preequilibrium><taus> time.tau0 must agree energy-loss start <Eloss><tStart> must not precede time.tau0

The liquefier's deposit parameters (tau_delay, time_relax, d_diff, width_delta) live only in <Liquefier><CausalLiquefier>; FastHydro reads them from the C++ object and records them in the output. Any YAML key can be overridden on the command line with --set, routed by its prefix: --set time.choose_ntau=41 (solver), --set fasthydro.hard_vertex.mode=centre (adapters), --set transport.mode=israel_stewart.

Where the hard scatterings happen is fasthydro.hard_vertex.mode: ncoll (default, the smeared binary-collision density, what a hard process follows), ncoll_mc, npart or centre (every vertex at the origin).

PGun ignores the vertex

X-SCAPE's PGun overwrites the sampled vertex with the origin, so with PGun every shower starts at (0, 0, 0) whatever hard_vertex.mode says. PythiaGun uses the vertex and is the default here.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Run from the X-SCAPE build directory; the framework resolves several paths relative to it.

cd $XSCAPE_BUILD
C=../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FastHydro
export OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive OMP_NUM_THREADS=8    # idle OpenMP threads otherwise spin

# 0. smoke test: hydro only, then check the medium queries against the stored grid
python $C/example/run_hydro_only.py --config $C/config/fasthydro_twostage.yaml

# 1. the real thing: background leg, Matter + LBT, jet leg -> one HDF5 file
python $C/example/run_two_stage.py \
    --config   $C/config/fasthydro_twostage.yaml \
    --user-xml $C/config/jetscape_user_fasthydro.xml \
    --main-xml ../config/jetscape_main.xml \
    --events 1 --out out/pair.h5 --dump-droplets out/run.droplets.npz

# 2. replay the same shower through other solver settings: no X-SCAPE, no Matter/LBT
python $C/example/run_replay.py --droplets out/run.droplets.npz \
    --config $C/config/fasthydro_twostage.yaml \
    --set transport.mode=israel_stewart --out out/pair_visc.h5
  • Give --out an .h5 name. It writes the FNO4d HDF5 layout, one event at a time, so the memory is one pair however many events you ask for. An .npz name writes plain arrays of one pair, for a quick look only.
  • The replay reads the droplet dump (small, numpy only) and runs both legs again, so it works on a machine without h5py or an X-SCAPE build. It answers "what does the same jet do in a different medium": the shower responds to the medium it crosses, so a live run on a viscous background gives a different jet, while a replay keeps the deposit fixed.
  • run.device in the YAML (or --set run.device=cuda) picks cpu, cuda or mps; MPS runs in float32. CPU runs are slower and bitwise reproducible.

For the wake notebook, one command makes both legs (ideal and viscous, the second replayed from the first's droplets), about a minute per leg on Apple MPS:

python $C/example/make_wake_data.py                      # -> out_wake/wake_{ideal,visc}.h5
python $C/example/make_wake_data.py --medium realistic   # dN_ch/deta about 650

It finds or downloads the EoS table it needs (--no-download refuses the network, --dry-run prints what it would do).

docs.title: Soft particlization: hadrons from one leg
docs.text:
FastHydro has no surface code of its own: when iSS finds no surface, X-SCAPE builds one from the stored evolution (Cornelius, in C++). One run particlizes one leg, chosen with <SoftParticlization><hydro_id>; run_particlize.py sets it:

cd $XSCAPE_BUILD
C=../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FastHydro
python $C/example/run_particlize.py --leg jet --events 10 --out-dir out_particlize
python $C/example/run_particlize.py --leg bg  --events 10 --out-dir out_particlize --oversample 200
python $C/example/delta_spectra.py --out-dir out_particlize --npz out_particlize/delta.npz

An event's initial condition depends only on the seed and the event index, so event k of the background run is the background of event k of the jet run; both record the initial condition's hash, and delta_spectra.py refuses to pair events whose hashes differ. It prints every (jet − background) difference with its compound-Poisson error: the wake's tens of GeV sit on about 10⁴ GeV of bulk, so the background's sampling noise decides how many oversamples a signal needs.

The driver refuses settings that cannot give a meaningful surface: frames zeroed after freeze-out (output.zero_after_freezeout / stop_at_freezeout must be off), and an EoS whose hadron list iSS does not decay. Use eos.kind: hotqcd (MUSIC EOS 9, the UrQMD list, decayed by iSS); hotqcd_smash (EOS 91) needs SMASH as an afterburner.

Checked with Israel–Stewart (η/s = 0.08), 2 central events × 200 oversamples, mid-rapidity:

FastHydro + iSS PHENIX 0–5 % dN_ch/dη 637 ~650–690 dN/dy π⁺, K⁺, p 292, 56, 17.4 ~286, ~49, ~18 ⟨p_T⟩ π⁺, K⁺, p [GeV] 0.51, 0.74, 1.03 ~0.45, ~0.67, ~0.95

⟨p_T⟩ is about 10 % harder than data: there is no δf and no hadronic cascade. The surface conserves entropy (98 % of the hydro's total at τ₀ on an ideal run).

docs.title: Comparison with MUSIC, and the 0–10 % tune
docs.text:
notebooks/bulk_vs_music.ipynb compares FastHydro's hadrons with 3D MC-Glauber + MUSIC + iSS, 0–10 % Au+Au (example/make_bulk_comparison_data.py makes its inputs). On 25 events per model:

  • The initial state alone is close. Against MUSIC with FastHydro's transport and no δf, FastHydro's multiplicity is 9 % lower, ⟨p_T⟩ 3–4 % softer for every species, and the dN/dη shape agrees to 1 % in width.
  • Transport matters more. MUSIC's calibrated bulk viscosity and δf add 23 % multiplicity and lower ⟨p_T⟩ by 7–13 %.
  • The tune. τ₀ = 0.5 fm/c, target_T = 0.418, η/s = 0.08, ζ/s = 0.12, b ∈ [0, 4.7] fm matches calibrated MUSIC in dN_ch/dη at mid-rapidity (−1 %) and in π and K ⟨p_T⟩ (+1.5 %, −0.6 %). Protons stay about 7 % soft and dN/dη 7–9 % wide at |η| ≈ 3.

The tune comes as two configuration pairs on the same medium:

pair for config/AuAu_FastHydro_tune_0_10_particles.{yaml,xml} spectra: iSS on one leg, every frame kept config/AuAu_FastHydro_tune_0_10_wake.{yaml,xml} jet-wake pairs (arr, arr_bg, source/), parton level 
python $C/example/run_particlize.py --leg bg --events 25 --oversample 100 --set run.device=cuda \
    --config $C/config/AuAu_FastHydro_tune_0_10_particles.yaml \
    --user-xml $C/config/AuAu_FastHydro_tune_0_10_particles.xml
python $C/example/make_wake_data.py --medium tune_0_10 --legs visc --device cuda
python $C/example/make_hadron_wake_data.py --medium tune_0_10 --device cuda

On this medium use only the viscous leg for wake runs: the "ideal" leg drops the tuned shear and bulk viscosity.

docs.title: Output format
docs.text:
The file is FNO4d's HDF5 layout, written with fast_data's own writer, so every FNO4d reader loads it:

arr               (N, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau) f4   the JET leg   [e, vx, vy, vz]
arr_bg            (N, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau) f4   the background leg
source/S          (N, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau) f4   what was injected (contravariant Milne)
source/droplets   (M, 8) f8                       tau, x, y, eta, E, px, py, pz
source/offsets    (N+1,) i8                       per-event slices into droplets
shower/partons, shower/vertices, shower/initiators, and their offsets
ntau_freezeout[_bg], tau_freezeout[_bg]           per leg
diag/                                             per-event scalars: n_droplets, ic_sha256, ...
  • e is in GeV/fm³, vx, vy, vz are Cartesian lab velocities; attributes record the full resolved configuration as JSON.
  • arr is the jet leg, following fast_data's convention: arr together with source/S is what a deposition FNO consumes. arr_bg is the same initial condition without the jet.
  • arr is not arr_bg + S. The fluid keeps responding after the last droplet has fired, and the response spreads far beyond the cells the source touched. That propagating difference, the wake, is the physics.
  • The shower costs about 9 kB per event against 5.5 MB for the hydro pair, and is stored by default (fasthydro.store_showers: false turns it off). Shower positions are Cartesian (x, y, z, t) and live on the partons; X-SCAPE's vertices carry only a time.

Read a pair with PairBrowser:

from fasthydro.browse import PairBrowser

p = PairBrowser("out_wake/wake_ideal.h5")
p.summary()                          # IC identical, first differing frame, deposit, freeze-out
p.diff(0, k)                         # e(jet) - e(background), event 0, frame k
p.source_at(0, tau)                  # where the jet was, from the droplet table
par, ver, ini = p.showers(0)         # the shower graph of event 0
start, tip, alive = p.shower_at(0, 3.0)   # the shower as it stands at t = 3 fm/c

PairBrowser also opens the MUSIC pair files of the Au+Au jet production, which use this layout. Two diagnostics are worth reading after every run: the energy of droplets that would deposit after the end of the τ window (often 20 % or more with a short window; fix with a longer time.choose_ntau or a smaller tau_delay), and the count of medium queries outside the grid (a grid too small silently removes quenching).

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text: notebook notebooks/jet_wake.ipynb the wake in the medium: Mach cone, damping, broadening, Mach angle (inputs: make_wake_data.py) notebooks/hadron_wake.ipynb the wake in the hadrons: Δφ and (Δη, Δφ) maps with significance, the near-side excess, the momentum balance (inputs: make_hadron_wake_data.py) notebooks/bulk_vs_music.ipynb bulk observables against 3D MC-Glauber + MUSIC, 0–10 % (inputs: make_bulk_comparison_data.py)

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Soft hadrons only, ideal Cooper–Frye. The viscous stresses are stored as zero, so iSS applies no δf (exact for ideal runs, an approximation for viscous ones). The jet's surviving partons are not hadronized.
  • No hadronic afterburner in the default build; iSS decays the resonances itself.
  • The η edges are open: analyse at mid-rapidity.
  • The surface lattice is coarser than the hydro grid (twice the spacing in the shipped XML) to keep the surface finder affordable.
  • Bulk viscosity is untested upstream, and the non-conformal viscous sector has no analytic benchmark.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
pytest tests -q
FAST_DATA_FULL_SELFTEST=1 pytest tests/test_fast_data_selftests.py   # the solver's physics gates

Tests that need pyjetscape_core skip cleanly without a build. Among them: zero droplets give a jet leg equal to the background bit for bit, four-momentum is conserved to 1e-10, and the Python deposit kernel matches the real C++ one.

The full documentation, with every measurement and design decision: contribs/FastHydro/README.md.

docs.title: Live PyTorch FNO hydro
docs.text: PyFNOHydro is a hydro module written in Python and backed by a PyTorch Fourier neural operator (FNO). It takes the initial condition from the pre-equilibrium stage, predicts the whole space-time evolution of the medium in one forward pass, stores it in X-SCAPE's evolution history and builds the freeze-out surface, so Matter, LBT and iSS run on the prediction exactly as they would on MUSIC. Use it to test a surrogate model against the full event: jet quenching and hadron observables on the predicted medium, side by side with MUSIC. Because the model can be a live torch.nn.Module, you can do this in the same Python session in which you train it, with no export step. The method and the 2+1D models are described in Phys. Rev. C 113, 014904 (2026) (arXiv:2507.23598).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    IS["initial state<br/>(e.g. TrentoInitial)"] --> PE["pre-equilibrium<br/>(e.g. NullPreDynamics)"]
    PE --> F["PyFNOHydro"]
    F --> J["Matter, LBT<br/>(read the medium)"]
    F --> S["iSS<br/>(freeze-out surface)"]

Inside EvolveHydro(), PyFNOHydro:

  1. takes the pre-equilibrium energy density and flow (e, ux, uy) and rebins them (nearest neighbour) onto the FNO grid: 3 features (e, vx, vy) or 4 (e, T, vx, vy);
  2. repeats that frame ntau times along the time axis and, for a 3-feature model, multiplies the energy density by τ₀ (the models are trained on e·τ);
  3. calls the model on a tensor of shape (1, n_features, nx, ny, ntau), under torch.no_grad(); the model must return the same shape;
  4. prepends the τ₀ frame, divides by τ again, and stores the ntau + 1 frames as a boost-invariant evolution starting at τ₀ (the pre-equilibrium module's end time);
  5. finds the freeze-out surface at the configured temperature.

docs.title: Three ways to give it a model
docs.text:
import torch                                   # always before jetscape
from jetscape.fno_hydro import PyFNOHydro

# 1. a JIT-traced TorchScript file (the format the C++ FnoHydro reads)
hydro = PyFNOHydro("models/traced.pt", config)

# 2. your model class plus a checkpoint (state_dict, or a dict with "model_state_dict")
from my_model import FNOModel
net = FNOModel(modes=12, width=20)
hydro = PyFNOHydro((net, "checkpoints/epoch50.pt"), config)

# 3. a live model object, used as it is: no serialisation
hydro = PyFNOHydro(net, config)

docs.title: The live model (approach 3)
docs.text:
Approach 3 is what makes the module useful while you develop a model. PyFNOHydro keeps a reference to your nn.Module, not a copy, so a model you have just trained, or are still training, runs inside a full X-SCAPE event:

import torch                                   # (1) before jetscape
import torch.nn as nn
from jetscape import create_module
from jetscape.fno_hydro import PyFNOHydro, fno_config_from_xml
from jetscape.run_jetscape import run_manual
from jetscape.utils import bulk_info_to_numpy

net = ...                                      # your nn.Module, e.g. the FNO you are training:
                                               # (1, F, nx, ny, ntau) -> (1, F, nx, ny, ntau)

user_xml = "jetscape_user_fno.xml"             # a user XML with a <Hydro><FNO> block
config = fno_config_from_xml(user_xml, device="mps")      # "cpu", "cuda" or "mps"
hydro = PyFNOHydro(net, config)                # (2) sets net.eval()

modules = [create_module("TrentoInitial"), create_module("NullPreDynamics"), hydro]
run_manual("jetscape_main.xml", user_xml, modules, n_events=1)

evo = bulk_info_to_numpy(hydro.get_bulk_info(), n_features=4)  # (ntau+1, nx, ny, [e, T, vx, vy])
surface = hydro.get_surface_cells()                             # what iSS samples

Run it from the X-SCAPE build directory (or inside a js.JobDir): TrentoInitial and the other C++ modules read their tables from there. run_manual takes a pipeline built in Python; the user XML must set <enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination>false</enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination>. FnoHydro's config/jetscape_user_root_bulk_test.xml is such a file, with a Trento initial state and a <Hydro><FNO> block. For jet energy loss and hadronization on the predicted medium, add the managers by hand as on Writing modules in Python, with create_module("Matter") and create_module("ColorlessHadronization") inside them, or use js.per_event(..., tasks=[...]) to read each event's results.

Pitfalls of the live model

  • Import torch before jetscape. PyTorch and the compiled extension each load an OpenMP runtime, and the one initialised second can crash the process. On macOS import jetscape imports torch first if it is installed; on Linux torch is otherwise only loaded when PyFNOHydro is constructed, after the extension. Put import torch at the top.
  • PyFNOHydro calls net.eval() when it is constructed. If you continue training the same object, call net.train() for the training steps and net.eval() again before the next event.
  • The grid must be the model's. nx, ny, ntau, x_min, y_min, dtau and n_features must match what the model was trained on; nothing checks this for you. dx = -2 x_min / nx.
  • The model runs on config["device"], and PyFNOHydro moves your model there (net.to(device) moves the object itself, not a copy).
  • A pre-equilibrium module is required before PyFNOHydro (NullPreDynamics will do); τ₀ is its end time, not a config key.
  • The evolution is 2+1D, boost-invariant. Higher-dimensional models need their own module (see FastHydro for a 3+1D Python hydro).
  • The log line Unrecognized hydro module id:PyFNOHydro is a harmless warning.
  • One forward pass per event runs with the GIL held; the heavy work is inside torch.

docs.title: The grid configuration
docs.text:
The config dict gives the FNO grid:

config = dict(
    nx=60, ny=60, ntau=59,          # required
    n_features=3,                   # required: 3 or 4
    x_min=-15.0, y_min=-15.0,       # required [fm]
    dtau=0.1,                       # required [fm/c]
    T_freeze=0.136,                 # required: freeze-out temperature [GeV]
    neta=1, deta=0.0,               # optional
    tau_normalise=True,             # optional: the model predicts e*tau (default for 3 features)
    device="cpu",                   # optional: "cpu", "cuda", "mps"
)

Instead of a dict, keep the grid in the user XML, next to the run: fno_config_from_xml(user_xml, device=...) parses the <Hydro><FNO> block before the run, and config=None lets PyFNOHydro read the same block from the loaded XML in InitializeHydro(), as the C++ module does:

<Hydro>
  <FNO>
    <model_file>models/traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt</model_file>
    <n_features>3</n_features>
    <freezeout_temperature>0.136</freezeout_temperature>
    <nx>60</nx>
    <ny>60</ny>
    <neta>1</neta>
    <ntau>59</ntau>
    <x_min>-15.0</x_min>
    <y_min>-15.0</y_min>
    <dtau>0.1</dtau>
    <deta>0</deta>
  </FNO>
</Hydro>

X-SCAPE's config/jetscape_main.xml (branch contrib) has the defaults of this block, so a user XML may carry it. PyFNOHydro takes the model from its constructor, not from <model_file>.

docs.title: Try it: python_fno_test.py
docs.text:
example/python_fno_test.py runs TrentoInitial → NullPreDynamics → PyFNOHydro with a traced model, prints the stored grid, the evolution as numpy and torch tensors and the number of surface cells, and saves python_fno_test_bulk.png (energy-density slices). Put the model file into contribs/FnoHydro/models/ or pass --model:

cd X-SCAPE/build_gpu
python ../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_fno_test.py \
  --model ../external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/FnoHydro/models/traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt \
  --events 1 --device cpu

--config-source dict|python-xml|jetscape-xml picks one of the three configuration routes above, --user another user XML (default: FnoHydro's config/jetscape_user_root_bulk_test.xml), --no-plots skips matplotlib.

PyTorch is not part of the container or the Mac wheel environment; install it there, or use the js_fno conda environment of a source build, which has it.

docs.title: Utilities: the evolution as arrays and tensors
docs.text:
jetscape.utils converts between X-SCAPE's evolution history and numpy / torch:

from jetscape.utils import (bulk_info_to_numpy, bulk_info_to_tensor,
                            numpy_to_bulk_info, tensor_to_bulk_info, rebin_preeq_to_fno_grid)

info = hydro.get_bulk_info()                               # EvolutionHistory, any hydro module
arr = bulk_info_to_numpy(info, n_features=4)               # (ntau, nx, ny, 4): e, T, vx, vy; float32
t = bulk_info_to_tensor(info, n_features=4, device="cpu")  # (1, 4, nx, ny, ntau), the FNO layout

tensor_to_bulk_info(t, hydro)                              # back into a FluidDynamics module
fno_input = rebin_preeq_to_fno_grid(preeq, ini, nx_fno, ny_fno, x_min_fno, y_min_fno,
                                    dx_fno, dy_fno, n_features=3)   # (3, nx, ny, 1)

bulk_info_to_numpy reads the transverse slice (2+1D). For a 3+1D evolution, e.g. from MUSIC, info.to_numpy_full(n_features) returns (ntau, nx, ny, neta, n_features) with the columns e, T, vx, vy, vz, s. The production writers store MUSIC's evolution directly in the HDF5 layout the FNO training reads (below).

docs.title: The C++ FnoHydro (LibTorch)
docs.text:
For runs without Python in the loop, the FnoHydro contrib is the same idea in C++: a FluidDynamics module registered as FnoHydro that loads a traced TorchScript model with LibTorch and runs it on the pre-equilibrium output. It reads the model file and the grid from the same <Hydro><FNO> block (<model_file>, nx, ny, ntau, ...), so a traced model and its XML work in both; the freeze-out temperature it takes from <Hydro><MUSIC><freezeout_temperature>. It needs LibTorch (about 2 GB) and ROOT at build time:

cmake .. -DUSE_MUSIC=ON -DUSE_ISS=ON -DUSE_JS_CONTRIB=ON -DUSE_JS_FNO_HYDRO=ON \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$(python -c 'import torch; print(torch.utils.cmake_prefix_path)')"
make -j FnoModule

It is not built in the container or the Mac wheel. The contrib also holds FnoRooIn (replays a stored evolution from ROOT) and the ROOT bulk writers of the original training pipeline; see its README.

docs.title: Where the models come from
docs.text:
The trained models are not in js-contrib, because they are too large for git (about 1.5 GB each). They are published with the paper on Zenodo, record 16647726, together with the training data in ROOT format:

Model file What it is traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt traced, 3 features, 60 × 60, 59 time steps, 40–60 % centrality; the default of python_fno_test.py traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_0_10_59bins.pt the same for 0–10 % traced_JS3.7_2k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_4types_59bins.pt traced, trained on four event types model_10K_central.pt, model_10K_peripheral.pt, model_500_of_four_types.pt the untraced models of the paper (central, peripheral, four event types) 
mkdir -p models && cd models
curl -L -o traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt \
  "https://zenodo.org/records/16647726/files/traced_JS3.7_10k_3feat_fno_model_cpu_40_60_59bins.pt?download=1"

In the future, trained models and training data will also be shared on the OSDF, next to the production outputs; see Data on the OSDF.

docs.title: Training data from the productions
docs.text:
A model is only as good as its training set, and js-contrib's productions write it directly in the HDF5 layout of the FNO4d training code (/arr of shape (nevents, 4, nx, ny, neta, ntau) with e, vx, vy, vz, plus the grid as attributes), with no ROOT step in between:

  • Hydro only: prod_AuAu_0_10 writes one MUSIC evolution per event (H5BulkWriter).
  • Jet + medium pairs: prod_AuAu_0_10_jet runs the two-stage hydro: MUSIC_1 evolves the background, Matter + LBT lose energy in it, and MUSIC_2 evolves the same initial condition with the lost energy deposited. Each event is written as a pair: arr (with the jet), arr_bg (without), the droplets that were deposited (source/droplets) and the parton shower (shower/). arr - arr_bg is the jet's effect alone, the target of a deposition model. How to run it, also on clusters: Au+Au jets (two stages).
  • FastHydro writes the same pair layout with a fast PyTorch solver, for large samples: FastHydro.

docs.text:
