  • FastHydro: a 3+1D hydro solver in PyTorch with the jet-deposition workflow.
  • Au+Au jets (two stages): the GPU production of training pairs.

docs.title: Writing modules in Python
docs.text:
Every stage of an X-SCAPE event (hard process, energy loss, hadronization, soft particlization, afterburner, writer, hydro, ...) can be a Python class. You subclass the C++ base class and override the method JETSCAPE calls; the framework then creates, copies, calls and writes your module exactly as it would a C++ one, next to the C++ modules of the run. Use this to prototype a new physics module, to wrap a model that lives in Python, or to tap the event at a stage the standard output does not cover. Because the bindings keep the C++ names and argument order, a working Python module ports to C++ line by line, and a C++ module ports to Python the same way.

Python modules need no compiler: they run with the production container and the Mac wheel as they are, against the compiled X-SCAPE inside. The examples on this page are in python_modules/ of the copied examples (xscape-examples DEST), or in the repository under contribs/PyJetscape/example/python_modules/.

docs.title: How JETSCAPE calls a module
docs.text:
when method Init() InitTask() once; read your XML parameters here every event ExecuteTask() gun, sampler, afterburner: the event's work every event, energy loss DoEnergyLoss(deltaT, time, Q2, pIn, pOut) once per parton per time step every event, jet hadronization DoHadronization(shower, hOut, pOut) once per event, all showers at once end of every event ClearTask() drop per-event state Finish() FinishTask() once; close files

Override only what you need: a method you leave out does what the C++ base class does. Call the base explicitly when you extend it, e.g. core.SoftParticlization.ClearTask(self).

docs.title: The base classes
docs.text:
All are in jetscape.pyjetscape_core (below core).

stage base class override gets / gives initial state InitialState ExecuteTask (+ GetNcoll, GetNpart, SampleABinaryCollisionPoint) set_entropy_density_from_numpy, set_num_of_binary_collisions_from_numpy hard process HardProcess ExecuteTask (+ GetSigmaGen, GetSigmaErr, GetPtHat, GetEventWeight) self.AddParton(...), self.AddHadron(...) pre-equilibrium PreequilibriumDynamics InitializePreequilibrium, EvolvePreequilibrium set_e_numpy, set_utau_numpy, ... hydro FluidDynamics InitializeHydro, EvolveHydro store_fluid_cells_from_numpy, the freeze-out surface (example) energy loss JetEnergyLoss DoEnergyLoss(deltaT, time, Q2, pIn, pOut) the parton in pIn; the partons at time out jet hadronization Hadronization DoHadronization(shower, hOut, pOut) one list of final partons per shower; hadrons out soft particlization SoftParticlization ExecuteTask self.GetHydroHyperSurface(); self.set_hadron_list([[Hadron, ...], ...]) afterburner Afterburner ExecuteTask, GetCurrentHadronList self.GatherAfterburnerHadrons() writer JetScapeWriter GetStatus, Write(obj), WriteEvent every Parton, PartonShower, Hadron the tasks write; self.GetHeader() liquefier LiquefierBase smearing_kernel(tau, x, y, eta, droplet) [j^tau, j^x, j^y, j^eta] shower growth PartonShowerGenerator DoShower(jloss)

toy_modules.py has one template per stage in the plain binding style (ToyGun, ToySplit, ToyHadronizer, ToySampler, ToyAfterburner, ToyWriter); toy_modules_pythonic.py has the same in the Pythonic style used below. The toys are not physics; they show the interface.

docs.title: A worked example: an energy-loss module
docs.text:
Three Python modules make a complete jet event: a gun that fires two back-to-back 40 GeV gluons, an energy-loss module that splits every parton above e_min into two halves once time >= t_split, and a hadronizer that turns every final parton into a π⁺. The classes are those of toy_modules_pythonic.py.

my_modules.py
import jetscape as js
from jetscape import pyjetscape_core as core


@js.module("CustomModuleToyGunV2", section="Hard")
class ToyGunV2(core.HardProcess):
    """Two back-to-back gluons of E (GeV) along x."""

    xml_parameters = {"E": 40.0}

    def ExecuteTask(self):
        position = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
        ini = js.JetScapeSignalManager.Instance().GetInitialStatePointer()
        if ini is not None and ini.GetNcoll() > 0:
            position = ini.sample_binary_collision_point()        # (t, x, y, z)
        for sign in (+1, -1):
            self.AddParton(js.make_parton(21, (self.E, sign * self.E, 0.0, 0.0), position))

    def GetSigmaGen(self):
        return 1.0


@js.module("CustomModuleToySplitV2", section="Eloss")
class ToySplitV2(core.JetEnergyLoss):
    """A parton above e_min splits into two halves at t >= t_split."""

    xml_parameters = {"t_split": 1.0, "e_min": 30.0}

    def DoEnergyLoss(self, deltaT, time, Q2, pIn, pOut):
        p = pIn[0]
        if time >= self.t_split and p.e() > self.e_min:
            E, px, py, pz = p.momentum
            return [js.make_parton(p.pid(), (E / 2, px / 2, s * 1.0, pz / 2),
                                   position=p.position) for s in (+1, -1)]


@js.module("CustomModuleToyHadronizerV2")
class ToyHadronizerV2(core.Hadronization):
    """Every final parton becomes a pi+ with its momentum and position."""

    def DoHadronization(self, shower, hOut, pOut):
        return [js.make_hadron(211, p.momentum, p.position, stat=1)
                for partons in shower for p in partons]

What the pieces do:

  • @js.module(name, section) registers the class in JETSCAPE's module factory, so an XML can name it, and turns xml_parameters into XML parameters (next sections). Inside the module they are plain attributes: self.E, self.t_split, self.e_min.
  • DoEnergyLoss returns the partons at time. Returning None (here, below e_min or before t_split) lets the parton go on unchanged; returning two partons makes a splitting vertex.
  • DoHadronization returns the hadrons. js.make_parton / js.make_hadron take the momentum as (E, px, py, pz) and the position as (t, x, y, z).

The run builds the pipeline by hand: the energy-loss and hadronization managers and their containers are made in Python and the modules put inside, as the XML would do.

run_my_modules.py
import numpy as np
import jetscape as js
from jetscape import paths
from jetscape import pyjetscape_core as core
from my_modules import ToyGunV2, ToySplitV2, ToyHadronizerV2

eloss_manager = core.JetEnergyLossManager()   # copies `eloss` once per shower
eloss = core.JetEnergyLoss()                  # the per-shower container (deltaT, maxT)
eloss.Add(ToySplitV2())                       # modules in order (Matter before LBT)
eloss_manager.Add(eloss)

hadronization_manager = core.HadronizationManager()
hadronization = core.Hadronization()
hadronization.Add(ToyHadronizerV2())
hadronization_manager.Add(hadronization)

tasks = [ToyGunV2(), eloss_manager, hadronization_manager]     # pipeline order
main_xml = paths.xscape_root() / "config" / "jetscape_main.xml"

with js.per_event(main_xml, "my_user.xml", tasks=tasks) as driver:
    for i in driver.events():
        fp = driver.energy_loss_manager.final_parton_array()
        had = driver.hadronization_manager.hadron_array()
        print(f"event {i}: {len(fp)} final partons, E = {fp['E'].sum():.1f} GeV;",
              f"{len(had)} hadrons, pT = {np.hypot(had.p[:, 1], had.p[:, 2]).round(2)}")
my_user.xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<jetscape>
  <nEvents>3</nEvents>
  <vlevel>0</vlevel>
  <Random><seed>1</seed></Random>
  <enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination> false </enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination>
  <Eloss>
    <deltaT>0.1</deltaT>
    <maxT>2</maxT>
  </Eloss>
</jetscape>

$ python run_my_modules.py
event 0: 4 final partons, E = 80.0 GeV; 4 hadrons, pT = [20.02 20.02 20.02 20.02]
event 1: 4 final partons, E = 80.0 GeV; 4 hadrons, pT = [20.02 20.02 20.02 20.02]
event 2: 4 final partons, E = 80.0 GeV; 4 hadrons, pT = [20.02 20.02 20.02 20.02]

Each 40 GeV gluon split once into two 20 GeV halves with ±1 GeV along y. Now set a parameter from the user XML: add

    <CustomModuleToySplitV2><e_min>50</e_min></CustomModuleToySplitV2>

inside <Eloss>. The 40 GeV gluons stay below e_min, nothing splits, and every event prints 2 final partons ... 2 hadrons, pT = [40. 40.].

docs.title: The same modules named in the XML
docs.text:
With the automatic task list (the default), the user XML names the modules, and X-SCAPE builds the managers itself. Import the module file so the decorators register the classes, then run:

my_user_xml.xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<jetscape>
  <nEvents>3</nEvents>
  <vlevel>0</vlevel>
  <Random><seed>1</seed></Random>
  <Hard>
    <CustomModuleToyGunV2><E>50</E></CustomModuleToyGunV2>
  </Hard>
  <Eloss>
    <deltaT>0.1</deltaT>
    <maxT>2</maxT>
    <CustomModuleToySplitV2><e_min>30</e_min></CustomModuleToySplitV2>
  </Eloss>
  <JetHadronization><name>CustomModuleToyHadronizerV2</name></JetHadronization>
</jetscape>

import jetscape as js
from jetscape import paths
import my_modules  # noqa: F401  (the decorators register the modules)

main_xml = paths.xscape_root() / "config" / "jetscape_main.xml"
with js.per_event(main_xml, "my_user_xml.xml") as driver:
    print([type(t).__name__ for t in driver.GetTaskList()])
    # ['ToyGunV2', 'JetEnergyLossManager', 'HadronizationManager']
    for i in driver.events():
        fp = driver.energy_loss_manager.final_parton_array()
        print(i, len(fp), fp["E"].sum())          # 4 partons, 100 GeV: E is 50 here

C++ and Python modules mix freely in both styles: replace ToyGunV2 by <Hard><PythiaGun>, or put your energy-loss module after <Matter> in <Eloss>.

docs.title: Named in the XML or built by hand
docs.text:
named in the XML built by hand user XML <enableAutomaticTaskListDetermination> true (the default) false the module registered (@js.module or register_module), named in its section an object you Add() managers made by X-SCAPE JetEnergyLossManager / JetEnergyLoss, HadronizationManager / Hadronization made in Python examples run_from_xml.py + user_from_xml.xml run_by_hand.py (plain bindings), run_by_hand_pythonic.py (--style old|new)

Names. Every XML section accepts a module whose element name contains CustomModule: <Hard><CustomModuleMyGun>, <Eloss><CustomModuleMyLoss>, <SoftParticlization><CustomModuleMySampler>, <Afterburner><CustomModuleMyAfterburner>. Jet hadronization takes it as text: <JetHadronization><name>CustomModuleMyHadronizer</name>. A module that does not contain CustomModule in its name is never created from the XML.

Every user-XML tag needs a default in the main XML. At Init(), X-SCAPE compares every tag of the user XML with config/jetscape_main.xml and stops the process (exit) on a tag the main XML lacks: your module's name and each of its parameters. For a C++ module that means adding default blocks to jetscape_main.xml (js-contrib's README explains it). A Python module needs no edit: registering it gives the defaults, and Init() adds <section><name>defaults</name> to the main XML in memory (the file is not changed).

  • With @js.module, the defaults are xml_parameters (int, float, str or bool). Before your InitTask runs, each is read into self.<key> from [section, name, key]: the user XML's value, else the default, converted to the default's type (bool: 0, false, off, no are false).

  • With the plain call, give the defaults as XML text and read them yourself in InitTask, as a C++ module does:

    class ToyGun(core.HardProcess):
    def InitTask(self):
        self.e = self.get_xml_element_double(["Hard", "CustomModuleToyGun", "E"], False)

core.register_module("CustomModuleToyGun", ToyGun, section="Hard", defaults="<E>40</E>")

get_xml_element_int and get_xml_element_text work alike; with True a missing element raises. - core.registered_modules() lists the factory (the build's C++ modules and the Python ones), core.unregister_module(name) removes a Python one.

A module built by hand needs no registration, but register it anyway if it reads XML parameters: without the main-XML default, setting them in the user XML stops the run.

docs.title: Energy loss in detail
docs.text:
DoEnergyLoss(deltaT, time, Q2, pIn, pOut) is called for every parton of every shower at every time step up to <Eloss><maxT>, in steps of <Eloss><deltaT> (fm/c).

  • time is the end of the step. Q2 is what the framework passes: the parton's pT, not a virtuality; the virtuality is pIn[0].virtuality().
  • pIn is a list with this step's parton, the C++ object itself: p.set_stat(...) changes it in place. It is valid during the call only; do not keep it.

  • The output (appended to pOut, or returned as a list):

    output the shower empty / None the parton (as changed) goes on unchanged into the next step one parton it replaces the parton (no new vertex) two or more a vertex at time; each parton is a new branch

    Partons with the liquefier's statuses (droplet −11, miss −13, negative −17) and non-partons (photons, leptons) do not go on. Return a list or append, not both (ValueError). - Several modules in <Eloss> (Matter then LBT, or yours after Matter) are called in turn on the same lists, as in C++. Leave alone a parton another module handles (p.GetController(), pOut already filled). - The medium: self.GetHydroCell(t, x, y, z) returns a FluidCellInfo (temperature, energy_density, pressure, vx, vy, vz, ...), or None without a hydro. - Copies: the energy-loss manager copies the module once per shower at the start of each event with Clone() and drops the copies at the end. The default copy runs the C++ copy constructor and copies the instance attributes shallowly; __init__ and InitTask are not called on copies. Override Clone for state that must not be shared between showers:

    def Clone(self):
    copy = core.JetEnergyLoss.Clone(self)   # the default copy
    copy.history = []                       # one list per shower
    return copy

docs.title: The other stages
docs.text:
• Jet hadronization, DoHadronization(shower, hOut, pOut): once per event, after the energy loss. shower is a list with one list of final partons per shower. Return (or append to hOut) the hadrons, or a tuple (hadrons, partons) for partons you leave unhadronized; for hadrons alone return a list, not a tuple. self.GetHydroHyperSurface(T) and self.GetHydroCell(...) give the medium.
  • Soft particlization, ExecuteTask(): self.GetHydroHyperSurface() is the freeze-out surface (a list of SurfaceCellInfo); store hadrons with self.set_hadron_list(samples), a list of oversamples, each a list of Hadrons.
  • Afterburner, ExecuteTask() and GetCurrentHadronList(): self.GatherAfterburnerHadrons() gives per oversample the soft hadrons, plus the jet hadrons when <Afterburner><include_fragmentation_hadrons> is 1.
  • Writer, GetStatus() and Write(obj) (+ WriteEvent()): per event the header is filled (self.GetHeader().GetSigmaGen(), ...), then Write receives the hard partons, per shower the initiating Parton and the PartonShower, then the jet Hadrons. Add a writer with driver.Add(writer) before Init(), also in XML mode. The C++ ASCII writer comes from core.create_module("JetScapeWriterAscii") + core.set_writer_output_file(w, name), and core.JetScapeReaderAscii(name) reads its file back.
  • Initial state, pre-equilibrium, hydro, liquefier: examples in example/inspect_bulk_info.py (GaussianIC), python/jetscape/fno_hydro.py (PyFNOHydro), python/jetscape/surface_replay.py, FastHydro's hydro.py and initial_state.py (FastHydro).

docs.title: Particles and lists
docs.text:
• js.make_parton(pid, momentum, position=(0, 0, 0, 0), stat=0, label=0, color=0, anti_color=0), js.make_hadron(pid, momentum, position, stat, label, mass=None) and js.make_photon(...) take momentum (E, px, py, pz) and position (t, x, y, z). The bound constructors keep C++'s order: core.Parton(label, pid, stat, p, x) with p = core.FourVector(px, py, pz, E) and x = core.FourVector(x, y, z, t).
  • Getters and setters as in C++: pid(), pstat(), e(), px(), pt(), eta(), p_in(), x_in(), set_stat(), set_form_time(), set_color(), ...; and p.momentum, p.position.
  • A particle's x(), y(), z(), t() are its position; a parton's virtuality is virtuality(), set with set_t().
  • Lists C++ passes by reference arrive as Python lists: the inputs are the C++ objects (valid during the call), the outputs are copied back into C++ after the call.

docs.title: Random numbers
docs.text:
• self.rng (Pythonic layer) is a numpy Generator seeded from the module's own C++ engine on first use: reproducible with <Random><seed>, with its own stream for each per-shower copy. Use it in InitTask or later; before the XML is loaded it raises.
  • self.GetMt19937Generator() is the engine itself, as in C++: g() is the next 32-bit draw, g.uniform() a draw in [0, 1).

The engines are seeded from the seed and the module's task number. Adding a Python module shifts the task numbers, and so the random streams, of the tasks created after it, exactly as adding a C++ module does.

docs.title: Checking a module against C++
docs.text: Run the C++ module and your Python version with the same seed and compare the output files, as tests/equivalence_driver.py does. For identical random numbers the Python version must create the same tasks in the same order; a Python module that holds a C++ module of its own gives it its task number back with core.next_task_number() / core.set_next_task_number() (see PyMatter there). Run each configuration in its own process: JETSCAPE keeps the XML, the seed and the module registry in process-wide singletons. Checked this way, a Python module handing each step to C++ Matter gives byte-identical hadrons to the C++ run, and a Python writer writes the same lines as the C++ one.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: A call into a Python energy-loss module costs about 1.4 µs on top of the module's own work: on a GB10, 715,438 calls in 500 events of a 100 GeV gluon in vacuum took 3.70 s through a Python module that hands each step to C++ Matter, against 2.72 s for Matter alone. A module written in Python costs what its Python code costs on top of that, per parton and time step. Python modules run in one thread (each call takes the GIL).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: symptom cause User XML tag <X> is unrecognized and the run stops the module or a parameter is not registered (@js.module / register_module with section= and defaults) before Init() a module named in the XML never runs its name does not contain CustomModule AttributeError: module 'jetscape' has no attribute 'JetEnergyLoss' most bound classes are in jetscape.pyjetscape_core, not re-exported by jetscape a parton's t() is not its virtuality t() is the position time; use virtuality() state shared between showers the default Clone() copies attributes shallowly; override Clone a liquefier attached from Python is gone C++ keeps only a weak reference; keep the Python object alive undefined symbol ... iColoredHadronization on import X-SCAPE built without -DUSE_3DGlauber=ON all 256 slots for Python modules are taken more than 256 registered Python modules in one process

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Live PyTorch FNO hydro: a complete Python hydro module backed by a neural network.
  • The Pythonic interface: reading what your module produced.
  • The full reference: PyJetscape's README, Writing modules in Python and example/python_modules/README.md.

docs.title: The Pythonic interface
docs.text: The Pythonic interface is the layer of PyJetscape you will use most. It runs X-SCAPE events in a Python loop and hands you each event's partons, hadrons and showers as numpy record arrays, awkward arrays with four-vector kinematics, or Python objects, ready for numpy, FastJet and histogramming. Use it for any study that reads what the modules produce: a script of your own, a notebook, or a small production. It is installed by import jetscape and only adds names to the bound C++ classes, so scripts written against the bare bindings keep working and keep their output. Where to get it: Python.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import fastjet
import jetscape as js

with js.per_event("jetscape_main.xml", "my_user.xml") as driver:
    for i in driver.events():
        partons = driver.energy_loss_manager.final_parton_array()   # numpy records
        jet = driver.hadronization_manager.hadron_array()          # HadronArray
        h = jet.to_awkward()                                        # samples x hadrons
        charged = h[js.select(h, "charged") & (abs(h.eta) < 2)]
        jets = fastjet.ClusterSequence(charged, fastjet.JetDefinition(
            fastjet.antikt_algorithm, 0.4)).inclusive_jets(min_pt=5.0)
        print(i, len(partons), "partons;", jets.pt.tolist())

The complete worked example is example/pythonic/oo_workflow.ipynb: three O+O events through the whole chain, the hadrons written to files and read back, spectra with errors, FastJet. Its simulation half is the script oo_workflow.py (--xml, --events, --seed, --outdir), a template for a production of your own.

Requirements. The bound classes need the compiled pyjetscape_core. Records and HadronArray need only numpy (they also work on files without a build); to_awkward() needs awkward and vector, select() needs particle, jets need the fastjet Python package, and the hadron files need h5py. All are in the container image, the Mac wheel's environment and the analysis environment; awkward and vector are imported only when used.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Names. A method ending in _array() returns numpy data for the current event (final_parton_array(), hadron_array(), edge_array()). A plain noun returns objects (showers, nodes). Properties (info, showers, momentum, last_random_seed) take no parentheses.
  • Four-vectors. Momentum is (E, px, py, pz), position (t, x, y, z), everywhere: records, HadronArray.p / .x, the hadron files, FourVector.comp(i). Two older calls keep their own order: the bound constructor FourVector(x, y, z, t) (for a momentum FourVector(px, py, pz, E)) and FourVector.to_list().
  • Units. GeV and fm (fm/c), as in X-SCAPE.
  • Flat first, nested on request. Every _array() is flat numpy plus offsets, the form the files use; to_awkward() gives the nested view.

docs.title: Running events
docs.text:
with js.per_event(main_xml, user_xml) as driver:     # Init() and ExecInit() on entry
    for i in driver.events():                         # ExecPerEvent() ... ClearPerEvent()
        ...                                           # this event's results are in memory
                                                      # Finish() on leaving the block

js.per_event(main_xml=None, user_xml=None, tasks=None, n_events=None) returns a JetScapePerEvent driver:

  • tasks=[...] adds a pipeline built by hand, in order; without it the XML's task list is used.
  • n_events overrides <nEvents>.
  • driver.events(n=None, on_error=None) yields the event index after the event ran and before it is cleared. n caps the count; break clears the current event. With on_error(i, exc), an event in which a module throws (for example Matter's rare "minus log of sudakov negative") is reported, cleared and skipped, as the productions do; without it the exception propagates.

The run's modules are driver properties (None when absent):

property what energy_loss_manager the final-state JetEnergyLossManager (in ISR runs, not the ISR chain's) hadronization_manager the HadronizationManager soft_particlization the first SoftParticlization (iSS) hydro the hydro module initial_state the initial state

Anything else: driver.GetTaskList() and, for sub-tasks, task.GetTaskList().

Run in a working directory of its own. MUSIC, 3dMCGlauber and iSS read inputs from and write side files to the current directory, and X-SCAPE's XMLs contain paths relative to the build. js.JobDir handles that for a script or notebook anywhere on disk:

with js.JobDir("out", "my_job.xml") as job:      # out/my_job.xml; runs in out/work/my_job
    with js.per_event(job.main_xml, job.user_xml) as driver:
        ...                                       # write your outputs to absolute paths

It copies the user XML to out/, makes its ../ paths absolute, copies music_input, links the build's tables, changes into out/work/<name> and back, and removes that directory after a run without an exception (keep=True keeps it). The build is found through jetscape.paths: $JETSCAPE_BUILD, else <X-SCAPE>/build_gpu, where X-SCAPE is $XSCAPE or the tree the package sits in. In the container XSCAPE=/opt/X-SCAPE is set, so scripts run unchanged in and out of it.

docs.title: The results of an event
docs.text:
Each method wraps a function of the bindings, and returns numpy copies or arrays taken over from C++, so the results stay valid after the event is cleared.

class member returns JetEnergyLossManager showers list of PartonShower, one per shower final_parton_array() final-parton records (what hadronization receives) initiator_array() the partons that started each shower SoftParticlization (iSS) hadron_array() HadronArray, one sample per oversample use_compact_output(on=True) from the next event on, hadrons as arrays (about 8x less memory) set_number_of_samples(n), set_next_random_seed(seed), last_random_seed oversamples and seeds primary_array() the undecayed hadrons (iSS <keep_primaries>), or None HadronizationManager, Hadronization hadron_array() HadronArray of the jet hadrons hadronize(partons, seed=None) hadronize stored partons again last_random_seed the jet hadronization's last seed colour_audit(), colour_totals(), set_colour_closure(mode) iColoredHadronization's colour bookkeeping, on builds that have it (hasattr(had, "colour_audit")) HardProcess parton_array(), info hard partons, hardest first; dict with pthat, sigma_gen, sigma_err, event_weight InitialState info dict with n_coll, n_part, centrality (what the module reports)

Compact output is taken once

After use_compact_output(), hadron_array() takes iSS's arrays over without a copy, so call it once per event. Without compact output it copies and can be called again.

docs.title: Record arrays
docs.text:
The small per-event tables are numpy structured arrays (jetscape.records): rec["px"] instead of rec[:, 4]. Each holds exactly the values of the older column array it reorders.

dtype from fields FINAL_PARTON_DTYPE final_parton_array() shower, pid, pstat, E, px, py, pz, t, x, y, z, mass, col, acol INITIATOR_DTYPE initiator_array() shower, pid, pstat, E, px, py, pz, t, x, y, z EDGE_DTYPE PartonShower.edge_array() src, tgt, pid, pstat, E, px, py, pz, t, x, y, z NODE_DTYPE PartonShower.node_array() id, t, x, y, z HARD_PARTON_DTYPE HardProcess.parton_array() pid, E, px, py, pz, pt, y

Records work with the usual tools: rec[rec["pstat"] >= 0], np.unique(rec["shower"]), np.hypot(rec["px"], rec["py"]), pandas.DataFrame(rec). Converters for arrays from files: final_parton_records(rows), final_parton_rows(rec), initiator_rows(rec), ... in jetscape.records.

docs.title: HadronArray
docs.text:
One event's hadrons (or a whole file's), one array per field, grouped into samples: one per iSS oversample, one for a jet hadronization.

attribute pid, pstat (n,) int32 p (n, 4) float32 E, px, py, pz x (n, 4) float32 or None t, x, y, z mass (n,) float32 or None None when read from a file sample_offsets (n_samples + 1,) int64 sample s is rows sample_offsets[s]:sample_offsets[s+1] info dict e.g. the seed; after from_h5: units, unit_offsets, attrs, path

len(h), h.n_samples, h.sample_counts; h.to_dict() gives the dict the hadron writer takes; h.to_awkward(...) the nested view; h.to_hadrons() a hadrons_h5.Hadrons for its histogram helpers.

Memory. HadronArray wraps the arrays the bindings return without a copy and stores no derived columns: pt, eta, phi and rapidity are computed by to_awkward() when you ask for them. to_hadrons() computes them all in float64 (about 2.4x the memory); use it for histograms, not to hold many events.

docs.title: Nested views: to_awkward
docs.text:
js.to_awkward(obj, position=False, charge=False, by_unit=False), also HadronArray.to_awkward(...):

input result HadronArray samples x hadrons, on the same buffers HadronArray.from_h5(...) with by_unit=True units (events) x samples x hadrons final-parton or initiator records showers x partons edge, node, hard-parton records a flat array of records

The records are vector Momentum4D objects, so kinematics come on demand:

import awkward as ak

h = driver.soft_particlization.hadron_array().to_awkward()
h.pt, h.eta, h.phi, h.rapidity, h.mass          # jagged, the shape of h
mid = h[abs(h.eta) < 0.5]
dndeta = ak.mean(ak.num(mid), axis=0)            # mean over the oversamples
  • position=True adds a nested h.position (Vector4D: h.position.t, h.position.rho). It is nested on purpose: vector would read flat fields named t, x, y, z as the coordinates of the momentum.
  • charge=True adds the PDG charge.
  • A stored mass appears as the field rest_mass; h.mass is vector's, computed from E and p.
  • ak.flatten(a, axis=1) merges units x samples into samples; ak.num(a, axis=k) counts.

docs.title: Selecting species: select
docs.text:
js.select(h, "pi+")                          # one PDG name
js.select(h, ["K+", "K-"])                   # any of several
js.select(h, "charged")                      # a class
js.select(h, ["p", "p~", "Lambda", "Lambda~"])

The result is a boolean mask of the input's shape (jagged for awkward input, so h[js.select(h, "charged")]). Classes: charged, neutral, hadron, meson, baryon, strange; names as the particle package spells them (pi0, K(S)0, Sigma+, Omega-, ...). Each distinct pid is looked up once.

"charged" and hadrons_h5.CHARGED

select(..., "charged") takes every pid with a nonzero PDG charge, resonances included. hadrons_h5.CHARGED, used by Hadrons.charged and the analysis scripts, lists the stable charged hadrons and leptons. They agree on decayed hadrons and differ only on files that keep undecayed primaries.

docs.title: Hadron files
docs.text:
The productions' hadron files (jetscape.hadrons_h5) take a HadronArray per unit (event) and give one back:

from jetscape.hadrons_h5 import HadronH5Writer
from jetscape.records import initiator_rows

with HadronH5Writer("x_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5", tag="bulk_bg", n_samples=20) as bulk_w, \
     HadronH5Writer("x_hadrons_jet_frag.h5", tag="jet_frag", n_samples=1,
                    initiators=True) as jet_w:
    for i in driver.events():
        iss, had = driver.soft_particlization, driver.hadronization_manager
        bulk_w.append_unit(iss.hadron_array().to_dict(), unit=i, event=i,
                           seed=iss.last_random_seed)
        jet_w.append_unit(had.hadron_array().to_dict(), unit=i, event=i,
                          initiators=initiator_rows(driver.energy_loss_manager.initiator_array()))

Keywords besides the hadrons (event=, seed=, pthat=, ...) become the file's per-unit table. Reading:

h = js.HadronArray.from_h5("x_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5")          # every unit, stored fields only
h.info["units"]["seed"]                                      # the per-unit table
a = h.to_awkward(by_unit=True)                               # units x samples x hadrons
first = js.HadronArray.from_h5("x_hadrons_bulk_bg.h5", units=[0])

For whole campaigns, with event-averaged histograms and compound-Poisson errors, use hadrons_h5.HadronFileReader and Hadrons: Hadrons.

docs.title: Jets with FastJet
docs.text:
FastJet's Python package clusters jagged awkward arrays directly: one call for every event, or every oversample.

import awkward as ak
import fastjet

jdef = fastjet.JetDefinition(fastjet.antikt_algorithm, 0.4)

# the jets of every event (a jet file: events x hadrons)
h = js.HadronArray.from_h5(jet_path).to_awkward()
acc = h[abs(h.eta) < 2]
jets = fastjet.ClusterSequence(acc, jdef).inclusive_jets(min_pt=5.0)   # events x jets
leading = ak.firsts(jets[ak.argsort(jets.pt, ascending=False)])

# charged jets
ch = acc[js.select(acc, "charged")]
ch_jets = fastjet.ClusterSequence(ch, jdef).inclusive_jets(min_pt=3.0)

# every oversample of every event (bulk: units x samples x hadrons)
b = js.HadronArray.from_h5(bulk_path).to_awkward(by_unit=True)
per_sample = ak.flatten(b, axis=1)                                     # samples x hadrons
bulk_jets = fastjet.ClusterSequence(per_sample[abs(per_sample.eta) < 2],
                                    jdef).inclusive_jets(min_pt=5.0)
bulk_jets = ak.unflatten(bulk_jets, ak.num(b, axis=1))                 # units x samples x jets

The jagged call gives the same jets as a loop over the samples. Jets are vector records too (.pt, .eta, .phi, .m); constituent_index() maps them back to hadrons. Areas, background subtraction and embedding are on Jets with FastJet.

docs.title: Particles and four-vectors
docs.text:
FourVector iterates, indexes and converts in comp() order (t, x, y, z) = (E, px, py, pz), compares by value, and pickles:

import numpy as np
from jetscape import pyjetscape_core as core

v = core.FourVector.momentum(10.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0)    # E, px, py, pz
E, px, py, pz = v
np.asarray(v)                                         # array([10., 1., 2., 3.])
v == core.FourVector(1, 2, 3, 10)                     # True (the constructor is x, y, z, t)

Because == compares values, a FourVector is not hashable; use tuple(v) as a key.

Particles (Parton, Photon, Hadron) gain momentum and position (FourVector copies) and keyword factories that take any 4-sequence:

p = js.make_parton(21, momentum=(50, 50, 0, 0), position=(0.5, 0, 0, 0),
                   stat=0, label=0, color=101, anti_color=102)
g = js.make_photon(momentum=(5, 0, 0, 5))
h = js.make_hadron(211, momentum=p.momentum, position=p.position, stat=1)   # PDG mass
E, px, py, pz = p.momentum
t, x, y, z = p.position

The bound methods stay methods (p.pt(), p.eta()). For properties, wrap a particle: from jetscape.particles import view; view(p).pt. Each is one call into C++ (about 1.4 µs), so for many particles use the arrays.

A particle's t() is its time

x(), y(), z(), t() of a particle are its position. A parton's virtuality is virtuality() (C++ Parton::t()).

docs.title: Parton showers
docs.text:
for shower in driver.energy_loss_manager.showers:
    for parton in shower:                              # the partons (graph edges)
        end = shower.end_node(parton)
        if end.is_one_to_two:
            print(parton.pid(), "splits at t =", end.position.t(),
                  "z =", end.split_z, "kt =", end.split_kt, "dR =", end.split_delta_r)
    edges = shower.edge_array()                        # EDGE_DTYPE records
    nodes = shower.node_array()                        # NODE_DTYPE records

PartonShower iterates over its partons and has nodes, start_node(p), end_node(p), edge_array() and node_array(); it has no len(), so an empty shower is still true in if shower:. A ShowerNode has id, vertex, position, parents, children, split_z, split_kt, split_delta_r, is_one_to_two and is_end. Showers and partons are C++ objects of the event: use them inside the loop. The record arrays are copies and outlive it.

docs.title: Cost and memory
docs.text:
Measured on a GB10:

iSS, 972,215 cells, 1000 oversamples (7.0M hadrons), resident memory after the step / peak dict from the bindings 686 / 916 MB; HadronArray 686 / 915 MB (no copy); to_awkward() + .pt 761 / 915 MB; Hadrons 1241 / 1240 MB a Python energy-loss module, 715,438 calls (500 events) 3.73 s against 3.70 s before the Pythonic layer (+0.9 %) one bound method call (p.pt(), view(p).pt) about 1.4 µs

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Read results inside the event loop. Call the _array() methods inside for i in driver.events():. Their numpy results outlive the event; C++ objects (showers, partons) do not.
  • No surface, no iSS hadrons. An event without a medium (O+O with no string) has no freeze-out surface; check len(driver.hydro.surface_to_numpy()) before hadron_array(), as oo_workflow.py does.
  • Field names and vector. Do not add fields named t, x, y, z, tau, rho, phi, eta, ... to a Momentum4D record; vector reads them as coordinates. Use nested records.
  • Bound classes are in pyjetscape_core. import jetscape as js re-exports only some of them (js.JetScapePerEvent, js.JetScapeSignalManager, js.FluidDynamics, ...). For the others write from jetscape import pyjetscape_core as core and core.FourVector, core.JetEnergyLoss, core.Parton.
  • ISR runs have two energy-loss managers; driver.energy_loss_manager is the final-state one.
  • Import torch before jetscape when you use PyTorch (see Python).

The full guide, with every member, the guarantees of the layer and a side-by-side table of the old and new calls: contribs/PyJetscape/PYTHONIC.md.

docs.title: 3D visualization
docs.text:
The contribs/Visualization scripts render an event's medium in 3D with PyVista: the hydro evolution resampled from Milne coordinates \((\tau, x, y, \eta_s)\) into the Cartesian lab frame \((t, x, y, z)\), so the fireball expands along the beam as it does in the lab, with the jet's parton shower, the jet wake, and the hadrons after freeze-out drawn in the same frame. Use them for talks and movies, and to check by eye that a run does what you think (where the jet went, where it deposited, what the surface looks like). The output is a GIF or MP4 movie, a ParaView time series, or an interactive window.

script draws needs hydro_pyvista.py the medium of a live MUSIC event, or of a saved dump a build (live), or a dump hydro_jet_pyvista.py the medium plus the jet's parton shower as growing arrows a build (live), or a dump + an ASCII output file wake_pyvista.py three panels: medium without the deposit, with it, and the difference a pair file (FastHydro or the Au+Au jet production) hydro_jet_particles_pyvista.py one production event from the hard scattering to the free-streaming hadrons a pair file and its hadron files

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• For stored files (wake_pyvista.py, hydro_jet_particles_pyvista.py) no X-SCAPE build is needed: the analysis environment has PyVista, VTK, imageio and MUSIC's EoS table (requirements_viz.txt, skipped with --no-viz). The container image has a -viz variant with PyVista (Production container).
  • For live runs (hydro_pyvista.py, hydro_jet_pyvista.py without --load) you need a build with pyjetscape_core for the same Python; the js_fno conda environment of a source build has the PyVista stack. Live runs execute in the X-SCAPE build directory (default <X-SCAPE>/build_gpu, --workdir to change it); the script changes there itself.
  • 3+1D events need the EvolutionHistory.to_numpy_full(n_features) binding, which returns the whole rapidity grid, (ntau, nx, ny, neta, nf) with the columns e, T, vx, vy, vz, s. It is in current pyjetscape_core; after pulling an older tree, rebuild it (cmake --build build_gpu --target pyjetscape_core).
  • .mp4 needs imageio-ffmpeg; without it the scripts fall back to .gif. Rendering is off-screen, so headless machines work (else run under xvfb-run).

docs.title: From Milne to the lab frame
docs.text:
For each lab time \(t\) the script sweeps \(z\) and maps back to Milne, as X-SCAPE's EvolutionHistory::get_tz() does:

\[ \tau = \sqrt{t^2 - z^2}, \qquad \eta_s = \tfrac12 \ln\frac{t+z}{t-z}, \qquad \text{fields} = \text{bulk}(\tau, x, y, \eta_s). \]

Cells outside the light cone or outside the stored \(\tau\) range are empty. A frame at \(t = \tau_\text{min}\) is therefore a thin sheet at \(z = 0\), and a frame after the last stored \(\tau\) a hollow, receding shell. The data kind is detected from the evolution:

  • 3+1D (neta > 1, e.g. the bundled config/OO_one_event.xml): interpolation in 4D \((\tau, x, y, \eta_s)\) on the full grid from to_numpy_full, with the stored lab-frame velocity.
  • 2+1D, boost-invariant: interpolation in 3D \((\tau, x, y)\), and the longitudinal flow is synthesised (\(v_z = z/t\)).

The render grid is independent of the hydro grid (--nxy, --nz, default 96³): higher is smoother and slower; the physics does not change. The resampling is the dominant cost and runs in parallel over frames (--jobs).

Flicker at early times

The medium starts at \(\tau_\text{min}\), a thin, very hot surface that sweeps through the \(z\) grid. If \(z\) is under-resolved its peak flickers from frame to frame. Use a high --nz (≳ 256) or --z-oversample 3 (extra samples uniform in \(\tau\), about 3–5× the resampling cost); the script warns when neither is set.

docs.title: The medium: hydro_pyvista.py
docs.text:
cd external_packages/js-contrib/contribs/Visualization

# live: one event with the bundled O+O config, a movie and a ParaView time series
python hydro_pyvista.py --events 1 --movie evt.gif --vtk-dir vti

# iterate on the picture without re-running MUSIC: dump the Milne array once, re-render from it
python hydro_pyvista.py --events 1 --save-milne /tmp/milne.npz
python hydro_pyvista.py --load /tmp/milne.npz --movie /tmp/hydro.gif --field both

# an interactive window with a lab-time slider
python hydro_pyvista.py --load /tmp/milne.npz --interactive

Main options: --field {e,T,both}, --freeze-temp 0.155 (an isosurface, repeatable), --velocity (flow arrows), --nxy/--nz/--nt (render resolution and frame count), --t-min/--t-max/--z-max/--xy-max (the box), --azimuth/--elevation (camera; the beam runs left to right), --main/--user/--workdir (the run), --manual (a pipeline built in Python). The speed of a movie is --framerate (frames per second, default 6) or --frame-duration (seconds per frame); --vtk-dir DIR writes .vti + .pvd for ParaView. The 3+1D array can be large; --save-milne compresses it well (a 643 MB grid to about 37 MB).

docs.title: The parton shower: hydro_jet_pyvista.py
docs.text:
# live: MUSIC + jets with the bundled config/OO_one_event_jet.xml
python hydro_jet_pyvista.py --events 1 --movie evt_jet.gif

# from a dump, with the shower from the ASCII writer's output
python hydro_jet_pyvista.py --load hydro.npz --jet-ascii test_out.dat --movie evt_jet.gif

The medium is drawn exactly as by hydro_pyvista.py; the partons are arrows in the same \((t, x, y, z)\) frame, colour-coded by pT and accumulating over lab time, so the shower tree builds up. The animation starts at \(t = 0\): the jets evolve in vacuum first, and the medium appears at \(\tau_0\). Live, the shower is read from the event at the per-event yield point (JetEnergyLossManager.get_showers(), then PartonShower.to_numpy() per shower), not parsed from a file. Options: --jet-radius (arrow width in fm), --jet-cmap, --jet-color, --jet-min-energy, --jet-ascii, plus everything hydro_pyvista.py accepts.

docs.title: The jet wake: wake_pyvista.py
docs.text:
┌────────────────────┬────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
│ medium, no deposit │  medium + deposit  │      the wake      │
│ arr_bg             │  arr               │   arr - arr_bg     │
│ + shower           │  + the SAME shower │  + the SAME shower │
└────────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────┘

# a FastHydro pair (FastHydro's make_wake_data.py writes one)
python wake_pyvista.py --file out_wake/wake_ideal.h5 --nt 48 --nz 160 --z-oversample 3 \
    --movie wake_ideal.mp4

# a MUSIC pair from the Au+Au jet production
python wake_pyvista.py --file <out>/AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5 --nt 48 --movie wake_music.mp4

Nothing is run: the pair file holds both legs on one initial condition and the shower.

  • The left panel is not "no jet". There is one shower, drawn in all three panels; the left panel leaves out only the medium's response to the energy the shower lost. The shower was quenched by that undisturbed medium (the background leg is the one Matter and LBT see).
  • The difference is absolute, \(\Delta e\) in GeV/fm³, on a colour scale set at the 99.9th percentile (--diff-clim overrides it), because a single early spike where the first droplets land would otherwise hide the wake. The first two panels share one colour scale on purpose: the deposit is small against the fireball's peak.
  • A relative panel \(\Delta e / e\) is opt-in: --panels bg,jet,diff,reldiff, with cells below --rel-floor (default 0.1) times each frame's peak drawn as zero.
  • Only frames where both legs are live are shown: the jet leg freezes out later, and past the background's freeze-out the difference would be the whole jet leg.
  • The temperature comes from the EoS: FastHydro files carry their table; for MUSIC files it is read from MUSIC's EOS/hotQCD under the production's build, or --eos-table / $MUSIC_EOS_TABLE. Without a table a conformal EoS is used, with a warning.
  • Z+jet pairs: the Z's decay leptons are drawn as straight green tracks with an arrow along the Z (--no-z, --z-color, --z-arrow).

Options: --panels, --event, --diff-cmap, --diff-clim, --diff-pct, --no-jet, plus everything hydro_jet_pyvista.py accepts. Each panel is resampled separately, so keep --nt small while iterating.

docs.title: Hadrons after freeze-out: hydro_jet_particles_pyvista.py
docs.text:
One event of an Au+Au jet production, from the hard scattering to the free-streaming hadrons: the jet leg's medium (with the deposit), the shower, then the hadrons.

python hydro_jet_particles_pyvista.py --file <out>/AuAu_0_10_jet_seed0001.h5 \
    --nt 60 --z-oversample 3 --movie jet_particles.mp4

It reads the pair file and, next to it, the hadron files that hadronize.py writes: <stem>_hadrons_bulk_jet.h5 (iSS on the jet leg's surface, small pale points) and <stem>_hadrons_jet_frag.h5 (the jet's fragmentation, large points coloured by pT).

  • One oversample is drawn, picked at random; the run prints which (--sample K --frag-sample J reproduces it, --rng-seed fixes the choice).
  • Bulk hadrons appear where iSS put them (the freeze-out cell, or a resonance's decay point) and then fly in straight lines. Many appear after the last frame, at large \(|z|\); --hadron-eta-max restricts the picture to mid-rapidity.
  • Jet hadrons have no position (Pythia's string fragmentation writes none). They start from the hard vertex at --frag-time (default: the shower's last vertex). --formation-tau0 TAU0 gives each its own formation time instead, \(t = \max(\text{frag-time}, t_\text{vertex} + \tau_0 E/m)\), so soft fragments appear first.
  • The beam view can foreshorten a dijet pointing at the camera: turn it with --azimuth -55.

More options: --stream-time, --hadron-pt-min, --parton-off, --no-bulk, --no-frag, --no-jet, --hadron-stem, --bulk-color, --bulk-size, --bulk-opacity, --frag-size, --eos-table.

The full documentation, with the reasoning behind every visual choice: contribs/Visualization/README.md.
